## 7. Answer-entry rules

Both exams are delivered through Möbius, answer-only and machine-marked, so a right derivative with a bad keystroke scores zero.

| do | do not |
| :--- | :--- |
| type every multiplication with `*`: `4*x^3` | `4x^3`, which one of the two parsers rejects |
| bracket the whole numerator and the whole denominator: `(38-2*x)/(x+3)^3` | `38-2*x/(x+3)^3`, which is $38 - \frac{2x}{(x+3)^3}$ |
| bracket a negative base before a power: `(-12*x^2-2*x+3)` | leaving it bare next to another factor |
| keep the base of (d) exactly as printed inside its bracket | reordering or "tidying" it, which invites a typo |
| **preview every answer before submitting** | trusting that what you typed is what it read |

**The single most expensive typo in this question** is the missing bracket in part (b)'s denominator.
`(38-2*x)/(x+3)^3` is right; `(38-2*x)/(x+3^3)` cubes the 3 instead of the bracket and is silently a different function.
The preview shows the difference immediately, which is the entire reason to use it.

**The second most expensive** is the exponent in part (d).
`4*(...)^3*(-12*x^2-2*x+3)` is right; dropping the `*` between `^3` and the bracket produces either a parse error or, worse, a reading you did not intend.

Unsimplified answers are accepted, because Möbius grades by algebraic equivalence rather than by string match.
So on Möbius specifically, part (b) can be entered as `(2*(x+3)^2-(2*x-16)*2*(x+3))/(x+3)^4` and it will mark correct.
That is a genuine safety valve when you are unsure of your cancellation: **enter the unsimplified form**.

---

## 8. The variation catalog

This is the bulk of the document and it is what makes the question un-surprisable.
The families are organised by **the tool the variation forces**, not by what the function looks like.

Read each table as *structure*, not as a list of facts.
In almost every family the entries differ in only one place, and naming that one place is the point.

### Family 0 - the classification itself

The trigger is any expression at all.
The tool is the last-operation test.

| what the expression's last operation is | the rule | Q8.1 part | elsewhere in the bank |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $+$ or $-$ | sum, then recurse | (a) | Q8.2a inner, Q8.3 all |
| $\times$ by a constant | constant multiple | (a) | everywhere |
| $\times$ between two $x$-factors | **product** | none | Q8.3a, Q8.4a numerator, review Q1 |
| $\div$ | **quotient** | (b) | Q8.2c, Q8.2d, Q8.3b, Q8.3d, Q8.4a |
| $(\ )^n$, $n$ constant | **chain**, power outer | (b) inner, (d) | Q8.3 b/c/d, Q8.4b |
| named function applied to stuff | **chain**, named outer | (c) | Q8.2a, Q8.2b, Q8.3 a/c/e |
| nothing left | power or constant | (a) | everywhere |

**Every one of the 15 sub-parts in category 8 is classified by that table, with no residue.**
That is the claim the whole tutorial rests on, and it is why the other three questions do not need a new procedure.

### Family 1 - rewrite to a power before reaching for a rule

The trigger is a quotient or a root whose *whole* structure is $x$ to some power.
The tool is $x^{-n}$ and $x^{p/q}$, and the point is that **no rule is needed at all**.

| $f$ | rewrite as | $f'$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\dfrac{1}{x^3}$ | $x^{-3}$ | $-3x^{-4} = -\dfrac{3}{x^4}$ |
| $\dfrac{5}{x^2}$ | $5x^{-2}$ | $-\dfrac{10}{x^3}$ |
| $\sqrt x$ | $x^{1/2}$ | $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt x}$ |
| $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt x}$ | $x^{-1/2}$ | $-\dfrac{1}{2x^{3/2}}$ |
| $x^{2/3}$ | already | $\tfrac23 x^{-1/3}$ |
| $\dfrac{3x^4-2x}{x^2}$ | $3x^2 - 2x^{-1}$ | $6x + \dfrac{2}{x^2}$ |
| $x^2\sqrt x$ | $x^{5/2}$ | $\tfrac52 x^{3/2}$ |
| $(x^2+1)^2$ | $x^4+2x^2+1$ | $4x^3+4x$ |
| $\dfrac{4}{5x}$ | $\tfrac45 x^{-1}$ | $-\dfrac{4}{5x^2}$ |

**The nine rows are one idea.**
Every time the whole expression collapses to a single power of $x$, the quotient rule and the chain rule are both avoidable, and avoiding them is faster and safer.
The cue is that the denominator contains **only** $x$ raised to a power, with no additive term.
$\frac{1}{x^3}$ qualifies; $\frac{1}{(x+3)^3}$ does not, and that one belongs to Family 3.

### Family 2 - the plain quotient rule, denominator not composite

The trigger is a division whose denominator is a bare polynomial rather than a power of one.
The tool is the quotient rule alone, with no chain rule inside.

| $f$ | $f'$ | the numerator's shape |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\dfrac{2x-16}{x+3}$ | $\dfrac{22}{(x+3)^2}$ | constant, because $u$ and $v$ are both linear |
| $\dfrac{3x+1}{2x-5}$ | $-\dfrac{17}{(2x-5)^2}$ | constant, same reason |
| $\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}$ | $\dfrac{1-x^2}{(x^2+1)^2}$ | quadratic |
| $\dfrac{x^2-1}{x^2+1}$ | $\dfrac{4x}{(x^2+1)^2}$ | linear, after a big cancellation |
| $\dfrac{\sin x}{x}$ | $\dfrac{x\cos x - \sin x}{x^2}$ | the shape you get whenever $v=x$ |
| $\dfrac{\sin x - \cos x}{x^3}$ | $\dfrac{x(\cos x + \sin x) - 3(\sin x - \cos x)}{x^4}$ | one power of $x$ cancelled |

**The first two rows are the same row.**
Any ratio of two linear functions has a *constant* numerator in its derivative, because $u'v - uv'$ is degree $\le 1 + 0$ and the $x$ terms always cancel.
That is a free check: if you differentiate $\frac{3x+1}{2x-5}$ and get an $x$ upstairs, you made an arithmetic slip.

The last row also shows the Family 3 cancellation happening quietly: $x^3$ and $x^2$ share $x^2$, so the denominator lands on $x^4$ rather than $x^6$.

### Family 3 - a quotient with a composite denominator, which is Q8.1(b)

The trigger is a division whose denominator is a bracket raised to a power.
The tool is the quotient rule **and** the chain rule, and a cancellation always follows.

| $f$ | $f'$ | check: denominator power went $2n \to n+1$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\dfrac{2x-16}{(x+3)^2}$ | $\dfrac{38-2x}{(x+3)^3}$ | $4\to 3$ |
| $\dfrac{x+1}{(x-2)^3}$ | $\dfrac{-2x-5}{(x-2)^4}$ | $6\to 4$ |
| $\dfrac{x}{(x^2+1)^2}$ | $\dfrac{1-3x^2}{(x^2+1)^3}$ | $4\to 3$ |
| $\dfrac{3x}{(2x-1)^2}$ | $-\dfrac{3(2x+1)}{(2x-1)^3}$ | $4\to 3$ |
| $\dfrac{x-4}{(x+1)^2}$ | $\dfrac{9-x}{(x+1)^3}$ | $4\to 3$ |
| $\dfrac{1}{(x^2+4)^3}$ | $-\dfrac{6x}{(x^2+4)^4}$ | no quotient rule needed; it is $(x^2+4)^{-3}$ |

**Read the six rows as one formula and one exception.**
The formula is section 2.4's, $\dfrac{u'w - n\,u\,w'}{w^{n+1}}$, and the first five rows are it with different letters.
It was verified over 144 $(a,b,c,n)$ combinations, so it is not five coincidences.

The exception is the last row, where the numerator is a **constant**.
A constant over a power is not a quotient problem at all: rewrite it as a negative power and use the chain rule, which is one step instead of three.
The cue is that $u' = 0$, which makes the whole first term of the quotient rule vanish.

**The most common variation of Q8.1(b) is a change of $n$.**
$n=2$ gives a denominator of $(x+3)^3$; $n=3$ gives $(x-2)^4$.
If you memorise "the answer has a cube on the bottom" you will get $n=3$ wrong.
The rule is $n+1$, always.

### Family 4 - the chain rule with a named-function outer, which is Q8.1(c)

The trigger is $\sin$, $\cos$, $\tan$, $\sec$, $\csc$, $\cot$ or $\sqrt{\ }$ wrapped around something that is not bare $x$.
The tool is the chain rule, and the only thing that varies is which outer derivative you write.

| $f$ | $f'$ | where it appears |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\sin\left(2x^2-x+1\right)$ | $(4x-1)\cos\left(2x^2-x+1\right)$ | **Q8.1c** |
| $\cos\left(3x^2+5\right)$ | $-6x\sin\left(3x^2+5\right)$ | |
| $\tan\left(x^3\right)$ | $3x^2\sec^2\left(x^3\right)$ | |
| $\sec\left(x^2-3x\right)$ | $(2x-3)\sec\left(x^2-3x\right)\tan\left(x^2-3x\right)$ | **Q8.2b** |
| $\cot(2x)$ | $-2\csc^2(2x)$ | **Q8.2a**, first derivative |
| $\csc\sqrt x$ | $-\dfrac{\csc\sqrt x\,\cot\sqrt x}{2\sqrt x}$ | |
| $\sin\left(\tfrac1x\right)$ | $-\dfrac{\cos\left(\frac1x\right)}{x^2}$ | |
| $\tan(2x)$ | $2\sec^2(2x)$ | **Q8.4a** numerator |

**Every row has exactly the same shape**: the outer derivative from the table in section 2.2, evaluated at the untouched inner, times the inner derivative.
There are eight rows and one idea.
The signs are not eight facts either: they are the three minus signs from $\cos$, $\cot$ and $\csc$, exactly as section 2.2 says.

**The variation that catches people is $\cot(2x)$**, where the answer picks up a factor of 2.
That factor is the chain rule and nothing else, and it is what makes Q8.2a's second derivative work out to $8\csc^2(2x)\cot(2x)$ rather than $2\csc^2(2x)\cot(2x)$.

### Family 5 - the chain rule with a power outer, which is Q8.1(d)

The trigger is a bracket, or a trig function, raised to a constant power.
The tool is $\frac{d}{dx}[g]^n = n[g]^{n-1}g'$.

| $f$ | $f'$ | where it appears |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\left(-4x^3-x^2+3x+7\right)^4$ | $4\left(-4x^3-x^2+3x+7\right)^3\left(-12x^2-2x+3\right)$ | **Q8.1d** |
| $\left(3x^2+1\right)^5$ | $30x\left(3x^2+1\right)^4$ | |
| $\sqrt{x^2-1}$ | $\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}$ | **Q8.3d** numerator |
| $(2x+1)^{-3}$ | $-6(2x+1)^{-4}$ | |
| $\sin^3 x$ | $3\sin^2 x\cos x$ | |
| $\cos^3\left(x^2\right)$ | $-6x\cos^2\left(x^2\right)\sin\left(x^2\right)$ | **Q8.4b** |
| $\left(x^2+1\right)^{1/3}$ | $\tfrac23 x\left(x^2+1\right)^{-2/3}$ | |
| $\sec^2 x$ | $2\sec^2 x\tan x$ | **Q8.3e** outer |

**The two rows to look at twice are $\sin^3 x$ and $\cos^3(x^2)$.**
The notation $\sin^3 x$ *means* $(\sin x)^3$, so the last operation is the cubing and the outer function is the power, not the sine.
$\cos^3(x^2)$ is the same thing with an extra layer, which is why it lives in Family 7 as much as here, and why Q8.4b is worth two points rather than one.

**The row that people over-work is $\sqrt{x^2-1}$.**
Writing it as $(x^2-1)^{1/2}$ gives $\frac12(x^2-1)^{-1/2}\cdot 2x$, and the 2s cancel to leave $\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}$.
That cancellation happens every single time the outer power is $\frac12$ and the inner is a quadratic, and knowing it saves a line.

### Family 6 - the product rule, which Q8.1 does not test and the other papers do

The trigger is two $x$-dependent factors multiplied.
The tool is $u'v + uv'$, which is symmetric, so there is no order to get wrong.

| $f$ | $f'$ | where it appears |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $x\cos\sqrt{x-3}$ | $\cos\sqrt{x-3} - \dfrac{x\sin\sqrt{x-3}}{2\sqrt{x-3}}$ | review question 1 |
| $x^2\tan x$ | $2x\tan x + x^2\sec^2 x$ | review question 2 |
| $(x^2+1)(x^3-2)$ | $5x^4+3x^2-4x$ | expanding first is faster here |
| $x^3\sin 2x$ | $3x^2\sin 2x + 2x^3\cos 2x$ | |
| $\sin x\cos\left(\sin x^2\right)$ | $\cos x\cos\left(\sin x^2\right) - 2x\sin x\sin\left(\sin x^2\right)\cos\left(x^2\right)$ | **Q8.3a** |

**Row 3 is the cautionary one.**
$(x^2+1)(x^3-2)$ *can* be done by the product rule, and it is faster to expand to $x^5+x^3-2x-2$ and differentiate term by term.
The product rule is for factors you cannot expand, which in practice means at least one of them is trigonometric or a root.

**Row 5 is Q8.3a and it is the hardest single derivative in the category**, because it is a product whose second factor is a three-layer composite.
It is still just $u'v + uv'$; the difficulty is entirely inside $v'$, and $v'$ is Family 7.

### Family 7 - the nested chain, two or more layers, which is Q8.3

The trigger is a composite whose inner function is itself a composite.
The tool is the same chain rule, applied outside-in, one layer at a time.

| $f$ | $f'$ | layers |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\sqrt{1+\sqrt{1+x}}$ | $\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{1+\sqrt{1+x}}\,\sqrt{1+x}}$ | 3 |
| $\cos\left(\sin x^2\right)$ | $-2x\cos\left(x^2\right)\sin\left(\sin x^2\right)$ | 3 |
| $\sec^2\left(\dfrac{x+1}{x-2}\right)$ | $-\dfrac{6\sec^2 u\,\tan u}{(x-2)^2}$, with $u = \dfrac{x+1}{x-2}$ | 3, and the innermost is a quotient |
| $\left(\dfrac{1+x^3}{1-x^2}\right)^{1/3}$ | $\dfrac13\left(\dfrac{1+x^3}{1-x^2}\right)^{-2/3}\cdot\dfrac{2x+3x^2-x^4}{(1-x^2)^2}$ | 2, with a quotient inside |

**Nothing new happens in this family.**
The procedure in section 3 recurses, and a three-layer function simply means step 3 runs three times instead of one.
The only practical change is bookkeeping: write each layer's derivative on its own line rather than trying to assemble the whole product in your head.

Row 1 is the cleanest illustration.
The outer $\sqrt{\ }$ gives $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+\sqrt{1+x}}}$, the middle $\sqrt{\ }$ gives $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+x}}$, the inner $1+x$ gives 1, and the answer is those three multiplied.
The 4 in the denominator is $2\times 2$, one from each square root.

### Family 8 - a quotient whose parts are themselves composites

The trigger is a division where $u$, $v$, or both, need a rule of their own.
The tool is the quotient rule with a sub-derivation for each piece.

| $f$ | $f'$ | where |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\dfrac{\sqrt{x^2-1}}{x^2-2x-8}$ | $\dfrac{\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}\left(x^2-2x-8\right) - \sqrt{x^2-1}\,(2x-2)}{\left(x^2-2x-8\right)^2}$ | **Q8.3d** |
| $\dfrac{x^2-\cos 3x}{x\sin 2x}$ | $\dfrac{(2x+3\sin 3x)(x\sin 2x) - \left(x^2-\cos 3x\right)(\sin 2x + 2x\cos 2x)}{(x\sin 2x)^2}$ | **Q8.2c** |
| $\dfrac{\tan 2x}{\sqrt x}$ | $\dfrac{2\sec^2(2x)\sqrt x - \frac{\tan 2x}{2\sqrt x}}{x}$ | **Q8.4a** |

**These are the questions where "you may not need to simplify" pays for itself.**
Every one of those three answers is final as written.
Q8.2c in particular has a denominator that is already $(x\sin 2x)^2$, and expanding it to $x^2\sin^2 2x$ gains nothing.

The one worth noticing is Q8.4a, whose denominator $\sqrt x$ makes the quotient rule produce a fraction inside a fraction.
Multiplying numerator and denominator by $2\sqrt x$ clears it to $\dfrac{4x\sec^2(2x) - \tan 2x}{2x^{3/2}}$, which is tidier and, per the policy in section 5, entirely optional.

### Family 9 - a derivative at a single named point, sometimes from given values

The trigger is a vertical bar with $x = a$ on it, or a question that hands you numbers instead of formulas.
The tool is: **differentiate symbolically first, substitute last**.

| asked | answer | the trap |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\left.\dfrac{d}{dx}\dfrac{f}{g}\right|_{x=1}$ with $f(1)=3$, $g(1)=6$, $f'(x)=\sqrt x$, $g'(x)=3\sin\frac{\pi x}{3}$ | $\dfrac{4-3\sqrt3}{24}\approx -0.04984$ | $g'(1) = 3\sin\frac\pi3 = \frac{3\sqrt3}{2}$, in **radians** |
| $\left.\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos^3\left(x^2\right)\right|_{x=\sqrt\pi/2}$ | $-\dfrac{3\sqrt{2\pi}}{4}\approx -1.87998$ | the point is chosen so $x^2 = \frac\pi4$ |
| $\left.\dfrac{d}{dx}\dfrac{f-x^2g}{f+g}\right|_{x=0}$ with $f(0)=1,f'(0)=2,g(0)=0,g'(0)=-1$ | $1$ | the $x^2g$ term needs the product rule before you substitute |
| $y'(0)$ for Q8.1(b) | $\dfrac{38}{27}$ | |
| $y'(1)$ for Q8.1(a) | $14$ | |
| $y'(0)$ for Q8.1(c) | $-\cos 1 \approx -0.5403$ | radians |
| $y'(0)$ for Q8.1(d) | $4\cdot 7^3\cdot 3 = 4116$ | |

**The one rule in this family is the order of operations.**
Substituting $x=1$ before you differentiate turns $f(x)$ into the constant 3 and gives you 0, which is the classic zero-mark answer.
Differentiate with the letters, then substitute.

The second row is the giveaway about how these are constructed: $\sqrt\pi/2$ looks arbitrary until you square it and get $\pi/4$, where cosine and sine are both $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$.
Whenever an evaluation point looks strange, square it or double it and see what it was designed to become.

### Family 10 - the second derivative, which is Q8.2a

The trigger is $\frac{d^2}{dx^2}$.
The tool is: run the procedure twice, on the **simplified** first derivative.

| $f$ | $f'$ | $f''$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\cot(2x)$ | $-2\csc^2(2x)$ | $8\csc^2(2x)\cot(2x)$ |
| $4x^5+3x^4-6x^3+6$ | $20x^4+12x^3-18x^2$ | $80x^3+36x^2-36x$ |
| $\dfrac{2x-16}{(x+3)^2}$ | $\dfrac{38-2x}{(x+3)^3}$ | $\dfrac{4(x-30)}{(x+3)^4}$ |
| $x^2\tan x$ | $2x\tan x + x^2\sec^2 x$ | $2\tan x + 4x\sec^2 x + 2x^2\sec^2 x\tan x$, which is $4\pi$ at $x=\pi$ |

**This is the one family where simplifying the first derivative is mandatory rather than optional.**
Differentiating an unsimplified $f'$ doubles the work and doubles the chance of an error, so the policy in section 5 flips: for a second derivative, tidy $f'$ first, then differentiate it.
Row 3 makes the point: differentiating $\frac{38-2x}{(x+3)^3}$ is one quotient rule, and differentiating the uncancelled $\frac{2(x+3)^2-2(2x-16)(x+3)}{(x+3)^4}$ is a much worse afternoon.

The Q8.1(b) row also produces a free bonus: $f''(19) < 0$, which confirms by the second-derivative test that the critical point found in section 4 is a maximum.

### Family 11 - naming the rules, which is Q8.4

The trigger is "state which rule(s) you are applying".
The tool is the last-operation test, which produces the name as a by-product.

| $f$ | rules, in the order you apply them |
| :--- | :--- |
| $\dfrac{\tan 2x}{\sqrt x}$ | **quotient**, then **chain** on $\tan 2x$, then **power** on $x^{1/2}$ |
| $\cos^3\left(x^2\right)$ | **chain** with a power outer, then **chain** again with a cosine outer, then **power** on $x^2$ |
| $\dfrac{2x-16}{(x+3)^2}$ | **quotient**, then **chain** on the denominator, then **power** |
| $\sin\left(2x^2-x+1\right)$ | **chain**, then **power** and **sum** on the inner |

**You never have to remember what you did.**
If you wrote the tree in section 3, the rule names are already on the page in the order the marker wants them, which is why the habit in section 5 costs nothing and pays off directly on Q8.4.

### Family 12 - the simplification step, as a source of marks lost

The trigger is having a correct derivative and choosing to tidy it.
The tool is care, and the point of this family is that **this is where the marks in category 8 actually go**.

| the raw form | the simplified form | the step that can go wrong |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\dfrac{2(x+3)^2-2(2x-16)(x+3)}{(x+3)^4}$ | $\dfrac{38-2x}{(x+3)^3}$ | distributing the $-2$ across $(2x-16)$ |
| $20x^4+12x^3-18x^2$ | $2x^2\left(10x^2+6x-9\right)$ | nothing; but it gains nothing either |
| $4u^3\left(-12x^2-2x+3\right)$ | $-4\left(12x^2+2x-3\right)u^3$ | flipping every sign inside |
| $\dfrac{(x-2)^3-3(x+1)(x-2)^2}{(x-2)^6}$ | $\dfrac{-2x-5}{(x-2)^4}$ | cancelling $(x-2)^2$, not $(x-2)^3$ |
| $\dfrac{(x^2+1)^2 - 4x^2(x^2+1)}{(x^2+1)^4}$ | $\dfrac{1-3x^2}{(x^2+1)^3}$ | the same |
| $5(3x^2+1)^4\cdot 6x$ | $30x(3x^2+1)^4$ | nothing |
| $\tfrac12(x^2-1)^{-1/2}\cdot 2x$ | $\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}$ | nothing |

**Every entry in this table was checked as an identity over 14 sample points**, not at one value, because two expressions can agree at a single point by accident.
Two seeded wrong versions, a sign slip in the numerator and an off-by-one in the denominator power, were both confirmed to be rejected by that check.

The row to study is row 1, because the sign error there is the single most common way to lose a mark on Q8.1.
$-2(2x-16)$ is $-4x + 32$, and the plausible wrong answer is $-4x - 32$, which produces $\frac{-2x - 26}{(x+3)^3}$ and looks entirely reasonable.
The section 6 check at $x=1$ catches it: the right answer is $+0.5625$ and the wrong one is $-0.4375$.

### Family 13 - an algebraic rewrite that removes the need for a rule

The trigger is an expression that looks like it needs the product or quotient rule but collapses.
The tool is algebra done before calculus.

| $f$ | rewrite as | $f'$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\sqrt x\cdot\sqrt{x^3}$ | $x^2$ | $2x$ |
| $\dfrac{x^3+x}{x}$ | $x^2+1$ | $2x$ |
| $\tan x\cos x$ | $\sin x$ | $\cos x$ |
| $\dfrac{\sin 2x}{2\sin x}$ | $\cos x$ | $-\sin x$ |
| $\dfrac{x^2-9}{x-3}$ | $x+3$, for $x\neq3$ | $1$ |

**This family is a habit rather than a technique.**
Spend three seconds looking for a collapse before you start, because when there is one it turns a two-rule problem into a one-line one.
Q8.1 contains no such collapse, which is itself worth confirming: $(2x-16)$ and $(x+3)^2$ share no factor, so part (b) really does need a rule.

### Family 14 - the derivative as input to the next question

The trigger is that the derivative is not the answer.
The tool is whatever the next question needs, and the point is that a derivative left unsimplified is often unusable downstream.

| asked | using | answer |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Q9.1: for which $x$ is the tangent to $f = 3x^2+4x-3$ perpendicular to $y=6x+2$? | $f' = 6x+4$, set equal to $-\frac16$ | $x = -\dfrac{25}{36}$ |
| the critical points of Q8.1(a) | $2x^2(10x^2+6x-9) = 0$ | $x=0$ and $x = \dfrac{-3\pm3\sqrt{11}}{10}$ |
| the critical point of Q8.1(b) | $38-2x = 0$ | $x = 19$, a maximum, with $y = \frac1{22}$ |
| where Q8.1(d) has a horizontal tangent | the base $=0$ or $-12x^2-2x+3=0$ | $x\approx 1.3269$, and $x = \dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt{37}}{12}$ |

**Row 1 is the one that trips people, and the mistake is not calculus.**
Perpendicular means the slopes multiply to $-1$, so the target slope is $-\frac16$ and not $-6$.
Row 2 and row 3 are where Family 12's "simplify only when the zeros matter" clause bites: you cannot read $x=19$ off an uncancelled quotient without doing the cancellation anyway.

## 9. The trap list

Ranked by how often each one actually costs marks in this family.

1. **Dropping the inner derivative in the chain rule.** Writing $\cos(2x^2-x+1)$ for part (c) or $4(-4x^3-x^2+3x+7)^3$ for part (d). This is the number one mark-loser in the entire course and it is caught in one second by the check in section 6.
2. **The quotient rule written backwards.** $uv' - u'v$ instead of $u'v - uv'$. It flips the sign of the whole answer and it looks completely plausible on the page. The guard is step 2 of the procedure: write the rule with blanks before you fill it in.
3. **A sign slip distributing the minus over the second numerator term.** $-2(2x-16) = -4x+32$, not $-4x-32$. Family 12, row 1.
4. **Taking $v' = 1$ instead of $2(x+3)$ in part (b).** This is trap 1 wearing a different hat: the denominator is a composite and it needs the chain rule too.
5. **Expanding part (d).** Not wrong, just expensive. Four minutes, twelve terms, no marks, and every term is a chance to slip. The question explicitly gives you permission not to.
6. **Leaving $(x+3)^4$ in part (b)'s denominator after cancelling the numerator.** Half a cancellation is worse than none, because the two halves no longer describe the same function. Either cancel properly or leave the whole thing raw.
7. **Differentiating the base inside the bracket in part (d).** Writing $4(-12x^2-2x+3)^3$. The outer derivative leaves the inner **completely untouched**; this is the same misunderstanding as trap 1 seen from the other side.
8. **Calculator in degrees on part (c).** Only matters when you evaluate, but section 6 tells you to evaluate, so it matters. The error factor is about 6.6 and the check catches it immediately.
9. **Writing $\frac{d}{dx}\sin = -\cos$.** The minus belongs to $\cos$, not to $\sin$. Section 2.2's "co-functions get the minus" generates it correctly every time.
10. **Missing brackets on Möbius entry.** `(38-2*x)/(x+3)^3` versus `(38-2*x)/(x+3^3)`. Preview catches this and nothing else will.
11. **Reaching for the product rule on $(x+3)(x+3)$ in part (b).** It works and it wastes thirty seconds.
12. **Simplifying part (c) or part (d) at all.** There is nothing there to simplify, so any algebra you do is pure risk.

## 10. Drill set

No answers beside the questions.
Do all twelve on paper in under twenty minutes, then check.

Score **rule choice**, **execution** and **simplification** as three separate columns, because they need three different fixes.
A wrong rule is a reading problem and section 3 fixes it.
A right rule executed wrongly is a memory problem and section 2 fixes it.
A right derivative simplified wrongly is an algebra problem and Family 12 fixes it, and it is the most common of the three.

1. $y = 7x^6 - 5x^4 + 2x - 9$
2. $y = \dfrac{3x-5}{(x+2)^2}$
3. $y = \cos\left(5x^3+2x\right)$
4. $y = \left(2x^2-5x+1\right)^6$
5. $y = \dfrac{4}{x^3} + 3\sqrt x$
6. $y = x^2\sin(3x)$
7. $y = \sqrt{4x^2+1}$
8. $y = \tan^2 x$
9. $y = \dfrac{x+1}{x^2+1}$
10. $y = \sin(\cos x)$
11. $y = \dfrac{x^3-2x}{x^2}$
12. $y = \dfrac{x}{(3x-1)^3}$

### Answer key

| # | answer | family and method |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | $42x^5 - 20x^3 + 2$ | 0, sum and power only; the $-9$ vanishes |
| 2 | $\dfrac{16-3x}{(x+2)^3}$ | 3, and the numerator is $3(x+2) - 2(3x-5)$, so the constant is $6+10=16$ |
| 3 | $-\left(15x^2+2\right)\sin\left(5x^3+2x\right)$ | 4, chain with a cosine outer; the minus is the cosine's |
| 4 | $6\left(2x^2-5x+1\right)^5(4x-5)$ | 5, generalized power rule; do **not** expand |
| 5 | $-\dfrac{12}{x^4} + \dfrac{3}{2\sqrt x}$ | 1, rewrite as $4x^{-3}+3x^{1/2}$ first |
| 6 | $2x\sin 3x + 3x^2\cos 3x$ | 6, product rule, with a chain inside the second term |
| 7 | $\dfrac{4x}{\sqrt{4x^2+1}}$ | 5, and the $\frac12$ cancels against the inner's $8x$ |
| 8 | $2\tan x\sec^2 x$ | 5, since $\tan^2 x$ means $(\tan x)^2$ |
| 9 | $\dfrac{1-2x-x^2}{\left(x^2+1\right)^2}$ | 2, plain quotient rule; the numerator is a full quadratic |
| 10 | $-\sin x\cos(\cos x)$ | 4, chain; the minus comes from the **inner** $\cos$ |
| 11 | $1 + \dfrac{2}{x^2}$ | 13, split to $x - 2x^{-1}$ first and no rule is needed |
| 12 | $-\dfrac{6x+1}{(3x-1)^4}$ | 3, and the denominator power is $n+1 = 4$, not 6 |

Every answer in this key was recomputed by two independent numerical methods before it was written down.

Three of the twelve are deliberately mis-shaped to catch a specific reflex.
Number 5 looks like it needs the quotient rule and does not.
Number 8 looks like a trigonometric derivative and is actually a power.
Number 11 looks like a quotient and collapses to two terms.
If you reached for a rule on any of those three, section 3 step 1 is the section to redo.

---

## 11. The one-page decision tree

```
"Compute the derivative of y = <expression>."
|
+-- STEP 1.  If I substituted a number, what would I do LAST?
|      + or -            -> do each term separately, then ask again
|      x by a constant   -> pull the constant out, then ask again
|      x between two     -> PRODUCT   u'v + uv'     (symmetric, no order risk)
|         x-factors
|      /                 -> QUOTIENT  (u'v - uv')/v^2   <- ORDER MATTERS
|      ( )^n             -> CHAIN     n( )^(n-1) * (inner)'
|      sin/cos/tan/sqrt  -> CHAIN     outer'(inner) * (inner)'
|      nothing left      -> POWER     n x^(n-1)   or   0
|
+-- STEP 2.  Write the rule with BLANKS first.  Then name u and v.
|            This is what stops the quotient rule coming out backwards.
|
+-- STEP 3.  Ask step 1 again about each piece.  Stop at x^n or a constant.
|
+-- STEP 4.  Assemble.  The question is now answered and the marks are earned.
|
+-- STEP 5.  Simplify ONLY if one factor cancels top and bottom.
|      quotient over a power  -> YES, one power of the base comes out,
|                               and the denominator goes 2n -> n+1
|      a bracket to a power   -> NO.  Never expand.
|      a trig chain result    -> NO.  There is nothing to do.
|      a SECOND derivative    -> YES, always tidy f' before differentiating it
|
+-- STEP 6.  CHECK.  On the calculator:  [f(1.001) - f(0.999)] / 0.002
             Compare with your y'(1).  Three matching figures is enough.

      SHAPE     a polynomial's degree drops by exactly 1
      POLES     a pole's order RISES by exactly 1
      INNER     the inside of a bracket or a trig function is UNCHANGED
      CHAIN     is the inner derivative actually written down?  Look.
      ORDER     quotient rule numerator starts with u', not u
      RADIANS   check the calculator mode before trusting any number
      TYPE IT   every * explicit, numerator and denominator bracketed
      PREVIEW   always
```

### Defects found in this file's own checks

Three checks failed on first run.
In all three the mathematics was right and the **check** was wrong, which is why the rule is to establish which of the two is broken before changing any answer.
That is now seven runs in a row in this series where every first-run failure was a verifier defect.

| the check | why it failed | the fix |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| the difference quotient at a fixed $h = 10^{-3}$, which reported **five** failures | a truncation error is an **asymptotic** statement, so pinning it to one $h$ measures the size of the next term instead. At $x = 0.05$ the function $1/x^3$ changes by 6 percent across that step, and $\cos(5x^3+2x)$ at $x=7.9$ has local wavenumber 938, so $h=10^{-3}$ is a 0.94 radian phase step. | test along a **ladder** in $h$ from $10^{-2}$ to $10^{-7}$ and report the best rung. The five errors fall from $\sim10^{-3}$ to $\sim10^{-13}$. A control confirms the ladder does **not** rescue a genuinely wrong derivative. |
| the Family 7 entry $\left(\frac{1+x^3}{1-x^2}\right)^{1/3}$, failing at a relative error of exactly **1.00** | an error of exactly 1 is the signature of a **branch** problem, not an algebra problem. The sample points 1.4, 2.2 and 4.0 all put the base below zero, and Python returns the principal **complex** cube root of a negative float, so the two sides were evaluated on different branches. | move the sample points inside $-1 < x < 1$, where the base is positive and the real cube root and the principal branch agree. A control confirms the trap is real by checking that the base at $x=2.2$ really does produce a complex value. |
| the figure gate demanding that at least 8 of the tree's lines carry a vertical connector | the tree has 7, and the threshold 8 was **invented rather than measured**. A gate asserting a number nobody derived tells you nothing when it passes and lies when it fails. | replace it with the structural property the figure actually has to satisfy: no rule node may be **orphaned**, meaning every announced rule has a connector glyph on the non-blank line above it. Two controls confirm the new gate both bites on a seeded orphan and clears when a connector is added. |

The first two are the same failure in two costumes: a numerical method used outside the regime where it is valid.
The third is a different and more insidious one, because it would have passed review: the number 8 looks like a measurement and was a guess, and it was only exposed because the figure happened to have 7.

A fourth defect was found and fixed before it could be counted: a bisection for the real root of $-4x^3-x^2+3x+7$ was bracketed on $[-2, 0]$, where the polynomial is $+29$ and $+7$ at the ends and has no root at all.
The fix was to sweep for sign changes over $[-4,4]$ first, which finds exactly one, in $[1.32, 1.33]$, and to assert that count as its own check rather than assuming it.

# Q8.2 - Four derivatives, including a second derivative

**The question (Midterm Exam 2, item 9, 16 points).**

> Find each of the derivatives listed below.
> Show your work.
>
> **Note:** You may not need to simplify your answer.
>
> a. $\dfrac{d^2}{dx^2}\,\cot(2x)$
> b. $\dfrac{d}{dx}\,\sec\left(x^2 - 3x\right)$
> c. $\dfrac{d}{dx}\,\dfrac{x^2 - \cos(3x)}{x\,\sin(2x)}$
> d. $\left.\dfrac{d}{dx}\,\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}\right|_{x=1}$ where $f(1) = 3$, $g(1) = 6$, $f'(x) = \sqrt{x}$ and $g'(x) = 3\sin(\pi x/3)$.

**The answers.**

| part | the derivative | what a marker expects to see |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| a | $\dfrac{d^2}{dx^2}\cot(2x) = 8\csc^2(2x)\cot(2x)$ | this, or the equivalent $\dfrac{8\cos(2x)}{\sin^3(2x)}$ |
| b | $(2x-3)\sec\left(x^2-3x\right)\tan\left(x^2-3x\right)$ | exactly this; nothing to simplify |
| c | $\dfrac{\left(2x+3\sin 3x\right)\left(x\sin 2x\right) - \left(x^2-\cos 3x\right)\left(\sin 2x + 2x\cos 2x\right)}{\left(x\sin 2x\right)^2}$ | exactly this, unsimplified |
| d | $\dfrac{4-3\sqrt3}{24} \approx -0.0498397$ | the exact surd, not the decimal |

**What to type into Möbius:**

```
a.  8*csc(2*x)^2*cot(2*x)          or  8*cos(2*x)/sin(2*x)^3
b.  (2*x-3)*sec(x^2-3*x)*tan(x^2-3*x)
c.  ((2*x+3*sin(3*x))*(x*sin(2*x))-(x^2-cos(3*x))*(sin(2*x)+2*x*cos(2*x)))/(x*sin(2*x))^2
d.  (4-3*sqrt(3))/24
```

Every multiplication carries an explicit `*`, and every answer is previewed before it is submitted.
If the preview on part (a) does not render `csc` and `cot`, the sine-and-cosine form on the right is the fallback that no parser can refuse.

**Provenance.**
Midterm Exam 2, item 9, worth **16 points** of that paper's 94.
Midterm 2 prints its point values on their **own line before** the item, so the `(16 points)` line sits above `9. Find each of the derivatives listed below`, and reading the document boundary is what settles the attribution.
Item 9 carries **no** "no credit" clause.
Midterm 2's two no-credit clauses are on items 4 and 7, and inventing a third one here would be a fiction.
It does carry the printed permission *"You may not need to simplify your answer"*, and section 5 is where that clause gets complicated, because part (a) is the one place in category 8 where you have to simplify something.

**Verification.**
Every derivative, every simplification, every table entry and every drill answer in this document was recomputed in Python before it was written down.
First derivatives were checked by a complex-step derivative and by a Richardson difference-quotient ladder, exactly as the Q8.1 section of the harness established.
Second derivatives got their own two independent arms, neither of which reads my own $f'$, because re-differentiating your own answer is not evidence.
**212 checks, 0 failures, 27 of them seeded controls that are required to fail and do.**
Section 12 gives the counts and the nine checker defects that had to be fixed along the way.

**Browser version of this tutorial:** https://claude.ai/code/artifact/af6ef5e9-36a0-4925-be3b-ef22ea896d48

## What Q8.2 adds, and what it inherits

Q8.1 was built as the foundation of this category and it deliberately holds three things that are **not** repeated here.
Go back to `notes\Q8.1 - Four derivatives, power chain and quotient rules.md` for them rather than looking for them below:

| inherited from Q8.1 | where it lives | why it is not restated |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| the **last-operation test** for choosing a rule | Q8.1 section 3 | it is mechanical and it recurses, so it needs no change to handle a second derivative; you just run it twice |
| the **simplification policy** | Q8.1 section 5 | all four Q8 items print the same permission, so the policy belongs to the category |
| the **eight-second centred-difference check** | Q8.1 section 6 | it works unchanged on parts (b), (c) and (d) of this question |
| the full **rule table** and the six trig derivatives | Q8.1 sections 2.1 and 2.2 | this document uses $\cot$, $\csc$, $\sec$ and $\tan$ and assumes you have them |

Q8.2's own contribution is **the second derivative**, and it is three specific ideas, not one:

1. **The simplification policy inverts.**
   Q8.1's policy is that simplifying has zero marginal reward and non-zero marginal risk, so you stop when the derivative is written.
   That is right when $f'$ is the *answer*.
   In part (a) $f'$ is an *input*, and the reward stops being zero, because every unsimplified factor you carry into the second differentiation multiplies into a bigger mess.
   Section 5 states the inverted policy and the one test that tells you which regime you are in.
2. **The rule choice can change between the first and the second differentiation.**
   $\cot(2x)$ is a chain rule with a named-function outer.
   Its derivative $-2\csc^2(2x)$ is a chain rule with a **power** outer.
   Nothing in Q8.1 prepares you for the rule name changing under your hands, and it is why people who get part (a)'s $f'$ right still get $f''$ wrong.
   Family 2 in section 8 is the whole catalog of how the rule changes, including the two cases where it becomes a **product** rule.
3. **A second derivative needs a different numerical check, and the check that works for $f'$ actively misleads you.**
   Q8.1's rule was that a smaller $h$ is safer.
   For a second difference you divide by $h^2$ instead of $h$, so the roundoff floor is a hundred times worse, and $h = 10^{-5}$ on a real calculator gives you **zero** correct figures.
   Section 6 gives the measured optimum and the table that produced it.

Where Q8.2's four parts sit in Q8.1's family map: (a) is Family 10 there and Family 2 here, (b) is Family 4 there and Family 7 here, (c) is Family 8 in both, (d) is Family 9 in both.
The renumbering is not carelessness.
Q8.1 organised its families around *which rule you pick*; this document organises them around *what happens on the second pass*, because that is the axis Q8.2 tests.

**Sixteen points for four derivatives is four points each, on a paper worth 94.**
That makes Q8.2 the second-heaviest item on Midterm 2 and 17 percent of the paper, so it is worth more attention than its difficulty suggests.
Part (a) is worth the same four points as part (b), and part (a) takes three times as long.

## 0. The 30-second version

```
FIRST DERIVATIVES (b, c, d):  run Q8.1's last-operation test once.  Done.

SECOND DERIVATIVE (a):  run it TWICE, with one step in between.

   PASS 1   last op of cot(2x) is a NAMED FUNCTION -> chain rule
            f' = -csc^2(2x) * 2 = -2 csc^2(2x)

   BETWEEN  is f' as short as it will get?  If not, shorten it NOW.
            This is the opposite of the rule for a first derivative.

   PASS 2   ask the last-operation question AGAIN, about f'.
            The answer may be a DIFFERENT rule than pass 1 gave you.
            -2 csc^2(2x) ends in a SQUARE, so pass 2 is a POWER chain.
            f'' = -2 * 2 csc(2x) * (-csc(2x) cot(2x) * 2)
                = 8 csc^2(2x) cot(2x)

   CHECK    [f(x+h) - 2 f(x) + f(x-h)] / h^2   with h = 0.001, NOT smaller.

GIVEN VALUES (d):  differentiate with the LETTERS, substitute LAST, radians.
```

That is the whole method and it is runnable from memory.
The only line worth rehearsing is the "between" line, because it is the one that has no analogue in a first-derivative question.

## 1. What this question is really testing

| the reflex being tested | where it comes back |
| :--- | :--- |
| running the rule-selection test a **second** time instead of pattern-matching | this is the only question in the bank that requires it |
| noticing that $\csc^2 u$ ends in a **square**, so the outer function is the power | Q8.3b, Q8.3e, Q8.4b, and every $\sin^n$ or $\sec^n$ you will ever meet |
| the product rule **inside** a quotient rule | Q8.2c, Q8.3a, Q8.3d |
| differentiating with letters and substituting last | Q8.2d, Q8.4b, and every related-rates question |
| radians, always | Q8.2d, Q8.4b, Q8.1c |
| $f''$ as a tool rather than an answer | Q5.1, Q5.2, Q5.3 (all three sketch questions state conditions on $f''$), Q11, Q12 |

**The four parts are a designed tour again, and this time the axis is depth rather than breadth.**
Part (a) is one function differentiated twice.
Part (b) is one chain rule, deliberately easy, to give you a cheap four points.
Part (c) is a quotient with a rule needed inside each half of it.
Part (d) has no functions at all, only numbers, which strips away the calculus and tests whether you know the quotient rule as a *formula* rather than as a procedure you can only execute on expressions.

| what each part is actually for | part |
| :--- | :--- |
| can you run the procedure twice, and notice the rule changed | a |
| can you do a clean chain rule at speed | b |
| can you nest a rule inside a rule without losing a term | c |
| do you know the quotient rule as a formula, and do you know what radians are | d |

**Part (b) is the cheapest four points on the paper and it should take you forty seconds.**
Do it first.
Part (a) is where the time goes, and part (d) is where the marks go, because the two traps in (d) are silent.

## 2. The four things you must have cold

Q8.1 section 2 has the five rules and the six trig derivatives, and this document assumes them.
These four are the additions that Q8.2 specifically needs.

### 2.1 The two Pythagorean identities, in the direction that helps

$$\csc^2 u = 1 + \cot^2 u, \qquad \sec^2 u = 1 + \tan^2 u$$

You need these read **left to right**, which is the unusual direction.
The point is that $\csc^2(2x)$, which looks like a squared reciprocal you cannot do anything with, is a constant plus $\cot^2(2x)$, which is a power of something whose derivative you know.
That is a second, completely independent route to part (a) and it is Family 4 in section 8.

Both were verified as identities over the sample points at $10^{-16}$ relative, not assumed.

### 2.2 Which of $\csc^2 u$ and $\csc\left(u^2\right)$ you are looking at

This is the single most consequential piece of notation in the question.

| written | means | last operation | rule |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\csc^2(2x)$ | $\left[\csc(2x)\right]^2$ | **squaring** | chain, **power** outer |
| $\csc\left((2x)^2\right)$ | $\csc\left(4x^2\right)$ | applying $\csc$ | chain, **named** outer |
| $\sec\left(x^2-3x\right)$ | as written | applying $\sec$ | chain, **named** outer |
| $\sec^2 x$ | $(\sec x)^2$ | **squaring** | chain, **power** outer |

$\csc^2(2x)$ is a square, and that single fact is what turns pass 2 of part (a) into a power-rule problem.
Read the superscript's **position**: on the function name it is an exponent applied last, and inside the bracket it is part of the argument.

### 2.3 The derivative of a squared trig function, which you will use twice

$$\frac{d}{dx}\left[T(u)\right]^2 = 2\,T(u)\cdot T'(u)\cdot u'$$

Three factors, and the third is the one that goes missing.
For part (a) with $T = \csc$, $u = 2x$:

$$\frac{d}{dx}\csc^2(2x) = 2\csc(2x)\cdot\left(-\csc(2x)\cot(2x)\right)\cdot 2 = -4\csc^2(2x)\cot(2x)$$

Note that the two $\csc$ factors multiply into $\csc^2$, which is why the answer looks like the thing you started with.
That coincidence is what makes part (a) feel circular, and it is worth expecting so it does not read as a mistake.

### 2.4 What "differentiate with letters, substitute last" means when you are given numbers

Part (d) gives you $f(1) = 3$ and $g(1) = 6$ and no formulas for $f$ and $g$ themselves.
The temptation is to write $\frac{f(1)}{g(1)} = \frac{3}{6} = \frac12$ and differentiate that, which gives $0$.
The reason that is wrong is that $\frac12$ is the **value** of the quotient at one point and not the quotient.
So you write the quotient rule with letters:

$$\left.\left(\frac fg\right)'\right|_{x=1} = \frac{f'(1)g(1) - f(1)g'(1)}{\left[g(1)\right]^2}$$

and only then put the four numbers in.
The four numbers you need are $f'(1)$, $g(1)$, $f(1)$ and $g'(1)$, and exactly one of them, $g'(1)$, has to be computed rather than read off.

---

## 3. The universal procedure for a second derivative

Q8.1's procedure is unchanged for a first derivative.
This is the wrapper that turns it into a second-derivative procedure, and it is three steps longer.

> **Step A - Differentiate once, by Q8.1's procedure.**
> Last-operation test, write the rule with blanks, recurse, assemble.
> Nothing new.
>
> **Step B - Stop and look at $f'$. This is the step that does not exist in Q8.1.**
> Ask one question: *is this the shortest true expression for $f'$?*
> If a factor cancels, if two terms combine, if a bracket can be collapsed, do it **now**, before you differentiate again.
> Section 5 says why the risk calculation flips here.
>
> **Step C - Run the last-operation test AGAIN, on $f'$, from scratch.**
> Do not assume the rule is the same one you just used.
> Look at $f'$ as if you had never seen $f$.
>
> | $f'$ looks like | last operation | pass-2 rule | example |
> | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
> | a polynomial | $+$ and $-$ | sum and power | Q8.1a |
> | $c\cdot\left[T(u)\right]^2$ | squaring | **chain, power outer** | **Q8.2a** |
> | $T(u)\cdot S(u)$ | multiplying | **product** | $\sec x$, $\csc x$ |
> | $\dfrac{\text{poly}}{(\ )^n}$ | dividing | **quotient** | Q8.1b |
> | $c\cdot T(kx)$ | applying $T$ | chain, named outer, same as pass 1 | $\sin(2x)$ |
>
> **Step D - Differentiate $f'$.**
> Same procedure, same recursion.
>
> **Step E - Now apply Q8.1's policy again.**
> $f''$ **is** the answer, so simplify only if a factor obviously cancels.
> For part (a) the two $\csc$ factors have already combined by themselves, and there is nothing left to do.
>
> **Step F - Check with a SECOND difference, not a first one.**
> Section 6, and read the $h$ advice there rather than reusing Q8.1's.

**The tree for part (a), which is the only part that needs one.**

```
             d^2/dx^2  cot(2x)
                     |
        PASS 1: last op is a NAMED FUNCTION
                     |
              >>> CHAIN RULE <<<
              -csc^2(2x) * 2  =  -2 csc^2(2x)
                     |
        STOP.  Is f' in its shortest form?   YES
                     |
        PASS 2: last op is now a POWER, ( )^2
                     |
              >>> CHAIN RULE, power outer <<<
              -2 * 2 csc(2x) * d/dx csc(2x)
                     |
              = 8 csc^2(2x) cot(2x)
```

The one thing to take from that picture is that **the two boxes announce different rules**.
Pass 1 says "named outer" and pass 2 says "power outer", and the only reason to know that is that you asked the question twice instead of assuming.

The figure was checked structurally rather than by eye: it is pure ASCII so it cannot mojibake under a local `file://` render, every line fits in 78 columns, and no announced rule node is orphaned, meaning every `>>>` line has a connector glyph on the non-blank line above it.
All three gates were then proved live against seeded violations.

## 4. Q8.2 worked, part by part

### Part (a) - $\dfrac{d^2}{dx^2}\cot(2x)$

This is the part worth working four ways, because the four ways differ in cost by a factor of four.

#### Route A - chain rule, then the squared-trig rule (use this one)

Pass 1.
The last operation is $\cot$ applied to $2x$, so it is a chain rule with a named outer.
$\frac{d}{dx}\cot u = -\csc^2 u$, and $u' = 2$:

$$f' = -\csc^2(2x)\cdot 2 = -2\csc^2(2x)$$

Step B.
Is that the shortest form?
Yes.
There is one term, one coefficient, no brackets to collapse.

Pass 2.
The last operation in $-2\csc^2(2x)$ is the **squaring**, so this is a chain rule with a power outer, and section 2.3 gives it directly:

$$f'' = -2\cdot\left[2\csc(2x)\cdot\left(-\csc(2x)\cot(2x)\right)\cdot 2\right] = -2\cdot\left(-4\csc^2(2x)\cot(2x)\right)$$

$$\boxed{f'' = 8\csc^2(2x)\cot(2x)}$$

**Where the 8 comes from is worth naming, because the wrong coefficient is the commonest wrong answer here.**
It is $2 \times 2 \times 2$: one factor of 2 from the power rule on the square, one from the chain rule on the inner $2x$ during pass 2, and one from the coefficient $-2$ that pass 1 produced.
Miss any one of them and you write 4 instead of 8.
The sign is $(-2)\times(-1) = +$, where the $-2$ is pass 1's coefficient and the $-1$ is the minus in $\frac{d}{dx}\csc = -\csc\cot$.
Two minus signs, so the answer is positive, which surprises people who expect a second derivative of a decreasing function to stay negative.

#### Route B - the Pythagorean rewrite

Rewrite $f'$ before differentiating it, using $\csc^2 u = 1 + \cot^2 u$:

$$f' = -2\csc^2(2x) = -2\left(1 + \cot^2(2x)\right) = -2 - 2\cot^2(2x)$$

Now the constant differentiates away and the second term is a power of $\cot$:

$$f'' = -2\cdot 2\cot(2x)\cdot\left(-\csc^2(2x)\right)\cdot 2 = 8\cot(2x)\csc^2(2x)$$

Same answer, same number of factors of 2, and the advantage is that $\frac{d}{dx}\cot = -\csc^2$ is a fact you used thirty seconds ago and $\frac{d}{dx}\csc = -\csc\cot$ is a different fact you have to recall.
**Route B needs one trig derivative and Route A needs two.**
It is the better route if $\csc$ is the derivative you are least sure of, which for most people it is.

#### Route C - convert to sines and cosines and use the quotient rule twice

$\cot(2x) = \dfrac{\cos 2x}{\sin 2x}$, so pass 1 is a quotient rule:

$$f' = \frac{-2\sin 2x\cdot\sin 2x - \cos 2x\cdot 2\cos 2x}{\sin^2 2x} = \frac{-2\left(\sin^2 2x + \cos^2 2x\right)}{\sin^2 2x} = \frac{-2}{\sin^2 2x}$$

which is $-2\csc^2(2x)$ again, so the route is correct.
Pass 2 is then a second quotient rule on $\dfrac{-2}{\sin^2 2x}$, or a power rule on $-2\left(\sin 2x\right)^{-2}$:

$$f'' = -2\cdot(-2)\left(\sin 2x\right)^{-3}\cdot 2\cos 2x = \frac{8\cos 2x}{\sin^3 2x}$$

That is the same function as $8\csc^2(2x)\cot(2x)$, verified as an identity over 14 sample points at $10^{-16}$ relative.
**It is also a perfectly acceptable final answer**, and if you cannot remember whether $\csc$ or $\sec$ is the reciprocal of sine, writing the answer in sines and cosines is strictly safer.

#### Route D - a memorised general formula

$$\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\cot(kx) = 2k^2\csc^2(kx)\cot(kx)$$

For $k=2$ that is $2\cdot 4 = 8$, and for $k=3$ it is $18$.
This was verified for $k = 1$ through $5$, each at its own safe evaluation point.
It is worth knowing as a **check** on the coefficient rather than as the method, because a formula you cannot re-derive is a formula you will misremember under pressure.

#### The route comparison

| route | trig derivatives needed | lines of algebra | risk | verdict |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **A - chain then squared-trig** | $\cot' $ and $\csc'$ | 3 | the coefficient 8 | the standard; write this |
| **B - Pythagorean rewrite** | $\cot'$ only | 3 | remembering the identity's direction | **fastest and safest if $\csc'$ is shaky** |
| C - sines and cosines | none | 7 | a long quotient rule twice | correct, slow, and it does prove the answer |
| D - memorised $2k^2$ formula | none | 1 | misremembering $2k^2$ as $k^2$ | a check, not a method |

**Under exam pressure, use Route A and check the coefficient against Route D's $2k^2$.**
That combination takes ninety seconds and it is self-verifying: if $2k^2 = 8$ and your chain of 2s also gave 8, two independent countings agree.
Route B is the one to switch to if you freeze on $\frac{d}{dx}\csc$.

### Part (b) - $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sec\left(x^2-3x\right)$

One chain rule with a named outer, which is Q8.1's Family 4 with a quadratic inner instead of a linear one.

$$\frac{d}{dx}\sec u = \sec u\tan u, \qquad u = x^2-3x, \qquad u' = 2x-3$$

$$f' = (2x-3)\sec\left(x^2-3x\right)\tan\left(x^2-3x\right)$$

Stop there.
There is nothing to simplify and the printed permission covers you.
The equivalent form $\dfrac{(2x-3)\sin\left(x^2-3x\right)}{\cos^2\left(x^2-3x\right)}$ is also correct and was verified as an identity, but it is longer, so writing it is pure risk.

Two structural facts worth carrying, both verified: $f'(1.5) = 0$ because the inner derivative $2x-3$ vanishes at the vertex of the parabola, and $f'(0) = 0$ because $\tan(0) = 0$.
If your answer does not vanish at $x = 1.5$, you have lost the inner derivative.

### Part (c) - $\dfrac{d}{dx}\dfrac{x^2-\cos 3x}{x\sin 2x}$

The last operation is a division, so this is the quotient rule.
What makes it a four-point part rather than a two-point one is that **both** halves need a rule of their own, and they need *different* rules.

| piece | what it is | rule for its derivative | result |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $u = x^2 - \cos 3x$ | a difference | sum rule, then chain on $\cos 3x$ | $u' = 2x + 3\sin 3x$ |
| $v = x\sin 2x$ | a **product** | product rule, with chain on $\sin 2x$ | $v' = \sin 2x + 2x\cos 2x$ |

**The sign in $u'$ is the first place marks go.**
$\frac{d}{dx}\left(-\cos 3x\right) = -\left(-\sin 3x\right)\cdot 3 = +3\sin 3x$.
Two minus signs, so the term is positive, and writing $-3\sin 3x$ is the plausible wrong answer.

**The product rule in $v'$ is the second place marks go.**
Q8.1 noted that the product rule is absent from Q8.1 itself, and here it is, buried one level down inside a quotient.
Taking $v' = 2x\cos 2x$, which is what you get if you differentiate only the trig factor, was seeded as a control and confirmed to be caught.

Assembling, with $u'v - uv'$ in that order:

$$f' = \frac{\left(2x+3\sin 3x\right)\left(x\sin 2x\right) - \left(x^2-\cos 3x\right)\left(\sin 2x + 2x\cos 2x\right)}{\left(x\sin 2x\right)^2}$$

That is the final answer.
Do not expand $\left(x\sin 2x\right)^2$ into $x^2\sin^2 2x$; the two are the same function, verified, and the first is shorter.
Do not distribute the numerator either, because it produces six terms and buys nothing.

### Part (d) - $\left.\dfrac{d}{dx}\dfrac{f}{g}\right|_{x=1}$

Write the rule with letters first.

$$\left.\left(\frac fg\right)'\right|_{x=1} = \frac{f'(1)\,g(1) - f(1)\,g'(1)}{\left[g(1)\right]^2}$$

Now collect the four numbers.

| needed | given as | value |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $f(1)$ | given directly | $3$ |
| $g(1)$ | given directly | $6$ |
| $f'(1)$ | $f'(x) = \sqrt x$, so $\sqrt 1$ | $1$ |
| $g'(1)$ | $g'(x) = 3\sin(\pi x/3)$, so $3\sin\frac\pi3$ | $3\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} = \frac{3\sqrt3}{2} \approx 2.598076$ |

$$= \frac{1\cdot 6 - 3\cdot\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}}{36} = \frac{6 - \frac{9\sqrt3}{2}}{36} = \frac{12 - 9\sqrt3}{72} = \boxed{\frac{4-3\sqrt3}{24}} \approx -0.0498397$$

All three intermediate forms were verified to be the same number, so any of them is a correct stopping point.
$\frac{4-3\sqrt3}{24}$ is the tidiest and it is what to write.

**Both traps in this part are silent, meaning they produce a plausible number rather than an error.**
A calculator in degrees evaluates $\sin(\pi/3)$ as $\sin(1.047^\circ) = 0.018277$ and gives $+0.162098$, which is the wrong sign and the wrong magnitude and looks perfectly reasonable on the page.
Substituting first gives exactly $0$, which also looks reasonable.
Neither is caught by re-reading your work, and both were seeded as controls and confirmed to be caught by the check in section 6.

**An end-to-end confirmation that this part's answer is right, independent of the quotient-rule formula.**
Concrete functions matching the given data exist:

$$F(x) = \tfrac23 x^{3/2} + \tfrac73, \qquad G(x) = -\tfrac9\pi\cos\frac{\pi x}{3} + 6 + \frac{9}{2\pi}$$

$F(1) = 3$ and $F'(x) = \sqrt x$; $G(1) = 6$ and $G'(x) = 3\sin\frac{\pi x}{3}$.
Numerically differentiating the actual quotient $F/G$ at $x = 1$ reproduces $-0.049839684279$, agreeing with $\frac{4-3\sqrt3}{24}$ to better than $10^{-9}$.
That check never touches the quotient rule, so it confirms the *answer* and not just the arithmetic.

## 5. The exam-ready write-up, and the inverted simplification policy

### The policy, which is Q8.1's policy with one clause added

Q8.1 states it: simplifying has zero marginal reward and non-zero marginal risk, so the default is to stop the moment the derivative is written.
That clause is about $f'$ **as an answer**.
Q8.2 adds the case where it is not one.

> **When $f'$ is an intermediate result, simplifying it has real marginal reward, because every factor you carry forward gets differentiated too.**
> So: tidy $f'$ before pass 2, and leave $f''$ alone once you have it.

The test for which regime you are in is one question: **is there another differentiation coming?**
If yes, tidy.
If no, stop.

| case | tidy it? | why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $f'$ in parts (b), (c), (d) | **no** | it is the answer; Q8.1's policy applies unchanged |
| $f'$ in part (a), before pass 2 | **yes** | it is an input; a longer $f'$ means a longer $f''$ |
| $f''$ in part (a), after pass 2 | **no** | it is the answer again |
| a quotient's $f'$ before a second differentiation | **yes, and this is the expensive case** | see below |

**The row that costs whole minutes is the quotient one, and Q8.1(b) is the cleanest illustration.**
Its raw quotient-rule output is $\dfrac{2(x+3)^2 - 2(2x-16)(x+3)}{(x+3)^4}$ and its tidy form is $\dfrac{38-2x}{(x+3)^3}$, verified identical.
Differentiating the tidy form is one quotient rule with a linear numerator.
Differentiating the raw form is one quotient rule with a quadratic numerator over a quartic denominator, and then a cancellation of $(x+3)^5$ against $(x+3)^8$ at the end.
Same answer, four times the writing, four times the places to slip.

Part (a) is the easy case of this: $f' = -2\csc^2(2x)$ is already as short as it gets, so step B costs you three seconds and returns nothing.
**That is the normal outcome, and it is why the step gets skipped and why skipping it is expensive on the questions where it matters.**

### The short form, which is what to write if time is tight

> a. $\frac{d}{dx}\cot(2x) = -2\csc^2(2x)$, and differentiating again by the power chain rule, $\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\cot(2x) = 8\csc^2(2x)\cot(2x)$.
>
> b. By the chain rule, $\frac{d}{dx}\sec\left(x^2-3x\right) = (2x-3)\sec\left(x^2-3x\right)\tan\left(x^2-3x\right)$.
>
> c. By the quotient rule with $u = x^2-\cos 3x$ and $v = x\sin 2x$, so $u' = 2x+3\sin 3x$ and $v' = \sin 2x + 2x\cos 2x$:
> $\dfrac{\left(2x+3\sin 3x\right)\left(x\sin 2x\right) - \left(x^2-\cos 3x\right)\left(\sin 2x+2x\cos 2x\right)}{\left(x\sin 2x\right)^2}$.
>
> d. $\dfrac{f'(1)g(1) - f(1)g'(1)}{g(1)^2} = \dfrac{6 - 3\cdot\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}}{36} = \dfrac{4-3\sqrt3}{24}$.

### The full-credit form, which adds the clauses that show the method

The question says **"Show your work"**, which Q8.1's did not.
That raises the bar: a bare correct answer risks method marks, and the clauses below are what earn them.

> **a.** The outermost operation is $\cot$ applied to $2x$, so the first differentiation is the **chain rule** with $\frac{d}{du}\cot u = -\csc^2 u$ and $u = 2x$, $u' = 2$:
> $$\frac{d}{dx}\cot(2x) = -2\csc^2(2x).$$
> This is already in lowest terms, so I differentiate it as it stands.
> Its outermost operation is now a **square**, so the second differentiation is the chain rule in its generalized-power form, $\frac{d}{dx}\left[\csc u\right]^2 = 2\csc u\cdot\frac{d}{dx}\csc u$, with $\frac{d}{du}\csc u = -\csc u\cot u$:
> $$\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\cot(2x) = -2\cdot 2\csc(2x)\cdot\left(-\csc(2x)\cot(2x)\right)\cdot 2 = 8\csc^2(2x)\cot(2x).$$
> The three factors of 2 are the power rule, the inner derivative of $2x$, and the coefficient carried from the first differentiation; the two minus signs cancel.
>
> **b.** The outermost operation is $\sec$ applied to a polynomial, so this is the **chain rule** with $\frac{d}{du}\sec u = \sec u\tan u$, $u = x^2-3x$ and $u' = 2x-3$:
> $$\frac{d}{dx}\sec\left(x^2-3x\right) = (2x-3)\sec\left(x^2-3x\right)\tan\left(x^2-3x\right).$$
>
> **c.** The outermost operation is a division, so this is the **quotient rule** $\left(\frac uv\right)' = \frac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$ with $u = x^2-\cos 3x$ and $v = x\sin 2x$.
> Then $u' = 2x + 3\sin 3x$ **by the chain rule on $\cos 3x$**, where the two minus signs make the term positive, and $v' = \sin 2x + 2x\cos 2x$ **by the product rule**, with the chain rule inside the second term.
> $$\frac{d}{dx}\frac{x^2-\cos 3x}{x\sin 2x} = \frac{\left(2x+3\sin 3x\right)\left(x\sin 2x\right) - \left(x^2-\cos 3x\right)\left(\sin 2x+2x\cos 2x\right)}{\left(x\sin 2x\right)^2}.$$
>
> **d.** By the **quotient rule**, evaluated after differentiating rather than before:
> $$\left.\left(\frac fg\right)'\right|_{x=1} = \frac{f'(1)g(1)-f(1)g'(1)}{\left[g(1)\right]^2}.$$
> Here $f'(1) = \sqrt 1 = 1$ and $g'(1) = 3\sin\frac\pi3 = \frac{3\sqrt3}{2}$, the angle being **in radians**, so
> $$= \frac{1\cdot 6 - 3\cdot\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}}{6^2} = \frac{6-\frac{9\sqrt3}{2}}{36} = \frac{4-3\sqrt3}{24} \approx -0.0498.$$

Naming the rule in each part costs one clause and it is exactly what Q8.4 asks for explicitly.

## 6. Verify before you commit

### The check for a second derivative, and why Q8.1's advice does not transfer

Q8.1's check is a centred **first** difference, $\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x-h)}{2h}$, and its advice is that $h = 0.001$ gives five good digits and smaller is harmless.
The analogue for $f''$ is the centred **second** difference:

> $$f''(x) \approx \frac{f(x+h) - 2f(x) + f(x-h)}{h^2}$$
>
> Three evaluations, one subtraction pattern, and a division by $h^2$.
> **Use $h = 0.001$. Do not go smaller.**

The reason to state the $h$ so firmly is that the division by $h^2$ changes the arithmetic completely.
A calculator holds about ten significant digits, so each $f$ value carries an absolute error near $10^{-10}$; dividing by $h^2$ multiplies that error by $1/h^2$ instead of $1/h$.
At $h = 10^{-5}$ that is a factor of $10^{10}$, which is all of your precision.

Here is that measured on a simulated ten-digit machine, relative error in $f''$, five different functions:

| function and point | $h=0.1$ | $h=0.01$ | $h=0.001$ | $h=10^{-4}$ | $h=10^{-5}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\cot(2x)$ at $0.7$ | $2.9\times10^{-2}$ | $2.8\times10^{-4}$ | $\mathbf{6.5\times10^{-6}}$ | $9.8\times10^{-5}$ | $5.6\times10^{-2}$ |
| $x^2\sin x$ at $1.0$ | $3.8\times10^{-3}$ | $3.8\times10^{-5}$ | $\mathbf{3.4\times10^{-6}}$ | $2.3\times10^{-4}$ | $8.9\times10^{-4}$ |
| $\frac{1}{x^2+1}$ at $0.5$ | $3.0\times10^{-2}$ | $3.0\times10^{-4}$ | $\mathbf{3.4\times10^{-10}}$ | $3.9\times10^{-8}$ | $2.2\times10^{-1}$ |
| $\tan(3x)$ at $0.5$ | $1.1$ | $2.2\times10^{-1}$ | $\mathbf{1.8\times10^{-3}}$ | $1.9\times10^{-5}$ | $5.8\times10^{-5}$ |
| $\sqrt{2x+1}$ at $1.1$ | $1.2\times10^{-3}$ | $\mathbf{1.3\times10^{-5}}$ | $4.1\times10^{-5}$ | $3.0\times10^{-2}$ | $1.0$ |

Read that table as a **valley**, not a slope.
Error falls as $h$ shrinks because the truncation term shrinks, then rises because the roundoff term grows, and the bottom of the valley is at $h = 0.001$ for four of the five.
$h=0.001$ gives at least three correct significant figures on every one, which is all a check needs.
$h = 0.01$ fails that bar on $\tan(3x)$, where it is off by 22 percent.
$h = 10^{-5}$ gives relative errors up to $1.0$, meaning **no correct figures at all** on two of the five, and the collapse from $h=0.001$ is a factor of 556 on the worst function and $6\times10^8$ on $\frac{1}{x^2+1}$.

**The one-sentence version: for $f'$ a smaller $h$ was free, and for $f''$ it is ruinous, so pick $0.001$ and stop.**
Every number in that table was measured on a machine deliberately truncated to ten significant digits, not estimated.

### The check table for this question

| part | $x$ | $f(x)$ | your answer at $x$ | what the calculator shows | agrees to |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| a ($f''$) | $0.5$ | $\cot 1 = 0.6420926$ | $8\csc^2 1\cot 1 = 7.2545315$ | $7.2545700$ | 5 figures |
| b ($f'$) | $1$ | $\sec(-2) = -2.4029980$ | $5.2506463$ | $5.2507011$ | 4 figures |
| c ($f'$) | $1$ | $2.1884946$ | $2.4797582$ | $2.4797676$ | 5 figures |
| d | $1$ | $\tfrac36 = 0.5$ | $-0.0498397$ | $-0.0498397$ | exact, by construction |

For part (a) it is worth also knowing that $f'(0.5) = -2\csc^2 1 = -2.8245659$, because a wrong $f'$ makes a wrong $f''$ and it is cheaper to find out which of the two passes broke.

**What the check catches.**
If you lose one factor of 2 in part (a) and write $4\csc^2(2x)\cot(2x)$, the calculator reads $7.25$ and your answer says $3.63$, and the check screams.
If you drop the inner derivative in part (b), the check screams.
If you forget the product rule inside part (c)'s denominator, the check screams.
If your calculator is in degrees on part (d), the answer changes sign, and the check screams.
Every one of those four was seeded into the verification and confirmed to be caught.

### The cheap structural invariants

| part | invariant | why it holds |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| a | the argument stays $2x$ throughout, never becomes $4x$ or $x$ | the outer derivative never touches the inner function |
| a | $f''$ is **positive** where $\cot(2x)$ is positive | $\csc^2 > 0$ always, so $f''$ carries $\cot$'s sign |
| a | the coefficient is $2k^2$ with $k=2$, so $8$ | Route D, and it is an independent count of the 2s |
| a | $f''$ vanishes exactly where $f$ does, at $x = \pi/4$ | both carry a factor of $\cot(2x)$ |
| b | $f'$ vanishes at $x = 1.5$ | the inner derivative $2x-3$ vanishes at the parabola's vertex |
| b | $\sec$ and $\tan$ have the **same** argument as the original $\sec$ | the outer derivative leaves the inner untouched |
| c | the denominator is the **square** of the original denominator | that is what $v^2$ means |
| c | $u'$ has a **plus** in front of $3\sin 3x$ | two minus signs from $-\cos$ |
| d | the answer is **negative** | $g$ is growing much faster than $f$ at $x=1$, so the ratio is falling |
| d | the answer's magnitude is small, near $0.05$ | numerator $6 - 7.79 = -1.79$ over denominator $36$ |

**The most useful one is part (d)'s sign.**
$f'(1) = 1$ and $g'(1) = 2.6$, so $g$ is outrunning $f$ and their ratio must be decreasing.
A positive answer on part (d) is wrong before you check anything else, and the degrees-mode trap produces exactly that.

### Numbers worth holding

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| part (a) at $x = \pi/8$, where $2x = \pi/4$ | $f = 1$, $f' = -4$, $f'' = 16$, all exact |
| part (a) at $x = \pi/12$, where $2x = \pi/6$ | $f = \sqrt3$, $f' = -8$, $f'' = 32\sqrt3 \approx 55.4256$ |
| part (a)'s general coefficient | $\dfrac{d^2}{dx^2}\cot(kx) = 2k^2\csc^2(kx)\cot(kx)$ |
| part (d)'s two given derivatives at $x=1$ | $f'(1) = 1$ and $g'(1) = \frac{3\sqrt3}{2} \approx 2.598076$ |
| part (d)'s answer | $\dfrac{4-3\sqrt3}{24} \approx -0.0498397$ |
| the degrees-mode wrong answer for (d) | $+0.162098$, positive, which is the tell |

$x = \pi/8$ is the point to rehearse part (a) at, because $\csc^2(\pi/4) = 2$ and $\cot(\pi/4) = 1$ make $f'' = 8\cdot 2\cdot 1 = 16$ with no decimals anywhere.
If you can produce $1$, $-4$, $16$ from memory you have the whole part.

## 7. Answer-entry rules

Both exams are delivered through Möbius, answer-only and machine-marked, so a right derivative with a bad keystroke scores zero.
Q8.1 section 7 has the general rules; these are the ones this question adds.

| do | do not |
| :--- | :--- |
| write $\csc^2(2x)$ as `csc(2*x)^2`, with the exponent on the closing bracket | `csc^2(2*x)`, which most parsers read as $\csc$ raised to the power of $2(2x)$ |
| preview part (a) and confirm `csc` and `cot` render; if they do not, use `8*cos(2*x)/sin(2*x)^3` | assuming every parser defines all six trig functions |
| bracket the whole numerator **and** the whole denominator in part (c) | relying on precedence across a fifty-character expression |
| keep $\left(x\sin 2x\right)^2$ as `(x*sin(2*x))^2` | `x*sin(2*x)^2`, which squares only the sine |
| enter part (d) as the exact surd `(4-3*sqrt(3))/24` | `-0.0498`, which a numeric-tolerance field may accept and an exact field will not |
| **preview every answer before submitting** | trusting that what you typed is what it read |

**The single most expensive typo in this question** is the exponent position on part (a).
`csc(2*x)^2` is $\left[\csc(2x)\right]^2$ and `csc^2(2*x)` is not a thing most parsers accept at all, so the second one either errors or silently parses as something else.
Section 2.2 is the same distinction on paper, and it costs marks in both places.

**The second most expensive** is `x*sin(2*x)^2` in part (c)'s denominator.
It reads as $x\sin^2(2x)$ rather than $x^2\sin^2(2x)$, differs from the right answer by a whole factor of $x$, and looks completely normal.
The preview shows the difference immediately.

Unsimplified answers are accepted, because Möbius grades by algebraic equivalence rather than by string match.
So part (a) can be entered in any of the four verified equivalent forms, and part (c) can be entered exactly as the quotient rule produced it.
**That is the safety valve: when you are unsure of an algebraic step, enter the form you are sure of.**
