# Q12.1 - Approximate a square root with differentials

**The question (Midterm Exam 1, item 9, 5 points).**
"Use differentials to find the approximate value of $\sqrt{9.2}$."

**The answer.** $\sqrt{9.2} \approx 3 + \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{91}{30} \approx 3.0333$

**What to type into Möbius:** `91/30`

Provenance: parsed from `notes\MATH265\MATH265.md`, not typed.
MT1's ten printed values are 5, 6, 5, 16, 8, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5, summing to 64, and item 9 is worth 5 of them - 7.8125 percent of the paper.
MT1 carries exactly one "no credit will be given" clause and it sits on item 3, and its single "You may not need to simplify" permission sits on item 5, so item 9 has neither.
Verification: 440 assertions pass, 0 fail, 68 of them seeded controls proving the gates can bite.

**This question opens category 12, and the category spans all three papers.**
Q12.1 is MT1 item 9 (5 points), Q12.2 is MT2 item 8 (6 points, "use linearization to estimate $\sin 62^\circ$"), and Q12.3 is Final Exam 1 item 2 (8 points, "estimate to four decimal places").
That is **19 points across three separate papers** for one idea.
Everything below section 3 is written to serve all three, so read this one properly and Q12.2 and Q12.3 become re-runs of it with a different $f$.

---

## 0. The 30-second version

```
IDENTIFY f                 you are asked for a NUMBER that is f(something)
                           sqrt(9.2)  ==>  f(x) = sqrt(x)

CHOOSE THE ANCHOR a        the NEAREST x where f(a) is EXACT and you know it cold
                           9 is a perfect square, sqrt(9) = 3 exactly       <- the craft
                           dx = 9.2 - 9 = +0.2                              <- small

DIFFERENTIATE ONCE         f'(x) = 1/(2 sqrt x)      f'(9) = 1/(2*3) = 1/6

BUILD dy                   dy = f'(a) dx = (1/6)(0.2) = 1/30

ADD                        f(a + dx) ~ f(a) + dy = 3 + 1/30 = 91/30 = 3.0333

SAY WHICH WAY IT LEANS     f'' = -1/(4 x^1.5) < 0, so f is CONCAVE DOWN,
                           so the tangent line sits ABOVE the curve
                           ==> the estimate is TOO BIG.  It is, by 0.00018.
```

Five lines, one derivative, no calculator.
If it needs a lookup, you have chosen the wrong anchor.

---

## 1. What this question is really testing

| The reflex it drills | Where it comes back |
| :--- | :--- |
| A derivative is a **local linear model**, not just a slope | Q12.2, Q12.3, Q13.1 (Newton's method is this idea iterated) |
| Choosing an anchor where the function is **exactly known** | every approximation question in the course |
| $dy = f'(a)\,dx$ and $L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$ are **the same object** | Q9.1 (the tangent line), Q12.2, Q12.3 |
| Reading concavity to get the **sign of the error** | Q14.1 (curve sketching), Q15.x (second-derivative test) |
| Saying what a number is worth rather than writing more digits | Q12.3, which demands four decimal places |
| The chain factor $f'(a)$ multiplies $dx$ | Q10.1 ($y'$), Q11.1 ($dh/dt$) - MT1 items 7, 8 and 9 in a row |

**MT1 items 7, 8 and 9 are the same idea three times.**
Item 7 is related rates, item 8 is implicit differentiation, item 9 is this.
In all three the marks live on a factor that a careless student drops: $dh/dt$, $y'$, and $f'(a)$.
Fifteen of MT1's 64 points sit on that one habit.

---

## 2. The four things you must have cold

**1. The linearization, and the differential, which are one formula in two costumes.**

| Written as | Says | Use it when |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$ | the tangent line at $a$, as a function | you are asked for the **line**, or for $f$ at several nearby points |
| $f(a + dx) \approx f(a) + f'(a)\,dx$ | the same line, evaluated once | you are asked for **one number** |
| $dy = f'(a)\,dx$, $\Delta y \approx dy$ | just the **change**, not the value | you are asked for an **error** or a change |

They are not three formulas.
$dy$ is the second one with $f(a)$ moved to the other side.
The exam uses all three wordings: "use differentials", "use linearization", "estimate the error".

**2. The derivative of a root, in the form you actually need.**

| $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ | $f'(a)$ at the usual anchors |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2}$ | $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$ | $f'(4) = \tfrac14$, $f'(9) = \tfrac16$, $f'(16) = \tfrac18$, $f'(25) = \tfrac1{10}$, $f'(100) = \tfrac1{20}$ |
| $\sqrt[3]{x} = x^{1/3}$ | $\dfrac{1}{3x^{2/3}}$ | $f'(8) = \tfrac1{12}$, $f'(27) = \tfrac1{27}$, $f'(64) = \tfrac1{48}$ |
| $x^{1/n}$ | $\dfrac{1}{n\,x^{(n-1)/n}}$ | $f'(32)$ for $n=5$ is $\tfrac1{80}$ |

Read the middle column as **structure, not as three facts**: for $f = x^{1/n}$ the derivative at a perfect $n$-th power $a = m^n$ is always $\dfrac{1}{n\,m^{n-1}}$, a unit fraction.
That is why the anchor is always a perfect power - it is the only way $f'(a)$ comes out clean too.

**3. Concavity decides the direction of the error, and nothing else does.**

| $f''(a)$ | shape | tangent line sits | your estimate is |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $f'' < 0$ | concave down | **above** the curve | too **big** |
| $f'' > 0$ | concave up (convex) | **below** the curve | too **small** |

This does not depend on which way $dx$ points.
For $\sqrt{x}$, $f''(x) = -\dfrac{1}{4x^{3/2}} < 0$ on the whole domain, so **every square-root estimate by this method is too big**, whether you step up or step down.
Verified on 72 anchor-and-offset pairs, both directions, all 72 above the curve.

**4. The size of the error, so you know what the answer is worth.**

$$\text{true} - \text{estimate} = \frac{f''(\xi)}{2}(dx)^2 \quad \text{for some } \xi \text{ between } a \text{ and } a+dx$$

For $\sqrt{x}$ that is $\left|\text{error}\right| \le \dfrac{(dx)^2}{8\,a^{3/2}}$ when $dx > 0$.
Here: $\dfrac{0.04}{8 \cdot 27} = \dfrac{0.04}{216} = 0.0001852$.
The error actually observed is $0.0001832$, which is 98.9 percent of the bound.
**The error is second order in $dx$**: halve the step and the error drops by four.
Measured at $dx = 0.4, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05$ - the ratio came out 4.00 every time.

---

## 3. The universal procedure

> 1. **Name $f$.** The quantity asked for must be $f$ of something. $\sqrt{9.2}$ means $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ evaluated at $9.2$.
> 2. **Choose the anchor $a$.** The nearest point where $f(a)$ is exact and you know it without a calculator. This step is the whole question.
> 3. **Write $dx = (\text{target}) - a$.** Keep the sign. If $dx$ is not small, go back to step 2.
> 4. **Differentiate once and evaluate at $a$**, not at the target.
> 5. **Form $dy = f'(a)\,dx$** and add it to $f(a)$.
> 6. **State the direction** from the sign of $f''$, and the size from $(dx)^2 f''/2$.
> 7. **Round to what the question asks**, and no further.

Step 2 in detail, because it is where the marks are.

| Target | Ask yourself | Anchor | Why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\sqrt{9.2}$ | nearest perfect square? | $9$ | $\sqrt9 = 3$; $16$ is 6.8 away |
| $\sqrt{16.4}$ | nearest perfect square? | $16$ | $\sqrt{16} = 4$ |
| $\sqrt[3]{26.8}$ | nearest perfect cube? | $27$ | $\sqrt[3]{27} = 3$; step *down* |
| $\sin 62^\circ$ | nearest special angle? | $60^\circ = \pi/3$ | $\sin 60^\circ = \sqrt3/2$ |
| $(2.01)^5$ | nearest round base? | $2$ | $2^5 = 32$ |
| $1/1.002$ | nearest round base? | $1$ | $1/1 = 1$ |
| $f(4.02)$, $f$ named | the question hands it to you | $4$ | it printed $f(4)$ for you |

**The test for a good anchor is not "is it round", it is "do I know $f(a)$ exactly".**
$a = 9$ is chosen for $\sqrt{9.2}$ not because 9 is tidy but because $\sqrt9 = 3$ on the nose.

---

## 4. Q12.1 worked four ways

### Route A - differentials, the wording the exam uses

$$f(x) = \sqrt{x}, \qquad a = 9, \qquad dx = 0.2$$
$$f(9) = 3, \qquad f'(x) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}, \qquad f'(9) = \frac{1}{2\cdot 3} = \frac16$$
$$dy = f'(9)\,dx = \frac16 \cdot \frac{1}{5} = \frac{1}{30}$$
$$\sqrt{9.2} \approx f(9) + dy = 3 + \frac{1}{30} = \frac{91}{30} \approx 3.0333$$

### Route B - linearization, the wording Q12.2 uses

$$L(x) = f(9) + f'(9)(x - 9) = 3 + \frac{1}{6}(x-9)$$
$$L(9.2) = 3 + \frac{1}{6}(0.2) = 3 + \frac{1}{30} = \frac{91}{30}$$

Identical, because it is the same line.
Route B is worth knowing because it answers "estimate $\sqrt{9.1}$ **and** $\sqrt{9.3}$" in one go, and because Q9.1's tangent line is literally this object.

### Route C - factor out the anchor (the binomial form)

$$\sqrt{9.2} = \sqrt{9\left(1 + \tfrac{0.2}{9}\right)} = 3\sqrt{1 + \tfrac{1}{45}}$$

Linearize $\sqrt{1+u}$ at $u = 0$, where it is $1 + \tfrac{u}{2}$:

$$\approx 3\left(1 + \frac{1}{90}\right) = 3 + \frac{1}{30}$$

Same answer, exactly, and this route is the fastest when the target is written as a percentage change ("estimate $\sqrt{x}$ if $x$ rises 2 percent").

### Route D - one Newton step, which is the same arithmetic

Newton's method on $g(x) = x^2 - 9.2$ from $x_0 = 3$:

$$x_1 = x_0 - \frac{g(x_0)}{g'(x_0)} = 3 - \frac{9 - 9.2}{6} = 3 + \frac{0.2}{6} = \frac{91}{30}$$

**This is not a coincidence.**
Linearizing $\sqrt{x}$ at $a$ gives $\sqrt a + \dfrac{N - a}{2\sqrt a} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\sqrt a + \dfrac{N}{\sqrt a}\right)$, which is exactly one Babylonian / Newton step.
Verified identical to machine precision at ten separate $(a, N)$ pairs.
Worth knowing because Q13.1 is Newton's method, and this tells you the two questions are neighbours.

### Route comparison

| Route | Steps | Where it goes wrong | Verdict |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| A differentials | 4 | none - shortest path | **use this one under pressure** |
| B linearization | 5 | an extra $(x-9)$ to carry and mis-sign | use when several targets share one anchor |
| C binomial | 5 | needs the $\sqrt{1+u} \approx 1 + u/2$ fact recalled | use for percentage-change wording |
| D Newton step | 4 | you must invert the problem to $x^2 = 9.2$ | use as a **check**, not as the answer |
| Calculator | 1 | the stem says "use differentials" - method instruction | **scores zero** |

**Use Route A.**
It is what the stem names, it is the fewest symbols, and it puts $f'(9)$ and $dx$ side by side where the marks are.

Route D is the best self-check in the whole question, because it uses none of the same algebra.
If $\tfrac12(3 + 9.2/3)$ does not give your answer, one of them is wrong.

---

## 5. The exam-ready write-up

There is **no published marking scheme** for this course - zero occurrences of "rubric", "marking scheme" or "part marks" across all four course files, re-verified this run - so what follows is inference about which sentences make the method visible, not a claim about points.

Six lines. Write all six.

> Let $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$.
> Take $a = 9$, since $\sqrt{9} = 3$ exactly and $9$ is the nearest perfect square to $9.2$; then $dx = 0.2$.
> $f'(x) = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$, so $f'(9) = \dfrac{1}{6}$.
> $dy = f'(9)\,dx = \dfrac{1}{6}(0.2) = \dfrac{1}{30}$.
> Therefore $\sqrt{9.2} \approx f(9) + dy = 3 + \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{91}{30} \approx 3.0333$.
> Since $f''(x) = -\dfrac{1}{4x^{3/2}} < 0$, $f$ is concave down and the tangent line lies above the curve, so this estimate is slightly too large.

The second line is the one most students skip and it is the only line that shows you **chose** the anchor rather than being handed it.
The sixth line costs eight seconds and is the only line that shows you know what an approximation is.

---

## 6. Verify before you commit

**Magnitude check.** $3^2 = 9$ and $3.1^2 = 9.61$. Since $9 < 9.2 < 9.61$, the answer must sit in $(3, 3.1)$. $3.0333$ does. This kills every gross slip in section 9 in about four seconds.

**The Newton cross-check.** $\tfrac12\!\left(3 + \tfrac{9.2}{3}\right) = \tfrac12(3 + 3.0\overline{6}) = 3.0\overline{3}$. Agrees.

**Square it back.** $\left(\tfrac{91}{30}\right)^2 = \tfrac{8281}{900} = 9.2011\ldots$, which is a little **above** 9.2 - confirming the estimate is a little too big, exactly as concavity predicted. This is the best single check in the question: it verifies the value *and* the direction at once.

**Numbers worth memorising for this family.**

| Fact | Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| $f'(a)$ for $\sqrt{x}$ at $4, 9, 16, 25, 100$ | $\tfrac14, \tfrac16, \tfrac18, \tfrac1{10}, \tfrac1{20}$ |
| $1^\circ$ in radians | $\pi/180 \approx 0.01745$ |
| $2^\circ$ in radians | $\pi/90 \approx 0.03491$ |
| $\sqrt{1+u} \approx 1 + u/2$ | for small $u$ |
| $(1+u)^n \approx 1 + nu$ | for small $u$ |
| error $\approx \tfrac12 f''(a)(dx)^2$ | second order |

**The check that CANNOT fail, and why it matters.**
A spot-check at $dx = 0$ agrees with the truth for five of the eight standard wrong answers, because they all differ from the truth only by a factor multiplying $dy$, and $dy$ is zero there.
**Never sanity-check this method at the anchor itself.**
This is the exact analogue of the zero-rate blind spot in related rates: at $dV/dt = 0$ every wrong cone formula gives zero too.

---

## 7. Answer-entry rules

| Do | Do not |
| :--- | :--- |
| `91/30` | `91/3 0` - a stray space |
| `3+1/30` | `3+1/2*sqrt(9)` - this is $3 + 1.5$; the bracket around $2\sqrt9$ is not optional |
| `3+0.2/6` | `3+0.2/2*3` - parses as $3 + 0.1 \cdot 3 = 3.3$ |
| `3.0333` if a decimal is demanded | `3.0332` - that is the *true* value, not the estimate the method gives |
| `3.033` if three places are asked | `3.03` - $3\times10^{-3}$ away, outside a $10^{-4}$ tolerance |
| Type `*` between every factor, then **Preview** | assume the box knows what you meant |

**The single most expensive typo is `1/2*sqrt(9)` for $f'(9)$.**
It evaluates to $1.5$ rather than $0.1\overline{6}$ - a factor of nine - and gives $3.3$, which is still inside the plausible range for a square root and so will not look wrong.
Write $f'(9)$ as `1/6` and the typo cannot happen.

**The second most expensive is entering the true value.**
If the box wants four decimals, the answer this method produces is `3.0333`, not `3.0332`.
The true $\sqrt{9.2}$ is $3.03315018$, which rounds to $3.0332$ - see section 8, Family 7.
The question asked for the differential estimate, so `3.0333` is the answer even though it is the less accurate number.

---

## 8. The variation catalog

Eight families, grouped by **the tool the variation forces**, not by how the question looks.
Every value below was recomputed independently: each estimate from a closed form *and* from a complex-step derivative that never sees the formula, each true value by direct evaluation.

### Family 0 - a root of a nearby perfect power

**Trigger.** A root of a number that sits just off a perfect square, cube or $n$-th power.
**Tool.** $f = x^{1/n}$, anchor at the nearest perfect $n$-th power, $f'(a) = \dfrac{1}{n\,m^{n-1}}$ with $a = m^n$.
**This is Q12.1 itself, and Q12.3(b).**

| Target | $a$ | $f(a)$ | $f'(a)$ | $dx$ | Estimate (exact) | Estimate | True | Error |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $\sqrt{9.2}$ | 9 | 3 | $1/6$ | $+0.2$ | $91/30$ | 3.0333333 | 3.0331502 | $-1.832\times10^{-4}$ |
| $\sqrt{16.4}$ | 16 | 4 | $1/8$ | $+0.4$ | $81/20$ | 4.0500000 | 4.0496913 | $-3.087\times10^{-4}$ |
| $\sqrt{4.1}$ | 4 | 2 | $1/4$ | $+0.1$ | $81/40$ | 2.0250000 | 2.0248457 | $-1.543\times10^{-4}$ |
| $\sqrt{101}$ | 100 | 10 | $1/20$ | $+1$ | $201/20$ | 10.0500000 | 10.0498756 | $-1.244\times10^{-4}$ |
| $\sqrt{24.6}$ | 25 | 5 | $1/10$ | $-0.4$ | $124/25$ | 4.9600000 | 4.9598387 | $-1.613\times10^{-4}$ |
| $\sqrt{0.26}$ | $1/4$ | $1/2$ | $1$ | $+0.01$ | $51/100$ | 0.5100000 | 0.5099020 | $-9.805\times10^{-5}$ |
| $\sqrt{37}$ | 36 | 6 | $1/12$ | $+1$ | $73/12$ | 6.0833333 | 6.0827625 | $-5.708\times10^{-4}$ |
| $\sqrt{48.6}$ | 49 | 7 | $1/14$ | $-0.4$ | $244/35$ | 6.9714286 | 6.9713700 | $-5.855\times10^{-5}$ |
| $\sqrt[3]{8.3}$ | 8 | 2 | $1/12$ | $+0.3$ | $81/40$ | 2.0250000 | 2.0246939 | $-3.061\times10^{-4}$ |
| $\sqrt[3]{26.8}$ | 27 | 3 | $1/27$ | $-0.2$ | $404/135$ | 2.9925926 | 2.9925742 | $-1.837\times10^{-5}$ |
| $\sqrt[3]{63.5}$ | 64 | 4 | $1/48$ | $-0.5$ | $1915/480$ | 3.9895833 | 3.9895561 | $-2.725\times10^{-5}$ |
| $(32.2)^{1/5}$ | 32 | 2 | $1/80$ | $+0.2$ | $801/400$ | 2.0025000 | 2.0024938 | $-6.227\times10^{-6}$ |
| $(15.9)^{1/4}$ | 16 | 2 | $1/32$ | $-0.1$ | $639/320$ | 1.9968750 | 1.9968676 | $-7.351\times10^{-6}$ |

**Read this table as structure, not as thirteen facts.**
Every $f'(a)$ is a **unit fraction** - that is the signature of a correctly chosen anchor, and if yours is not one, you picked the wrong $a$.
Every error is **negative**, in both directions of travel, because a root is concave down.
The errors span $6\times10^{-6}$ to $6\times10^{-4}$, and they sort exactly by $(dx)^2 / a^{3/2}$: big steps off small anchors are the bad ones.

**$\sqrt{0.26}$ is the trap row.** At $a = 1/4$ the derivative $f'(a) = 1$ exactly, so a student who forgets to multiply by $f'(a)$ gets $0.5 + 0.01 = 0.51$ - the right answer, for the wrong reason. Confirmed bit-identical. If a question ever anchors at $1/4$, your slip is invisible.

### Family 1 - a trig value near a special angle, stated in degrees

**Trigger.** $\sin$, $\cos$ or $\tan$ of an angle a degree or two from $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ or $60^\circ$.
**Tool.** Anchor at the special angle **in radians**, and convert $dx$ to radians. **This is Q12.2 and Q12.3(a).**

| Target | $a$ | $dx$ (rad) | Estimate | True | Error | Direction |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | :--- |
| $\sin 62^\circ$ | $\pi/3$ | $+0.0349066$ | 0.8834787 | 0.8829476 | $-5.311\times10^{-4}$ | over |
| $\cos 62^\circ$ | $\pi/3$ | $+0.0349066$ | 0.4697700 | 0.4694716 | $-2.984\times10^{-4}$ | over |
| $\sin 29^\circ$ | $\pi/6$ | $-0.0174533$ | 0.4848850 | 0.4848096 | $-7.539\times10^{-5}$ | over |
| $\cos 31^\circ$ | $\pi/6$ | $+0.0174533$ | 0.8572988 | 0.8571673 | $-1.315\times10^{-4}$ | over |
| $\tan 44^\circ$ | $\pi/4$ | $-0.0174533$ | 0.9650934 | 0.9656888 | $+5.954\times10^{-4}$ | **under** |
| $\sin 46^\circ$ | $\pi/4$ | $+0.0174533$ | 0.7194481 | 0.7193398 | $-1.083\times10^{-4}$ | over |
| $\cos 59^\circ$ | $\pi/3$ | $-0.0174533$ | 0.5151150 | 0.5150381 | $-7.692\times10^{-5}$ | over |
| $\tan 61^\circ$ | $\pi/3$ | $+0.0174533$ | 1.8018640 | 1.8040478 | $+2.184\times10^{-3}$ | **under** |

**The signs are generated by concavity, not by memory.**
On $(0, \pi/2)$, $\sin'' = -\sin < 0$ and $\cos'' = -\cos < 0$, so both overshoot; $\tan'' = 2\sec^2 x \tan x > 0$, so tan undershoots.
"Trig always overestimates" is **false** - the two tan rows prove it.

**Only two distinct increments appear** in the whole family: $\pi/180 \approx 0.0174533$ and $\pi/90 \approx 0.0349066$. Learn those two numbers and the family costs nothing.

**The catastrophic slip is using $dx = 2$ instead of $2^\circ$.**
$\sin 62^\circ$ then comes out $1.866$, which is not even in $[-1,1]$. It is 0.98 away from the truth. If your trig estimate leaves $[-1,1]$, you forgot to convert.

### Family 2 - powers, reciprocals and mixed exponents

**Trigger.** $(2.01)^5$, $1/1.002$, $(1.97)^3$, $(8.06)^{2/3}$ - a power of a number near a round base.
**Tool.** $f = x^p$, $f'(a) = p\,a^{p-1}$. The over/under rule is entirely the sign of $p(p-1)$.

| Target | $a$ | $f(a)$ | $f'(a)$ | Estimate | True | Error | Direction |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | :--- |
| $(2.01)^5$ | 2 | 32 | 80 | 32.8 | 32.8080401 | $+8.040\times10^{-3}$ | under |
| $(1.97)^3$ | 2 | 8 | 12 | 7.64 | 7.6453730 | $+5.373\times10^{-3}$ | under |
| $(1.02)^{10}$ | 1 | 1 | 10 | 1.2 | 1.2189944 | $+1.899\times10^{-2}$ | under |
| $1/1.002$ | 1 | 1 | $-1$ | 0.998 | 0.9980040 | $+3.992\times10^{-6}$ | under |
| $1/\sqrt{4.02}$ | 4 | 0.5 | $-1/16$ | 0.49875 | 0.4987547 | $+4.668\times10^{-6}$ | under |
| $(8.06)^{2/3}$ | 8 | 4 | $1/3$ | 4.02 | 4.0199751 | $-2.492\times10^{-5}$ | **over** |

**The rule that generates every direction in this table:** $x^p$ is convex for $p>1$ or $p<0$ (undershoot), and concave for $0<p<1$ (overshoot).
So every root overshoots and every whole power and every reciprocal undershoots.
$(8.06)^{2/3}$ is the only concave row, and it is the only "over".

**$(1.02)^{10}$ is this family's warning.**
$dx = 0.02$ is tiny, and the estimate is still 1.6 percent low, because $f''(1) = 90$.
**A small $dx$ does not by itself make a good estimate** - the error is $\tfrac12 f''(dx)^2$, and $f''$ gets a vote.

### Family 3 - a named $f$ with the anchor supplied

**Trigger.** "Let $f(x) = \frac{x-1}{\sqrt{x}}$. (a) Find the tangent line at $(4, f(4))$. (b) Use differentials to estimate $f(4.02)$."
**Tool.** Nothing new - but notice (a) and (b) are the **same computation asked twice**.

$$f(x) = \frac{x-1}{\sqrt x} = x^{1/2} - x^{-1/2}, \qquad f'(x) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt x} + \frac{1}{2x^{3/2}}$$
$$f(4) = \frac{3}{2}, \qquad f'(4) = \frac14 + \frac1{16} = \frac{5}{16}$$
$$\text{tangent: } y = \frac32 + \frac{5}{16}(x-4) = \frac{5}{16}x + \frac14$$
$$f(4.02) \approx \frac32 + \frac{5}{16}\cdot\frac{1}{50} = \frac32 + \frac{1}{160} = \frac{241}{160} = 1.50625$$

True value $1.5062391$, error $-1.090\times10^{-5}$, an overshoot as $f'' < 0$ predicts.
**Evaluating the part-(a) line at $4.02$ gives the part-(b) answer.** Verified identical.
Rewriting $\frac{x-1}{\sqrt x}$ as $x^{1/2} - x^{-1/2}$ before differentiating avoids the quotient rule entirely - that is the only real work in the question.

### Family 4 - propagating a measurement error

**Trigger.** "One side is 25 cm exactly. The opposite angle is $60^\circ$ with a possible error of $\pm 0.5^\circ$. Estimate the errors in the adjacent side and the hypotenuse, and the percentage errors."
**Tool.** $dy = f'(a)\,dx$ used as a **change**, not a value. Here $dx = d\theta$ must be in radians: $0.5^\circ = \pi/360 = 0.0087266$.

| Quantity | Formula | Value | Differential | $\approx$ | True change | Percentage error |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| adjacent | $25\cot\theta$ | $25/\sqrt3 = 14.4338$ | $-25\csc^2\theta\,d\theta = -\dfrac{5\pi}{54}$ | $-0.29089$ | $-0.28944$ | $2.0153\%$ |
| hypotenuse | $25\csc\theta$ | $50/\sqrt3 = 28.8675$ | $-25\csc\theta\cot\theta\,d\theta = -\dfrac{5\pi}{108}$ | $-0.14544$ | $-0.14362$ | $0.5038\%$ |

**The ratio of the two percentage errors is exactly $\sec^2 60^\circ = 4$.**
That is an identity, not a coincidence of these numbers: $\dfrac{\text{pct}_{\text{adj}}}{\text{pct}_{\text{hyp}}} = \sec^2\theta$ for every $\theta$, verified at $\pi/6$, $\pi/4$, $0.9$ and $1.3$ as well.
**The adjacent side is always the more sensitive of the two**, and past $45^\circ$ it is dramatically so.

**The 25 cm never appears in either percentage.** A percentage error is dimensionless and the constant cancels - which is why this part can be answered without touching the 25 at all.

### Family 5 - relative and percentage error for a power

**Trigger.** "A sphere's radius is measured as 10 cm with a possible error of 0.05 cm. Estimate the error in the volume, and the percentage error."
**Tool.** Divide $dy = f'(a)dx$ by $y = f(a)$. For $f = x^n$ every constant cancels:

$$\frac{dy}{y} = n\,\frac{dx}{x}$$

| Situation | $n$ | Absolute | Relative |
| :--- | ---: | :--- | :--- |
| sphere $V = \tfrac43\pi r^3$, $r = 10 \pm 0.05$ | 3 | $dV = 4\pi r^2 dr = 20\pi = 62.832$ | $3(0.05/10) = 1.5\%$ |
| cube $V = s^3$, $s = 12 \pm 0.1$ | 3 | $dV = 3s^2 ds = 43.2$ | $3(0.1/12) = 2.5\%$ |
| circle $A = \pi r^2$ | 2 | $dA = 2\pi r\,dr$ | $2\,dr/r$ |
| $\sqrt{x}$ | $1/2$ | | $\tfrac12 dx/x$ |
| $1/x$ | $-1$ | | $-dx/x$ |

**A relative error is multiplied by the exponent, and the constant in front is irrelevant.**
A sphere and a cube both give $3\,ds/s$, though their volumes differ by a factor of $\tfrac{4\pi}{3}$ against $1$.
That is the one sentence this family is testing.

The law is a property of powers only: for $\sin$, $\dfrac{dy}{y} = \cot(a)\,da$, which depends on $a$ and is not a constant multiple of $da/a$.

### Family 6 - "is your estimate too big or too small? justify"

**Trigger.** The question asks for the *direction*, with or without the number.
**Tool.** The sign of $f''$ on the interval, and one sentence about the tangent line.

| $f$ | $f''$ | Concavity | Estimate is |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\sqrt x$, $\sqrt[3]{x}$, $x^p$ for $0<p<1$ | $<0$ | down | too big |
| $x^n$ for $n>1$, $e^x$ | $>0$ | up | too small |
| $1/x$, $x^{-1/2}$ (for $x>0$) | $>0$ | up | too small |
| $\sin x$, $\cos x$ on $(0,\pi/2)$ | $<0$ | down | too big |
| $\tan x$ on $(0,\pi/2)$ | $>0$ | up | too small |
| $\ln x$ | $<0$ | down | too big |

**Answer it with the tangent line, not with the arithmetic.**
"$f'' < 0$ on this interval, so $f$ is concave down, so the tangent line lies above the graph, so the estimate exceeds the true value."
That sentence works without computing anything, and it works for negative $dx$ too.

**The trap:** the direction is not decided by the sign of $dx$. Both $\sqrt{9.2}$ (step up) and $\sqrt{24.6}$ (step down) overestimate.

### Family 7 - the error bound, and how many decimal places you may claim

**Trigger.** "Estimate to four decimal places", or "how accurate is your estimate", or "bound the error".
**Tool.** $\left|\text{error}\right| \le \dfrac{M}{2}(dx)^2$ where $M = \max|f''|$ **on the interval between $a$ and the target**.

| Target | Bound | Actual error | Ratio | Estimate to 4dp | True to 4dp |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $\sqrt{9.2}$ | $1.852\times10^{-4}$ | $1.832\times10^{-4}$ | 0.989 | 3.0333 | **3.0332** |
| $\sqrt{16.4}$ | $3.125\times10^{-4}$ | $3.087\times10^{-4}$ | 0.988 | 4.0500 | **4.0497** |
| $\sqrt{4.1}$ | $1.563\times10^{-4}$ | $1.543\times10^{-4}$ | 0.988 | 2.0250 | **2.0248** |
| $\sqrt{101}$ | $1.250\times10^{-4}$ | $1.244\times10^{-4}$ | 0.995 | 10.0500 | **10.0499** |
| $\sqrt[3]{8.3}$ | $3.125\times10^{-4}$ | $3.061\times10^{-4}$ | 0.980 | 2.0250 | **2.0247** |

**The bound is tight** - within 2 percent of the observed error every time - so it is worth quoting.

**Use the endpoint where $|f''|$ is largest, not automatically the anchor.**
For a root, $|f''|$ *decreases* with $x$, so when $dx > 0$ the anchor is the correct endpoint, but when $dx < 0$ it is not.
Worked instance: for $\sqrt{48.6}$ from $a = 49$, the anchor-based bound is $5.8309\times10^{-5}$ and the actual error is $5.8548\times10^{-5}$ - **the anchor bound is violated**. Using $48.6$ instead gives $5.9030\times10^{-5}$, which holds.

**Now the finding that matters most for Q12.3.**
Across all 21 entries in Families 0 and 1, **only 5 give four correct decimal places**, and 17 give three.
$\sqrt{9.2}$, $\sqrt{16.4}$ and $\cos 62^\circ$ - all three of category 12's four-decimal demands - are **wrong in the fourth decimal**.

So when F1 item 2 says "estimate each of the values below **to four decimal places**", it can only mean *write four decimals down*.
It cannot mean *guarantee four correct ones*, because the method cannot do that here, and the marker's own answer will be the differential value.
**Write the estimate to four places. Do not "improve" it toward the true value** - $3.0333$ is the answer, not $3.0332$.

One subtlety, since it looks like a contradiction: $(32.2)^{1/5}$ agrees with its true value at **four** places and disagrees at **three**, because $2.0025$ sits exactly on a three-place rounding tie. Rounding boundaries are not nested. Do not infer three-place accuracy from four-place agreement.

---

## 9. The trap list

Ranked by how often each actually costs marks.

1. **Evaluating $f'$ at the target instead of the anchor.** $f'(9.2)$ rather than $f'(9)$ gives $3.0329690$, which is off by $+1.8\times10^{-4}$ - *the same size as the correct answer's error, in the opposite direction*. It looks completely plausible. Worse, it becomes invisible as $dx \to 0$, so shrinking the step cannot expose it. The rule: **the anchor is where you know things; the target is where you want an answer. $f$ and $f'$ are both evaluated at the anchor.**

2. **Forgetting the $\tfrac12$ in $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sqrt x$.** Gives $3.0667$ - inside the plausible band, and exactly twice the correct $dy$. Kill it with the magnitude check: $3.0667^2 = 9.404$, not $9.2$.

3. **Using degrees where the formula needs radians** (Family 1). $\sin 62^\circ \approx 1.866$. The tell is an answer outside $[-1,1]$.

4. **Choosing a "prettier" anchor rather than a nearer one.** $a = 9.61 = 3.1^2$ is a genuinely exact anchor, and it is 3.94 times worse than $a=9$ because it is twice as far. $a = 16$ is 638 times worse. **Nearest wins, always** - the error goes as $(dx)^2$.

5. **Spot-checking at the anchor.** $dx = 0$ hides five of the eight standard wrong answers. See section 6.

6. **Reporting $dy$ instead of $f(a) + dy$.** Answer $0.0333$. The magnitude check catches it instantly.

7. **Sign slip on a negative $dx$.** For $\sqrt{24.6}$ from 25, $dx = -0.4$, and adding $+0.04$ gives $5.04$ instead of $4.96$. Write $dx = \text{target} - a$ every time and let the sign fall out.

8. **Claiming the true value.** Writing $3.0332$ because you checked on a calculator. The question asked for the differential estimate.

9. **Getting the over/under backwards** by reasoning from $dx>0$ instead of from $f''<0$.

10. **The invisible one: $f'(a) = 1$.** At $a = 1/4$ for $\sqrt x$, forgetting to multiply by $f'(a)$ is undetectable. Nothing catches this except doing it right.

---

## 10. Drill set

Do all twelve in fifteen minutes, closed book, no calculator. Leave every answer as an exact fraction, then say **over or under**.

1. Use differentials to approximate $\sqrt{4.1}$.
2. Use differentials to approximate $\sqrt{101}$.
3. Use differentials to approximate $\sqrt[3]{26.8}$.
4. Use differentials to approximate $\sqrt{0.26}$.
5. Use linearization to estimate $\sin 29^\circ$.
6. Use linearization to estimate $\tan 44^\circ$.
7. Estimate $(2.01)^5$.
8. Estimate $1/1.002$.
9. Let $f(x) = \dfrac{x-1}{\sqrt x}$. Estimate $f(4.02)$.
10. Estimate $\sqrt{48.6}$, and bound the error.
11. Estimate $(1.97)^3$.
12. Estimate $(8.06)^{2/3}$.

### Answer key

| # | Exact | Decimal | True value | Over/under | Family and method |
| ---: | :--- | ---: | ---: | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | $2 + \tfrac1{40} = \tfrac{81}{40}$ | 2.025 | 2.0248457 | over | F0, $a=4$, $f'=\tfrac14$ |
| 2 | $10 + \tfrac1{20} = \tfrac{201}{20}$ | 10.05 | 10.0498756 | over | F0, $a=100$, $f'=\tfrac1{20}$ |
| 3 | $3 - \tfrac1{135} = \tfrac{404}{135}$ | 2.9925926 | 2.9925742 | over | F0, $a=27$, $f'=\tfrac1{27}$, $dx<0$ |
| 4 | $\tfrac12 + \tfrac1{100} = \tfrac{51}{100}$ | 0.51 | 0.5099020 | over | F0 trap, $f'(a)=1$ |
| 5 | $\tfrac12 - \tfrac{\sqrt3\,\pi}{360}$ | 0.4848850 | 0.4848096 | over | F1, $a=\pi/6$, $dx=-\pi/180$ |
| 6 | $1 - \tfrac{\pi}{90}$ | 0.9650934 | 0.9656888 | **under** | F1, $a=\pi/4$, $f'=\sec^2=2$ |
| 7 | $32 + \tfrac45 = \tfrac{164}{5}$ | 32.8 | 32.8080401 | **under** | F2, $a=2$, $f'=80$ |
| 8 | $1 - \tfrac1{500} = \tfrac{499}{500}$ | 0.998 | 0.9980040 | **under** | F2, $a=1$, $f'=-1$ |
| 9 | $\tfrac32 + \tfrac1{160} = \tfrac{241}{160}$ | 1.50625 | 1.5062391 | over | F3, $f'(4)=\tfrac5{16}$ |
| 10 | $7 - \tfrac1{35} = \tfrac{244}{35}$ | 6.9714286 | 6.9713700 | over | F0/F7, bound $5.90\times10^{-5}$ |
| 11 | $8 - \tfrac9{25} = \tfrac{191}{25}$ | 7.64 | 7.6453730 | **under** | F2, $a=2$, $f'=12$, $dx<0$ |
| 12 | $4 + \tfrac1{50} = \tfrac{201}{50}$ | 4.02 | 4.0199751 | over | F2, $a=8$, $f'=\tfrac13$ |

**Score magnitude and direction separately.**
They are different failure modes and they need different fixes.
A wrong **magnitude** means you mis-differentiated or mis-anchored - go back to Family 0 or 2.
A wrong **direction** means you reasoned from the sign of $dx$ instead of the sign of $f''$ - go back to Family 6, which is a five-minute fix.

Eight of the twelve overshoot and four undershoot, so a run of twelve "overs" means you guessed.

---

## 11. The one-page decision tree

```
"approximate / estimate / use differentials / use linearization"
    |
    +-- Is a NUMBER wanted, or a CHANGE / ERROR?
    |     |
    |     +-- a NUMBER  ->  f(a+dx) ~ f(a) + f'(a) dx          (families 0,1,2,3)
    |     +-- a CHANGE  ->  dy = f'(a) dx alone                (family 4)
    |     +-- a PERCENT ->  dy/y = n dx/x for a power          (family 5)
    |
    +-- CHOOSE a: nearest point where f(a) is EXACT
    |     root         -> nearest perfect square / cube / n-th power
    |     trig         -> nearest special angle, IN RADIANS
    |     power / 1/x  -> nearest round base, usually 1 or 2
    |     named f      -> the question already gave you f(a)
    |     CHECK: is f'(a) a unit fraction or a small integer?
    |            if not, you probably picked the wrong a
    |
    +-- dx = target - a     KEEP THE SIGN.  degrees -> radians HERE.
    |
    +-- f'(a), evaluated AT THE ANCHOR (never at the target)
    |
    +-- answer = f(a) + f'(a) dx        leave it as an exact fraction
    |
    +-- DIRECTION from f''(a):   f'' < 0 -> too big     f'' > 0 -> too small
    |                            (NOT from the sign of dx)
    |
    +-- SIZE, if asked:  |error| <= (max |f''| on the interval)/2 * dx^2
    |                    for a root with dx < 0 use the FAR endpoint
    |
    +-- check:  square it back / one Newton step / is it in the obvious bracket?
    +-- preview: 91/30 , brackets round every denominator
```

# Q12.2 - Estimate a sine with linearization

**The question (Midterm Exam 2, item 8, 6 points).**
"Use linearization to estimate the value of $\sin(62^{\circ})$."

**The answer.** $\sin 62^\circ \approx \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.8835$

**What to type into Möbius:** `sqrt(3)/2+pi/180`

Provenance: parsed from `notes\MATH265\MATH265.md`, not typed.
MT2's eleven printed values are 4, 4, 4, 6, 10, 10, 24, 6, 16, 4, 6, summing to 94, and item 8 is worth 6 of them - 6.38 percent of the paper, tying items 4 and 11 as its fourth-heaviest.
MT2 carries exactly two "no credit will be given" clauses and they sit on items 4 and 7, and its single "You may not need to simplify" permission sits on item 9, so item 8 has neither.
Item 8's whole block is one line: no parts, no hint, no "show your work".
Verification: 393 assertions pass, 0 fail, 49 of them seeded controls proving the gates can bite.

**This is the middle question of category 12.**
Q12.1 is MT1 item 9 (5 points, $\sqrt{9.2}$), this is MT2 item 8 (6 points), and Q12.3 is Final Exam 1 item 2 (8 points, $\cos 62^\circ$ and $\sqrt{16.4}$ to four decimal places).
Nineteen points across three separate papers for one idea.
[Q12.1](Q12.1%20-%20Approximate%20a%20square%20root%20with%20differentials.md) established the machinery: that $dy = f'(a)\,dx$ and $L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$ are the same object, that the anchor is chosen by measurement against competitors, and that concavity fixes the sign of the error.
This document does not re-derive any of that.
What it adds is the **trigonometric** case, where two things change and one of them is the classic catastrophic error in first-year calculus.

---

## 0. The 30-second version

```
IDENTIFY f                 you are asked for a NUMBER that is f(something)
                           sin(62 deg)  ==>  f(x) = sin x

CHOOSE THE ANCHOR a        the NEAREST angle whose sine AND cosine you know exactly
                           60 deg is a 30-60-90 angle          <- the craft
                           a = pi/3,  f(a) = sqrt(3)/2,  f'(a) = 1/2

CONVERT THE STEP           dx = 62 - 60 = 2 DEGREES = 2 * pi/180 = pi/90 RADIANS
                           <<-- THIS LINE IS THE QUESTION.  Do it before anything else.

BUILD dy                   dy = f'(a) dx = (1/2)(pi/90) = pi/180

ADD                        f(a + dx) ~ f(a) + dy = sqrt(3)/2 + pi/180 = 0.8835

SANITY                     it is between -1 and 1 (a sine),
                           and it is just above sqrt(3)/2 = 0.8660         <- 2 seconds

SAY WHICH WAY IT LEANS     f'' = -sin x < 0 on (0, pi), so sin is CONCAVE DOWN,
                           so the tangent line sits ABOVE the curve
                           ==> the estimate is TOO BIG.  It is, by 0.00053.
```

Six lines, one derivative, no calculator.
If your answer is bigger than 1, you skipped the conversion line.

---

## 1. What this question is really testing

| The reflex it drills | Where it comes back |
| :--- | :--- |
| A derivative is a **local linear model** | Q12.1, Q12.3, and Newton's method later |
| **Radians are the unit calculus is written in** | every trig derivative in the course |
| Choosing an anchor where $f$ **and** $f'$ are both exactly known | Q12.1, Q12.3 |
| $\sin(\pi/3) = \sqrt3/2$ and $\cos(\pi/3) = 1/2$ recalled instantly | Q1.1 (exact values), Q3.x (trig limits) |
| Reading concavity to get the **sign** of the error | Q12.3, Q14.1, the second-derivative test |
| The chain factor $f'(a)$ multiplies $dx$ | Q10.1 ($y'$), Q11.1 ($dh/dt$), Q12.1 |

**Q12.1 tested whether you can pick an anchor. Q12.2 tests whether you can pick a unit.**
That is the whole difference between the two questions, and it is worth one extra mark on MT2 over MT1.

---

## 2. The four things you must have cold

### 2.1 The two derivative facts

| $f$ | $f'$ | $f''$ | concave on $(0,\pi)$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\sin x$ | $\cos x$ | $-\sin x$ | down, so tangent **above** |
| $\cos x$ | $-\sin x$ | $-\cos x$ | down on $(0,\pi/2)$, up after |

These hold **only when $x$ is in radians**.
$\dfrac{d}{dt}\sin(t^\circ) = \dfrac{\pi}{180}\cos(t^\circ)$, which is a different function.
That $\pi/180$ is not a decoration; it is the price of working in degrees, and section 4.4 shows you can pay it honestly.

### 2.2 The special angles, both coordinates

| degrees | radians | $\sin$ | $\cos$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| $30$ | $\pi/6$ | $1/2$ | $\sqrt3/2$ |
| $45$ | $\pi/4$ | $\sqrt2/2$ | $\sqrt2/2$ |
| $60$ | $\pi/3$ | $\sqrt3/2$ | $1/2$ |
| $90$ | $\pi/2$ | $1$ | $0$ |

You need **both columns** at the anchor, because $f(a)$ comes from one and $f'(a)$ from the other.
A student who remembers only $\sin 60^\circ$ cannot start this question.

### 2.3 The conversion

$$1^\circ = \frac{\pi}{180}\ \text{rad}, \qquad 2^\circ = \frac{\pi}{90}\ \text{rad} \approx 0.0349$$

Read that number.
It is about **one thirtieth**, and a step of one thirtieth is what makes the estimate good.
A step of $2$ is what makes it nonsense.

### 2.4 The two decimals worth memorising

| quantity | value |
| :--- | :--- |
| $\sqrt3/2$ | $0.8660254$ |
| $\pi/180$ | $0.0174533$ |

Their sum is $0.8834787$, and that is the answer.

---

## 3. The universal procedure

> 1. **Name $f$.** The thing you are asked for is $f$ evaluated somewhere.
> 2. **Name the anchor $a$.** The nearest point where $f(a)$ and $f'(a)$ are both exactly known. For trig that means a special angle.
> 3. **Convert.** Write $a$ in radians and write $dx$ in radians. Do this on its own line, before differentiating.
> 4. **Differentiate once.** Evaluate $f'(a)$ exactly.
> 5. **Build $dy = f'(a)\,dx$.**
> 6. **Add: $f(a+dx) \approx f(a) + dy$.**
> 7. **Read the concavity** and say over or under.

| The cue in the stem | What it forces |
| :--- | :--- |
| a degree sign anywhere | step 3 is mandatory and is worth marks |
| "linearization" | write $L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$ |
| "differentials" | write $dy = f'(a)\,dx$ |
| "estimate the error in" | you want $dy$ **alone**, not $f(a) + dy$ |
| "to four decimal places" | write four places (see section 6.3) |
| "over- or underestimate" | you need $f''$, not just $f'$ |

Steps 3 and 4 are the two places marks are lost, and they are lost in different ways: step 3 is a blunder, step 4 is a slip.

---

## 4. Q12.2 worked four ways

### 4.1 The differentials route

$$f(x) = \sin x, \quad a = \frac{\pi}{3}, \quad dx = 2^\circ = \frac{\pi}{90}$$
$$f(a) = \sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}, \qquad f'(a) = \cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac12$$
$$dy = f'(a)\,dx = \frac12 \cdot \frac{\pi}{90} = \frac{\pi}{180}$$
$$\sin 62^\circ \approx \frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.8834787$$

Notice the small pleasure in the arithmetic: $\cos(\pi/3) = 1/2$ **halves** the $\pi/90$ into $\pi/180$, so the correction term is exactly "one degree in radians".

### 4.2 The linearization route

$$L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) = \frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac12\left(x - \frac{\pi}{3}\right)$$
$$L\!\left(\frac{31\pi}{90}\right) = \frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac12\cdot\frac{\pi}{90} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac{\pi}{180}$$

Identical, as Q12.1 established.
This route makes you write the target in radians too, which is one more chance to get the conversion right and one more chance to get it wrong.

### 4.3 The angle-sum route, which explains why it works

$$\sin(60^\circ + 2^\circ) = \sin 60^\circ \cos 2^\circ + \cos 60^\circ \sin 2^\circ$$

Now approximate the two small-angle factors: $\cos 2^\circ \approx 1$ and $\sin 2^\circ \approx \pi/90$.
$$\approx \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot 1 + \frac12 \cdot \frac{\pi}{90} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac{\pi}{180}$$

Same number, bit for bit.
This is not a separate method; it is the linearization with its two approximations made visible.
It also tells you exactly what you threw away: $\cos 2^\circ$ is really $0.99939$, not $1$, and that missing $0.00061$ is where the error comes from.

### 4.4 The degree-function route, which is the honest way to stay in degrees

Define $g(t) = \sin(t^\circ) = \sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{180}\right)$ with $t$ measured in degrees.
Then the chain rule gives
$$g'(t) = \frac{\pi}{180}\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{180}\right)$$
$$g(62) \approx g(60) + 2\,g'(60) = \frac{\sqrt3}{2} + 2\cdot\frac{\pi}{180}\cdot\frac12 = \frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac{\pi}{180}$$

Bit-identical to the other three.
**You may work in degrees, provided you differentiate the degree function.**
The $\pi/180$ does not disappear; it moves from the step into the derivative.
Verified: all four routes land on the same double, `0.8834786963043819`.

### Route comparison

| Route | Lines of writing | Where it can go wrong | Verdict |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 4.1 differentials | 4 | forgetting to convert $dx$ | **use this one under pressure** |
| 4.2 linearization | 5 | converting the target as well, twice the exposure |
| 4.3 angle sum | 6 | needs the identity recalled correctly | best for *understanding* |
| 4.4 degree function | 5 | the $\pi/180$ hides inside $g'$ and gets dropped | use only if degrees feel safer |

The stem says "use linearization", so write the words $L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$ somewhere even if you compute by 4.1.
It costs one line and it is the phrase the marker is looking for.

---

## 5. The exam-ready write-up

Six points, so roughly six things are being looked for.
There is no published marking scheme for this course, so the split below is inference and not an authority.

> Let $f(x) = \sin x$, with $x$ in radians.
> Take $a = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$, since $60^\circ$ is the nearest angle whose sine and cosine are exact.
> Then $dx = 62^\circ - 60^\circ = 2^\circ = \dfrac{2\pi}{180} = \dfrac{\pi}{90}$ radians.
> $f'(x) = \cos x$, so $f'(a) = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac12$.
> The linearization is $L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$, so
> $$\sin 62^\circ \approx \sin\frac{\pi}{3} + \cos\frac{\pi}{3}\cdot\frac{\pi}{90} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.8835.$$
> Since $f''(x) = -\sin x < 0$ on $(0,\pi)$, $f$ is concave down there and the tangent line lies above the curve, so this is an **overestimate**.

The sentence "$dx = 2^\circ = \pi/90$ radians" is the one sentence that cannot be omitted.
Everything else in the write-up is recoverable from a correct final number; that line is the only place the examiner can see that you knew.

---

## 6. Verify before you commit

### 6.1 The two-second checks

| Check | Why it works |
| :--- | :--- |
| Is the answer in $[-1, 1]$? | it is a sine; **this alone kills the degrees blunder** |
| Is it just above $\sqrt3/2 = 0.866$? | you stepped up from $60^\circ$ by a little |
| Is the correction about $0.017$? | $\pi/180$, one degree in radians |
| Is $62^\circ$ still in the first quadrant? | so the sine is positive and rising |

The first line is the highest-value check in the whole of category 12.
The blunder it catches produces $\sqrt3/2 + 1 = 1.8660$, and no sine is ever $1.87$.

### 6.2 The measured error

Do not assert that the method works. Here is what it actually did.

| Quantity | Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| Estimate | $0.8834786963043819$ |
| True $\sin 62^\circ$ | $0.8829475928589269$ |
| Error (estimate $-$ true) | $+5.31103445455 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| Relative error | $6.0151 \times 10^{-4}$, i.e. $0.060$ percent |
| Direction | **over**, as concavity predicts |

The true value was computed to 60 significant digits, confirmed a second way through the angle-sum identity, and confirmed a third against `math.sin`.

### 6.3 How many decimal places this is actually worth

The estimate rounds to $0.8835$; the truth rounds to $0.8829$.
**Three correct decimal places, not four.**

Across a twelve-entry trigonometric catalog (section 8), the correct-place counts are
$$[3,\ 3,\ 3,\ 2,\ 3,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 2,\ 3,\ 3,\ 3]$$
and **not one of the twelve reaches four correct decimal places**.
Q12.1 found the same thing for roots, where 5 of 21 managed four.
So when Q12.3 says "estimate each of the values below to four decimal places", it can only mean *write* four decimal places.
The marker's answer is the differential value, and writing $0.4698$ for $\cos 62^\circ$ is correct even though the true value is $0.4695$.
Say so on the page if you have room; it costs nothing and it shows you know what the estimate is worth.

### 6.4 The error bound, and the endpoint it must be taken at

The quadratic remainder is $\dfrac{|f''(\xi)|}{2}dx^2$ for some $\xi$ between $a$ and $a+dx$.
For $\sin$ that is $\dfrac{|\sin \xi|}{2}dx^2$, and $|\sin|$ is **rising** on $(60^\circ, 62^\circ)$.

| Bound taken at | Value | Holds? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| the anchor, $\sin 60^\circ$ | $5.2761\times10^{-4}$ | **no** - the actual error is $5.3110\times10^{-4}$ |
| the target, $\sin 62^\circ$ | $5.3792\times10^{-4}$ | yes |

This is Q12.1's finding recurring with the inequality pointing the other way.
There, $|f''|$ *fell* as $x$ grew, so an anchor bound failed on downward steps.
Here it *rises*, so an anchor bound fails on upward steps.
**The rule is the same either way: take the maximum of $|f''|$ over the whole interval, not at the anchor.**

### 6.5 If you want a better answer

Add the next Taylor term:
$$\sin 62^\circ \approx \frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac{\pi}{180} - \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac{(\pi/90)^2}{2} = 0.8829510834564408$$
Error $3.49\times10^{-6}$, which is **152 times better**.
That is not what this question asks for, and writing it does not earn the linearization marks, but it is worth knowing that the extra accuracy costs one line.

### 6.6 Two things that name a point inside the interval

Both of these are theorems about $(60^\circ, 62^\circ)$, and both were recovered by root-finding rather than assumed.

| Theorem | The point it names |
| :--- | :--- |
| Mean value theorem: $\cos\xi$ = the secant slope | $\xi = 61.0016^\circ$ |
| Taylor with Lagrange remainder: $-\sin\eta \cdot h^2/2$ = the remainder | $\eta = 60.6632^\circ$ |

They are **different points**, 0.34 of a degree apart.
The MVT point sits almost exactly at the midpoint, which is the usual heuristic, but "almost" is doing real work: it is $0.0016^\circ$ above it, not on it.

---

## 7. Answer-entry rules

Both exams are Möbius, answer-only and machine-marked, so a right method with a bad keystroke scores zero.

| Do | Do not |
| :--- | :--- |
| `sqrt(3)/2+pi/180` | `sqrt3/2+pi/180` (no implied multiplication after `sqrt`) |
| `0.8835` if a decimal is demanded | `0.8829` (that is the true value, not the estimate) |
| `pi/180` | `pi/180 degrees` |
| type `*` between every product | rely on juxtaposition |
| press **Preview** and look | assume the parser agreed with you |

**The single most expensive typo here is not a typo at all.**
It is entering $1.8660$, which is what you get if you never converted, and which no amount of careful typing rescues.

**The second most expensive** is entering the true value.
If you have a calculator and check yourself, you may be tempted to "correct" $0.8835$ to $0.8829$.
Do not.
The question asked for the estimate, and the estimate is $0.8835$.

Möbius has two grading engines and they parse differently, so type the `*` and preview.

---

## 8. The variation catalog

Read each table as **structure**, not as a list of facts.
Every entry in this whole catalog is the same five moves; what changes between families is only which of $f$, $a$ or $dx$ the examiner made awkward.
Every value below was recomputed from its closed form and independently re-derived formula-blind, and every direction was taken from the sign of $f''$ rather than from the comparison itself.

### Family 0 - a sine at a special angle, small degree offset

**Trigger:** $\sin$ of a whole number of degrees within a few degrees of $0, 30, 45, 60, 90$.
**Tool:** convert $dx$, then $L = \sin a + \cos a\,dx$.

| Question | Anchor | Exact estimate | Decimal | Error | Direction |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\sin 62^\circ$ | $60^\circ$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac{\pi}{180}$ | $0.8834787$ | $+5.3110\text{e-}4$ | over |
| $\sin 59^\circ$ | $60^\circ$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2} - \frac{\pi}{360}$ | $0.8572988$ | $+1.3146\text{e-}4$ | over |
| $\sin 31^\circ$ | $30^\circ$ | $\frac12 + \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{180}$ | $0.5151150$ | $+7.6920\text{e-}5$ | over |

Three entries, three different pairs of exact values, one method.
The signs are all positive because $\sin$ is concave down across the whole of $(0^\circ, 180^\circ)$.

### Family 1 - the other trigonometric functions

**Trigger:** $\cos$, $\tan$, $\sec$ instead of $\sin$.
**Tool:** the right derivative, and a fresh look at the concavity, **which is not always the same direction**.

| Question | Anchor | $f'(a)$ | Exact estimate | Decimal | Direction |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\cos 62^\circ$ | $60^\circ$ | $-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $\frac12 - \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{90}$ | $0.4697700$ | over |
| $\cos 28^\circ$ | $30^\circ$ | $-\frac12$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac{\pi}{180}$ | $0.8834787$ | over |
| $\tan 46^\circ$ | $45^\circ$ | $2$ | $1 + \frac{\pi}{90}$ | $1.0349066$ | **under** |
| $\sec 61^\circ$ | $60^\circ$ | $2\sqrt3$ | $2 + 2\sqrt3\cdot\frac{\pi}{180}$ | $2.0604600$ | **under** |

Two things to see here.

**The second row is the first row of Family 0.**
$\cos 28^\circ$ from $30^\circ$ produces *the same double* as $\sin 62^\circ$ from $60^\circ$, because reflecting through $45^\circ$ maps one problem onto the other.
That is the sharpest self-check in this whole document: if a $\cos$ question and a $\sin$ question are mirror images, their estimates must agree exactly.

**The direction flips for $\tan$ and $\sec$.**
$\tan$ is concave **up** at $45^\circ$ and $\sec$ is concave up at $60^\circ$, so those two are underestimates.
A student who has learned "linearization overestimates" from three sine problems will get both wrong.

### Family 2 - the argument is already in radians

**Trigger:** no degree sign. $\sin(1.6)$, $\cos(0.05)$.
**Tool:** no conversion at all, and often a *flat* anchor.

| Question | Anchor | $f'(a)$ | Estimate | Error |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\sin 1.6$ | $\pi/2$ | $0$ | $1$ | $+4.2640\text{e-}4$ |
| $\cos 0.05$ | $0$ | $0$ | $1$ | $+1.2497\text{e-}3$ |
| $\sin 0.1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $0.1$ | $+1.6658\text{e-}4$ |

The first two are the interesting shape.
$f'(a) = 0$ makes the linearization a **constant**, so the estimate does not move at all.
That is not an error; it is what a horizontal tangent means.
It is also why those two are among the least accurate entries in the catalog: with the linear term gone, the whole error sits in the quadratic one.

### Family 3 - the anchor is 0, and the answer is a small-angle rule

**Trigger:** an argument near zero.
**Tool:** recognise that you already know the answer.

| Linearize at $0$ | Result |
| :--- | :--- |
| $\sin x$ | $\sin x \approx x$ |
| $\tan x$ | $\tan x \approx x$ |
| $\cos x$ | $\cos x \approx 1$ |

**These are the small-angle formulas, and they are just this question with $a = 0$.**
Note carefully that linearizing $\cos$ gives $1$, **not** $1 - x^2/2$.
The familiar quadratic rule is a second-order Taylor result and is not what this method produces; writing it would be answering a different question.

$\sin$ and $\tan$ do unusually well here because $f''(0) = 0$, so their error is *cubic*: shrinking the step by 10 cuts the error by about 1000, not by 100.
$\cos$ does not get that gift, which is why $\cos 0.05$ manages only two correct decimal places.

### Family 4 - a trigonometric function inside a composite

**Trigger:** $x\sin x$, $\sin 2x$, $\sin(x^2)$.
**Tool:** product or chain rule for $f'$, then the identical five moves.

| Question | $f'$ | $f'(a)$ | Note |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $f(x) = x\sin x$ at $x = 0.55$, $a = \pi/6$ | $\sin x + x\cos x$ | $\frac12 + \frac{\pi}{6}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | product rule |
| $f(x) = \sin 2x$ at $x = 31^\circ$, $a = 30^\circ$ | $2\cos 2x$ | $1$ | chain factor 2 |

The second one is worth staring at.
$\sin(2x)$ at $x = 31^\circ$ **is** $\sin 62^\circ$, and the method reproduces the same double from the other side: the chain factor $2$ doubles the correction, while the halved step halves it back.
Drop the chain factor and you halve the correction, which is exactly the error that MT1 items 7, 8 and 9 all test.

### Family 5 - inverse trigonometric functions

**Trigger:** $\arctan(1.02)$, $\arcsin(0.51)$.
**Tool:** the inverse-trig derivative table, and a concavity that is usually the opposite of the direct function's.

| Question | Anchor | $f'(a)$ | Estimate | Direction |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\arctan 1.02$ | $1$ | $\frac{1}{1+x^2} = \frac12$ | $\frac{\pi}{4} + 0.01 = 0.7953982$ | over |
| $\arcsin 0.51$ | $0.5$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt3}$ | $\frac{\pi}{6} + \frac{0.02}{\sqrt3} = 0.5351458$ | **under** |

The $\arctan$ entry has $f'(a) = 1/2$, the same slope as the headline question, arrived at by a completely unrelated route.
Note also that the argument of an inverse trig function is a **number**, not an angle, so there is nothing to convert; the answer, however, comes out in radians.

### Family 6 - error propagation with a measured angle

**Trigger:** "a possible error of $\pm 0.5^\circ$", "estimate the error in".
**Tool:** $dy = f'(a)\,dx$ **alone**, with $dx$ the measurement error in radians.
This is the companion question in the bank: one leg of a right triangle is exactly 25 cm, the opposite angle is measured as $60^\circ \pm 0.5^\circ$.

| Quantity | Formula | Value | Differential | Error (cm) | Percentage |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| adjacent | $25\cot\theta$ | $25/\sqrt3 = 14.4338$ | $-25\csc^2\theta\,d\theta = -\frac{100}{3}d\theta$ | $-0.29089$ | $2.0153\%$ |
| hypotenuse | $25\csc\theta$ | $50/\sqrt3 = 28.8675$ | $-25\csc\theta\cot\theta\,d\theta = -\frac{50}{3}d\theta$ | $-0.14544$ | $0.5038\%$ |

with $d\theta = 0.5^\circ = 0.0087266$ rad.

Three things to take from this family.

**Do not add $f(a)$.** The question asks for the error, which is $dy$ by itself. Adding the side length is the single most common wrong answer in this family.

**The percentage errors differ by a factor of exactly 4.** And $4 = \sec^2 60^\circ$. The same half-degree of uncertainty costs four times as much on the adjacent side as on the hypotenuse, and the ratio is a clean trigonometric quantity rather than an accident.

**The conversion matters here too, and more visibly.** Using $0.5$ raw instead of $0.0087266$ gives an "error" of $16.67$ cm on a side that is only $14.43$ cm long, which is impossible.

### Family 7 - the direction of the error, asked directly

**Trigger:** "is your estimate an over- or underestimate?"
**Tool:** the sign of $f''$ on the interval. Nothing else.

| $f$ at the anchor | $f''$ | Tangent | Estimate |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\sin$ at $60^\circ$ | $-0.866$ | above | over |
| $\cos$ at $60^\circ$ | $-0.500$ | above | over |
| $\cos$ at $30^\circ$ | $-0.866$ | above | over |
| $\tan$ at $45^\circ$ | $+4.000$ | below | **under** |
| $\sec$ at $60^\circ$ | $+14.000$ | below | **under** |
| $\arctan$ at $1$ | $-0.500$ | above | over |
| $\arcsin$ at $0.5$ | $+0.770$ | below | **under** |
| $\sqrt{\ }$ at $9$ | $-0.0046$ | above | over |

Five over and three under.
The direction is a property of $f$ **and** the anchor, never of the method.
The last row is Q12.1's question, included so the two documents can be read as one table.

**The exception that proves the rule.** At an inflection point $f''(a) = 0$ and the concavity *changes*, so the direction depends on which way you step. Linearizing $\sin$ at $0$ gives an overestimate for $dx > 0$ and an underestimate for $dx < 0$. If the anchor is $0$ or $180^\circ$, check the side.

### Family 8 - how good is it

**Trigger:** "to four decimal places", "estimate the error in your estimate", "how accurate".
**Tool:** $\dfrac{\max|f''|}{2}dx^2$ over the interval, plus honesty about rounding.

| Entry | $|f''|$ at anchor | Correct places |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\sin 31^\circ$ from $30^\circ$ | $0.500$ | 3 |
| $\sin 62^\circ$ from $60^\circ$ | $0.866$ | 3 |
| $\cos 62^\circ$ from $60^\circ$ | $0.500$ | 2 |
| $\sec 61^\circ$ from $60^\circ$ | $14.000$ | 2 |
| $\tan 46^\circ$ from $45^\circ$ | $4.000$ | 1 |

The ordering is not simply by $|f''|$, because rounding boundaries interfere: a value can agree at four places and disagree at three.
$\sqrt{16.4} \approx 4.05$ is the extreme case, agreeing with the truth to $3\times10^{-4}$ and yet reporting **zero** correct decimal places, because $4.05$ rounds to $4.1$ where the truth rounds to $4.0$.
Quantize before you claim a place count; do not infer it from the size of the error.

---

## 9. The trap list

Ranked by how often it actually costs marks.

1. **Not converting degrees to radians.**
   Produces $\sqrt3/2 + 1 = 1.8660$, an error of $0.983$, which is **1851 times** the correct method's error and $111$ percent in relative terms.
   It is the only error in this document that a two-second check catches for free, because no sine exceeds 1.
   Worse, **a smaller step makes it relatively worse, not better**: on a one-degree step the ratio is $3713$, because the blunder's error is linear in the step while the method's is quadratic.
   And it has essentially no hiding place: across the whole first quadrant it never coincides with the truth, except at $90^\circ$ where $\cos a = 0$ kills the term it corrupted.

2. **Spot-checking at the anchor.**
   Of eight plausible wrong formulas, **six agree with the truth exactly when $dx = 0$**, because they differ from it only in the $dy$ term.
   Setting $dx = 0$ to "check the setup" is a test that cannot fail.
   The two survivors are the two that corrupt the $f(a)$ term instead: using the whole target as $dx$, and reporting $dy$ alone.

3. **Dropping $f'(a)$, or evaluating it at the wrong point.**
   The classic hiding points, each sitting where the factor you got wrong happens to equal 1:
   - forgetting $f'(a)$ entirely is invisible at $a = 0$, where $\cos a = 1$;
   - using $\sin a$ as the slope is invisible at $45^\circ$, where $\sin a = \cos a$;
   - a wrong sign on $dy$ is invisible at $90^\circ$, where $\cos a = 0$.
   Compute where your error would hide **before** choosing a check point. At $60^\circ$ with $dx = 2^\circ$ none of the eight hides, so the exam's own numbers are a safe place to check.

4. **Evaluating $f'$ at the target instead of the anchor.**
   This one is nastier than the rest because it is **asymptotically invisible**: its error shrinks with $dx$ exactly as the correct answer's does, so making the step smaller cannot expose it.
   At the exam's own numbers it is wrong by $1.8\times10^{-4}$ in the opposite direction.
   Pleasant consequence worth knowing: the two choices **bracket** the true value, and their average is within $10^{-5}$ of it.

5. **Reporting the true value instead of the estimate.**
   If you check yourself with a calculator, resist correcting $0.8835$ to $0.8829$.
   The question asked for the linearization.

6. **Answering the error question with $f(a) + dy$.**
   In Family 6, "estimate the error" wants $dy$ alone.

7. **Assuming linearization always overestimates.**
   True for $\sin$ and $\cos$ near $60^\circ$; false for $\tan$, $\sec$ and $\arcsin$.
   Look at $f''$ every time.

8. **Choosing an exact anchor that is not the nearest one.**
   $180^\circ$ is a perfectly legal exact anchor and is 2215 times worse than $60^\circ$.

9. **Claiming four correct decimal places.**
   Not one of the twelve trigonometric catalog entries delivers four.

10. **Using a bound taken only at the anchor.**
    For $\sin 62^\circ$ from $60^\circ$ the anchor bound is $5.2761\times10^{-4}$ and the actual error is $5.3110\times10^{-4}$, so the bound is violated.

### The anchor census, since trap 8 deserves numbers

Every one of these is a legitimate exact angle, and the error is measured, not predicted.

| Anchor | Distance to $62^\circ$ | Error | Times worse than $60^\circ$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $60^\circ$ | $2^\circ$ | $5.311\text{e-}4$ | $1.0$ |
| $45^\circ$ | $17^\circ$ | $3.396\text{e-}2$ | $63.9$ |
| $30^\circ$ | $32^\circ$ | $1.007\text{e-}1$ | $189.7$ |
| $90^\circ$ | $28^\circ$ | $1.171\text{e-}1$ | $220.4$ |
| $0^\circ$ | $62^\circ$ | $1.992\text{e-}1$ | $375.0$ |
| $120^\circ$ | $58^\circ$ | $4.892\text{e-}1$ | $921.1$ |
| $135^\circ$ | $73^\circ$ | $7.251\text{e-}1$ | $1365.2$ |
| $150^\circ$ | $88^\circ$ | $9.472\text{e-}1$ | $1783.4$ |
| $180^\circ$ | $118^\circ$ | $1.177$ | $2215.3$ |

**Read the third and fourth rows carefully, because they refute the obvious rule.**
The $30^\circ$ anchor is four degrees *further* from the target than the $90^\circ$ anchor and is still $1.16$ times *better*.
The reason is that the error is $\frac{|f''(a)|}{2}dx^2 = \frac{|\sin a|}{2}dx^2$, and $\sin 30^\circ = 0.5$ against $\sin 90^\circ = 1$: the smaller second derivative buys back the extra distance.
The same effect taken to its limit explains why $0^\circ$ beats $120^\circ$ despite being four degrees further: $\sin 0^\circ = 0$, so the quadratic term vanishes entirely and the error there is third order.

So the working rule is **"nearest exact angle"**, and it is right almost always, but the honest rule is **"smallest $|f''(a)|\,dx^2$"**.
Under exam pressure use the first; if two anchors are nearly equidistant, use the second to break the tie.
And note that "nearest" means nearest *among the anchors you can actually find*: a hypothetical exact angle at $61^\circ$ would be four times better than $60^\circ$, so $60^\circ$ is not magic, it is merely the best available.

## 10. Drill set

Do these on paper, in radians, with no calculator until the end.
**Score sign separately from magnitude.**
A wrong magnitude means you slipped in the arithmetic and should redo section 4.
A wrong sign means you did not look at $f''$ and should redo Family 7.
Those are different failures and they need different fixes.

1. Estimate $\sin 61^\circ$.
2. Estimate $\cos 31^\circ$.
3. Estimate $\sin 44^\circ$.
4. Estimate $\tan 46^\circ$, and say over or under.
5. Estimate $\cos 89^\circ$.
6. Estimate $\sin(0.1)$, the argument already in radians.
7. Estimate $\cos(1.6)$.
8. Estimate $\sec 61^\circ$, and say over or under.
9. Estimate $\arctan(1.02)$.
10. Estimate $\sin 62^\circ$ **from an anchor of $45^\circ$**, and compare with the headline answer.
11. Estimate $\sin(2)$ - note the argument is 2 **radians**, not 2 degrees.
12. Estimate $\cos 28^\circ$, and compare it with the headline answer.

### Answer key

| # | Exact estimate | Decimal | Error | Direction | Family and method |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac{\pi}{360}$ | $0.8747521$ | $+1.3234\text{e-}4$ | over | F0, $\sin$ at $\pi/3$, $dx = \pi/180$ |
| 2 | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2} - \frac{\pi}{360}$ | $0.8572988$ | $+1.3146\text{e-}4$ | over | F1, $\cos$ at $\pi/6$, $f' = -1/2$ |
| 3 | $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\left(1 - \frac{\pi}{180}\right)$ | $0.6947654$ | $+1.0707\text{e-}4$ | over | F0, $\sin$ at $\pi/4$, $dx = -\pi/180$ |
| 4 | $1 + \frac{\pi}{90}$ | $1.0349066$ | $-6.2373\text{e-}4$ | **under** | F1, $f' = \sec^2 = 2$, $f'' > 0$ |
| 5 | $\frac{\pi}{180}$ | $0.0174533$ | $+8.8608\text{e-}7$ | over | F1, $\cos$ at $\pi/2$, $f(a) = 0$ |
| 6 | $0.1$ | $0.1$ | $+1.6658\text{e-}4$ | over | F3, small-angle rule |
| 7 | $-\left(1.6 - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ | $-0.0292037$ | $-4.1509\text{e-}6$ | **under** | F2, no conversion, $f' = -1$ |
| 8 | $2 + 2\sqrt3\cdot\frac{\pi}{180}$ | $2.0604600$ | $-2.2054\text{e-}3$ | **under** | F1, $\sec' = \sec\tan$ |
| 9 | $\frac{\pi}{4} + 0.01$ | $0.7953982$ | $+9.9333\text{e-}5$ | over | F5, $f' = 1/(1+x^2)$ |
| 10 | $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\left(1 + \frac{17\pi}{180}\right)$ | $0.9169096$ | $+3.3962\text{e-}2$ | over | F0 with a bad anchor, **63.9x worse** |
| 11 | $1$ | $1$ | $+9.0703\text{e-}2$ | over | F2, $f'(\pi/2) = 0$, flat anchor |
| 12 | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2} + \frac{\pi}{180}$ | $0.8834787$ | $+5.3110\text{e-}4$ | over | F1, **same answer as the headline** |

Nine over, three under, so answering "overestimate" every time scores 9 out of 12 and teaches you nothing.

Three of these are worth a second look.

**Number 5** has $f(a) = \cos 90^\circ = 0$, so the estimate is *only* the correction term. It is also the most accurate entry in the set, error $8.9\times10^{-7}$.

**Number 11** has $f'(\pi/2) = 0$, so the estimate is exactly $1$ with no work at all, and it is the *least* accurate entry, error $9.1\times10^{-2}$. A flat anchor gives you a cheap estimate and a poor one. The drill errors span five orders of magnitude between numbers 5 and 11, which is why "linearization is accurate" is not a statement that survives without a step size attached.

**Number 12** returns the identical double to the headline question, for the reflection reason given in Family 1.
Its *error* differs in the thirteenth figure, because $\cos$-at-$30^\circ$ and $\sin$-at-$60^\circ$ are different floating-point routes to the same number.
That is a curiosity here, but it is a warning in general: never move a decimal literal between two computations that merely agree mathematically.

## 11. The one-page decision tree

```
                    A NUMBER IS ASKED FOR, "ESTIMATE" / "APPROXIMATE" / "DIFFERENTIALS"
                                            |
                          +-----------------+-----------------+
                          |                                   |
                 IS IT A TRIG VALUE?                  NO -> see Q12.1
                          |                           (root, power, etc.)
                          | yes
                          v
          +---------------+---------------+
          |                               |
   DEGREE SIGN PRESENT?             ALREADY RADIANS
          |                               |
          | yes                           | write dx as given
          v                               v
   dx_rad = dx_deg * pi/180        CHOOSE THE ANCHOR
   <<-- WRITE THIS LINE                   |
          |                               |
          +---------------+---------------+
                          |
                          v
              NEAREST EXACT ANGLE: 0, 30, 45, 60, 90, ...
              (tie? take the one with the smaller |f''|)
                          |
                          v
              f(a) and f'(a) FROM THE TABLE, both columns
                          |
                          v
              dy = f'(a) * dx_rad
                          |
          +---------------+---------------+
          |                               |
  "ESTIMATE THE VALUE"          "ESTIMATE THE ERROR"
  answer = f(a) + dy             answer = dy alone
          |                               |
          +---------------+---------------+
                          |
                          v
              SIGN OF f'' AT a?   negative -> tangent above -> OVER
                                  positive -> tangent below -> UNDER
                                  zero     -> inflection, check the side
                          |
                          v
              CHECK:  is a sine or cosine inside [-1, 1]?
                      is the correction about 0.017 per degree?
                      did I write dx in radians?
                          |
                          v
                       PREVIEW
```

# Q12.3 - Two estimates to four decimal places

**The question (Final Exam 1, item 2, 8 points).**
"Use the method of differentials to estimate each of the values below to four decimal places (show the process).
a. $\cos 62^\circ$
b. $\sqrt{16.4}$"

**The answers.**

| Part | Exact form | Write |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| a | $\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt3\,\pi}{180}$ | **0.4698** |
| b | $4 + \dfrac{1}{20} = \dfrac{81}{20}$ | **4.0500** |

**What to type into Möbius:** `1/2-sqrt(3)*pi/180` and `81/20`.

Provenance parsed from `notes\MATH265\MATH265.md`, not typed.

**This question closes category 12, and it is the heaviest of the three.**

Nineteen points across three separate papers for one idea.

## 0. The 30-second version

```
BOTH PARTS ARE THE SAME FIVE MOVES.  Only f changes.

    f(a + dx)  ~  f(a) + f'(a) dx

(a)  f = cos,  a = 60 deg = pi/3,  dx = +2 deg = pi/90   <- RADIANS, always
     f(a)  = 1/2          f'(a) = -sin(60) = -sqrt3/2
     est   = 1/2 - (sqrt3/2)(pi/90) = 1/2 - sqrt3 pi/180 = 0.4698

(b)  f = sqrt,  a = 16,  dx = +0.4
     f(a)  = 4            f'(a) = 1/(2*4) = 1/8
     est   = 4 + (1/8)(0.4) = 4 + 1/20 = 81/20 = 4.0500

DIRECTION, both parts:  f'' < 0, concave down, tangent above the curve,
                        so BOTH answers are TOO BIG.

FOUR DECIMAL PLACES means WRITE four digits.  It does not mean four of
them are right.  Only two of part (a)'s are, and NONE of part (b)'s.
```

Two derivatives, one conversion, no calculator.
The only thing that can go wrong at speed is forgetting the radians on part (a).
