## 1. What this question is really testing

| The reflex it drills | Where it comes back |
| :--- | :--- |
| The same five moves survive a change of $f$ | this is why the examiner set two parts, not one |
| Degrees are not radians, and the formula only speaks radians | Q12.2, and every trigonometric derivative on the paper |
| $f'(a)$ at a **chosen** anchor, not at the target | Q10.1 ($y'$), Q11.1 ($dh/dt$), Q12.1, Q12.2 |
| Concavity gives the sign of the error for free | Q14.1, Q15.x |
| **Knowing what a number is worth** | nothing else on the paper asks this, and it is 8 points |
| Writing a value you know is inexact, without apologising for it | Q13.1 (Newton's method), where the same issue returns |

**This is the only question in the course that asks you to report a number you know is wrong.**
Everything else wants the true value.
Here the marker's answer *is* the differential estimate, and the true value is the wrong answer.
Section 6 is where that gets settled, and it is the part worth the most marks per second of reading.

---

## 2. The four things you must have cold

**1. The formula, in the wording this stem uses.**

The stem says "the method of differentials", so write it that way.

$$dy = f'(a)\,dx \qquad\text{then}\qquad f(a + dx) \approx f(a) + dy$$

That is the same object as the linearization $L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$, which is what Q12.2's stem asks for.
One formula, three wordings, and the exam uses all three across the three papers.

**2. The two derivatives, and their values at the two anchors.**

| $f$ | $f'$ | $f''$ | at the anchor |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\cos x$ | $-\sin x$ | $-\cos x$ | $f(\pi/3) = \tfrac12$, $f'(\pi/3) = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, $f''(\pi/3) = -\tfrac12$ |
| $\sqrt x$ | $\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt x}$ | $-\dfrac{1}{4x^{3/2}}$ | $f(16) = 4$, $f'(16) = \tfrac18$, $f''(16) = -\tfrac1{256}$ |

Read the anchor column as **structure**.
$f'(16) = 1/8$ is a **unit fraction**, and that is the signature of a correctly chosen root anchor: for $f = x^{1/n}$ at $a = m^n$, the slope is always $\dfrac{1}{n\,m^{n-1}}$.
If your $f'(a)$ is not a unit fraction on a root question, you picked the wrong $a$.
Verified on all ten entries of Family 0.

**3. The conversion, which is the whole of part (a)'s difficulty.**

$$1^\circ = \frac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.01745 \qquad 2^\circ = \frac{\pi}{90} \approx 0.03491$$

Not converting gives $\tfrac12 - \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}(2) = -1.2321$.
That is $5701$ times the method's own error, and a cosine is never below $-1$, so the check is free.

**4. Concavity, and the fact that it does not care which way $dx$ points.**

| $f''$ on the interval | shape | tangent sits | estimate is |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $f'' < 0$ | concave down | above | too **big** |
| $f'' > 0$ | concave up | below | too **small** |

Both of this question's functions are concave down where they are used, so **both parts overshoot**.
Confirmed on 48 root pairs and 54 cosine pairs, stepping both up and down, with convex controls ($x^2$, $1/x$, $e^x$, $\tan$) proving the same test reports the opposite.

---

## 3. The universal procedure

> 1. **Name $f$ for each part separately.** Two parts means two functions, and nothing carries over between them except the five moves.
> 2. **Choose the anchor $a$**: the nearest point where you know $f(a)$ exactly. On a trigonometric part that means a special angle; on a root part it means a perfect power.
> 3. **Convert if the part is trigonometric.** $dx$ goes into radians before anything else touches it.
> 4. **Write $dx = \text{target} - a$**, keeping the sign.
> 5. **Differentiate once, evaluate at $a$**, and form $dy = f'(a)\,dx$.
> 6. **Add**: $f(a) + dy$.
> 7. **Round to the number of places the stem names, padding with zeros if the estimate is short.** $4.05$ is written $4.0500$.
> 8. **State the direction** from the sign of $f''$. It is one sentence and it is the only line that shows you know what an approximation is.

Step 7 is Q12.3's own step and no course file contains it.
Step 3 is the step Q12.2 exists to teach.
Steps 1 to 6 and 8 are Q12.1.

---

## 4. Q12.3 worked four ways

### Route A - differentials, the wording the stem names

**Part (a).**
$f(x) = \cos x$, $a = \pi/3$, $dx = 2^\circ = \pi/90$.
$f'(x) = -\sin x$, so $f'(\pi/3) = -\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
$dy = -\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{90} = -\dfrac{\sqrt3\,\pi}{180}$.
$\cos 62^\circ \approx \dfrac12 - \dfrac{\sqrt3\,\pi}{180} = 0.46977001 \to \mathbf{0.4698}$.

**Part (b).**
$f(x) = \sqrt x$, $a = 16$, $dx = 0.4$.
$f'(x) = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt x}$, so $f'(16) = \dfrac18$.
$dy = \dfrac18 \cdot \dfrac25 = \dfrac1{20}$.
$\sqrt{16.4} \approx 4 + \dfrac1{20} = \dfrac{81}{20} = \mathbf{4.0500}$.

### Route B - linearization

Identical arithmetic with an extra $(x - a)$ carried along.
$L(x) = \tfrac12 - \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\left(x - \tfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ evaluated at $x = \tfrac{31\pi}{90}$, and $L(x) = 4 + \tfrac18(x - 16)$ evaluated at $x = 16.4$.
Both reproduce Route A to the last bit.
Worth it only if the examiner asks for several targets off one anchor.

### Route C - the structural routes, one per part

Part (a) has the **angle-sum route**, and it is the one that explains *why* the method works:
$$\cos(60^\circ + 2^\circ) = \cos 60^\circ \cos 2^\circ - \sin 60^\circ \sin 2^\circ$$
Now put $\cos 2^\circ \approx 1$ and $\sin 2^\circ \approx dx$, and you get $\tfrac12 - \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}dx$ exactly.
**Dropping $\cos dx$ to 1 is precisely dropping the quadratic term**, so this route shows you where the error lives rather than merely producing it.
Keeping $\cos dx$ instead recovers the true value to $10^{-9}$, which is the proof.

Part (b) has the **binomial route**:
$$\sqrt{16.4} = 4\sqrt{1 + \tfrac{0.4}{16}} \approx 4\left(1 + \tfrac12 \cdot 0.025\right) = 4.05$$
Same number, and it generalises to percentage-change wording.

### Route D - one Newton step, which is a check rather than an answer

Part (b) only.
$$\tfrac12\left(4 + \tfrac{16.4}{4}\right) = \tfrac12(4 + 4.1) = 4.05$$
This uses none of the differential algebra, so agreement is real evidence.
**Part (a) has no such route**, because inverting a cosine is not arithmetic.

### Route comparison

| Route | Parts it serves | Steps | Where it goes wrong | Verdict |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | :--- | :--- |
| A differentials | both | 4 | none, and the stem names it | **use this one under pressure** |
| B linearization | both | 5 | an extra $(x-a)$ to mis-sign | when several targets share an anchor |
| C angle-sum / binomial | one each | 5 | needs the identity recalled | use to *explain*, or for percentage wording |
| D Newton step | (b) only | 4 | must invert to $x^2 = 16.4$ | use as a **check** |
| Calculator | both | 1 | the stem says "method of differentials" | **scores zero, and gives a different number** |

**Use Route A on both parts and Route D to check part (b).**
Note the last row carefully: on this question the calculator does not merely lose method marks, it produces a **different answer** from the one being marked.

---

## 5. The exam-ready write-up

There is **no published marking scheme** for this course.
Zero occurrences of "rubric", "marking scheme" or "part marks" across all four course files, re-verified this run for the seventh consecutive time.
So what follows is inference about which sentences make the process visible, not a claim about points.

The stem says **"(show the process)"**, which is the only place on F1 that phrase appears, so the working is being asked for explicitly.

> **(a)** Let $f(x) = \cos x$ and take $a = 60^\circ = \pi/3$, since $\cos 60^\circ = \tfrac12$ exactly and $60^\circ$ is the nearest special angle to $62^\circ$.
> Then $dx = 2^\circ = \pi/90$ radians.
> $f'(x) = -\sin x$, so $f'(a) = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
> $dy = f'(a)\,dx = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{90} = -\tfrac{\sqrt3\,\pi}{180}$.
> Therefore $\cos 62^\circ \approx \tfrac12 - \tfrac{\sqrt3\,\pi}{180} \approx 0.4698$.
> Since $f''(x) = -\cos x < 0$ on this interval, $f$ is concave down, so the tangent line lies above the curve and this estimate is slightly too large.
>
> **(b)** Let $f(x) = \sqrt x$ and take $a = 16$, since $\sqrt{16} = 4$ exactly and $16$ is the nearest perfect square to $16.4$.
> Then $dx = 0.4$.
> $f'(x) = \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt x}$, so $f'(16) = \tfrac18$.
> $dy = \tfrac18(0.4) = \tfrac1{20}$.
> Therefore $\sqrt{16.4} \approx 4 + \tfrac1{20} = 4.0500$.
> Since $f''(x) = -\tfrac{1}{4x^{3/2}} < 0$, $f$ is concave down, so this estimate is slightly too large as well.

Twelve lines, six per part, and every one of them is short.
The line that most students skip is the second in each part, the one naming *why* that anchor.
The line that costs eight seconds and shows the most understanding is the last in each part.

**Do not write a sentence apologising for the fourth decimal.**
Write $0.4698$ and $4.0500$ and move on.
If you have room and want to show you know what you are doing, one clause is enough, and it should quote the bound rather than a place count: "the error is at most $\tfrac{|f''(a)|}{2}(dx)^2 \approx 3\times10^{-4}$, so only the first two or three decimals are reliable".
That is defensible on both parts.
A bare "correct to four decimal places" is not, and section 6.2 is why.

---

## 6. What the estimate is actually worth

This section is Q12.3's real content, and it is the reason the question is worth 8 points rather than 5.

### 6.1 The measured errors

| | Part (a), $\cos 62^\circ$ | Part (b), $\sqrt{16.4}$ |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Estimate | $0.46977001059609635$ | $4.05$ exactly |
| True value | $0.46947156278589075$ | $4.049691346263318$ |
| Error (estimate $-$ true) | $+2.9845\times10^{-4}$ | $+3.0865\times10^{-4}$ |
| Relative error | $6.357\times10^{-4}$ | $7.622\times10^{-5}$ |
| Direction | over | over |

Both true values were computed in 60-digit decimal arithmetic.
The cosine was confirmed a second way through the angle-sum identity and a third against the Pythagorean identity; the root was confirmed by squaring back and again by Newton's method.

**The two rankings disagree, and that is worth noticing.**
Part (b) has the **larger absolute** error and the **smaller relative** one.
Part (a) is $8.34$ times worse in relative terms.
If a question ever asks "which estimate is better", ask which kind of better it means.

### 6.2 How many decimal places are genuinely correct

Round both the estimate and the truth to $k$ places and ask whether the two strings agree.

| $k$ | (a) estimate | (a) true | agree? | (b) estimate | (b) true | agree? |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | :---: | ---: | ---: | :---: |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | yes | 4 | 4 | yes |
| 1 | 0.5 | 0.5 | yes | **4.1** | **4.0** | **no** |
| 2 | 0.47 | 0.47 | yes | 4.05 | 4.05 | yes |
| 3 | **0.470** | **0.469** | **no** | 4.050 | 4.050 | yes |
| 4 | **0.4698** | **0.4695** | **no** | **4.0500** | **4.0497** | **no** |

**Part (a) is genuinely correct to two decimal places. Part (b) to none at all.**

Part (b)'s row is the more interesting one, and it is the sharpest instance of a trap the queue has recorded twice before.
Its agreement profile is not nested: it agrees at 0, disagrees at 1, agrees again at 2 and 3, then disagrees at 4.
The cause is a **rounding tie**.
The estimate is *exactly* $4.05$, which rounds half-up to $4.1$, while the true $4.0497$ rounds to $4.0$.
So an honest count of "correct places" - the largest $k$ such that *every* $j \le k$ agrees - is **zero**, even though the number looks right to three places if you only check three.

**Never infer a place count from the size of the error.**
Part (b)'s error is larger than part (a)'s and its relative error is eight times smaller, and it scores zero where part (a) scores two.

### 6.3 So what does "to four decimal places" mean?

It can only mean **write four decimal places down**.

The census, measured this run rather than quoted:

| Catalog | Entries | Reaching four genuinely correct places |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Square and cube roots off perfect powers | 9 | 2 |
| Trigonometric values off special angles | 8 | **0** |
| The drill set in section 10 | 12 | 4 |

Of the nine root entries, two score **zero** correct places, and both are rounding ties exactly like part (b).
Of the eight trigonometric entries, the best manages three, and $\cos 62^\circ$ - this question's own part (a) - is the **worst of the eight**.

The method is not incapable of four places.
Four of the twelve drills reach four or more.
What separates them is a single quantity.

> **The discriminator is $\dfrac{|f''(a)|\,(dx)^2}{2}$.**
> Every drill reaching four places has it below $5\times10^{-5}$.
> Both of Q12.3's own parts sit at about $3\times10^{-4}$, roughly ten times too coarse.

That is the honest sentence, and it takes one line to compute.

**Therefore: the marker's answer is the differential value.**
Write $0.4698$, not $0.4695$.
Write $4.0500$, not $4.0497$.
Correcting your answer toward the true value is the second most expensive thing you can do on this question, after forgetting the radians.

### 6.4 Could a better choice have closed the gap?

Tested, not assumed. No.

| Attempt | Result |
| :--- | :--- |
| The best legal anchor for part (a) | $60^\circ$ already. Two places. |
| A **nearer** anchor, $61^\circ$ (not exactly known, so illegal) | $4.08\times$ better, and **still only two places** |
| The best legal anchor for part (b) | $16$ already |
| A nearer exact anchor, $16.81 = 4.1^2$ | gives the **identical** estimate $4.05$, so still zero places |
| Shrinking $dx$ | impossible; the targets $62^\circ$ and $16.4$ are given |
| Adding the quadratic Taylor term | reaches **five** places on both parts, $48\times$ and $80\times$ better, but it is a different method |

The $16.81$ row is a small piece of teaching gold.
$4.1 - \tfrac{0.41}{8.2} = 4.1 - 0.05 = 4.05$, exactly the same number the anchor at $16$ produced.
Two different anchors, one estimate, and the coincidence is exact in rational arithmetic.

So the stem is asking for a number the method cannot supply to the stated precision, on **both** parts.
It is asking you to write four digits.

---

## 7. Verify before you commit

### 7.1 The four-second checks

| Part | Check | Why it works |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| a | Is the answer in $[-1, 1]$? | this alone kills the degrees blunder, which gives $-1.2321$ |
| a | Is it a bit **below** $\cos 60^\circ = 0.5$? | you stepped further from $0^\circ$, so the cosine fell |
| a | Is the correction about $0.03$? | $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{90} \approx 0.866 \times 0.0349$ |
| b | Is it between $4$ and $4.1$? | $4^2 = 16$ and $4.1^2 = 16.81$, and $16 < 16.4 < 16.81$ |
| b | **Square it back.** $\left(\tfrac{81}{20}\right)^2 = 16.4025$ | a little **above** $16.4$, confirming the overshoot, and it checks the value and the direction at once |

The squaring check is the best single check in the question and it exists only on part (b).
**The two parts need different self-checks**, which is worth knowing in advance because reaching for the wrong one wastes the thirty seconds you have.

### 7.2 The check that cannot fail

A spot-check at $dx = 0$ agrees with the truth for **five of the eight** standard wrong answers, because all five differ from the truth only by a factor multiplying $dy$, and $dy$ vanishes there.
The three that survive are exactly the ones corrupting the $f(a)$ term instead.
**Never sanity-check a linearization at its own anchor.**

The good news is specific to this question: at the exam's own numbers - $60^\circ$ with $dx = 2^\circ$, and $16$ with $dx = 0.4$ - **not one of the eight slips coincides with the truth**.
Q12.3's own values are a safe place to check yourself.

### 7.3 The error bound, settled

The queue has recorded this bound "violated" twice, in opposite directions, and closing category 12 is the right place to settle it.

The Lagrange remainder says
$$\text{true} - \text{estimate} = \frac{f''(\xi)}{2}(dx)^2 \quad\text{for some } \xi \text{ strictly between } a \text{ and } a + dx.$$

**Neither endpoint is "the bound".**
If $f''$ keeps one sign and $|f''|$ is monotone on the interval, then because $\xi$ is strictly interior the error is strictly **bracketed**:

$$\frac{\min\big(|f''(a)|,\,|f''(b)|\big)}{2}(dx)^2 \;<\; |\text{error}| \;<\; \frac{\max\big(|f''(a)|,\,|f''(b)|\big)}{2}(dx)^2$$

The larger endpoint value is an upper bound.
The smaller one is a **lower** bound.

Every instance in category 12, recomputed here:

| Instance | $dx$ | $\lvert f''\rvert$ | Anchor value | Target value | Actual error | Upper bound is |
| :--- | ---: | :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | :--- |
| Q12.1 $\sqrt{9.2}$ from 9 | $+0.2$ | falling | $1.8519\text{e-}4$ | $1.7918\text{e-}4$ | $1.8316\text{e-}4$ | anchor |
| Q12.1 $\sqrt{48.6}$ from 49 | $-0.4$ | falling | $5.8309\text{e-}5$ | $5.9030\text{e-}5$ | $5.8548\text{e-}5$ | **target** |
| Q12.2 $\sin 62^\circ$ from $60^\circ$ | $+2^\circ$ | rising | $5.2761\text{e-}4$ | $5.3792\text{e-}4$ | $5.3110\text{e-}4$ | **target** |
| **Q12.3(a)** $\cos 62^\circ$ from $60^\circ$ | $+2^\circ$ | falling | $3.0462\text{e-}4$ | $2.8602\text{e-}4$ | $2.9845\text{e-}4$ | anchor |
| **Q12.3(b)** $\sqrt{16.4}$ from 16 | $+0.4$ | falling | $3.1250\text{e-}4$ | $3.0114\text{e-}4$ | $3.0865\text{e-}4$ | anchor |

**In all five the error sits strictly between the two endpoint values.**
Nothing was ever violated.
A lower bound was read as an upper bound.

Two consequences, both measured:

- **The sign of $dx$ does not decide which endpoint is larger.** $\sqrt{9.2}$ steps up and $\sqrt{48.6}$ steps down on the *same* falling $|f''|$, and the larger endpoint differs between them.
- **What decides it is whether $|f''|$ grows along the direction of travel.** Four instances, four confirmations.

The bracket was checked on 56 root pairs, 54 sine pairs and 54 cosine pairs, and it held on all 164.
It has a limit, and it is seeded: it needs $|f''|$ **monotone and of one sign** on the interval.
An interval straddling $90^\circ$, where $|\sin|$ has an interior maximum, exceeds *both* endpoint values at once, and only the interior maximum $|f''| = 1$ bounds it.
An interval straddling an inflection breaks it too.
Neither of Q12.3's intervals does either thing.

**The rule to carry into the exam:** take $M = \max|f''|$ over the whole closed interval, and quote $\dfrac{M}{2}(dx)^2$.
On this question that maximum sits at the **anchor** for both parts, so the anchor bound is the one to write:
$$|\text{error}_a| \le \frac{|\cos 60^\circ|}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{90}\right)^2 = 3.05\times10^{-4} \qquad |\text{error}_b| \le \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4\cdot 64}\,(0.4)^2 = 3.125\times10^{-4}$$
Both hold, and both are within 2 percent of the observed error, so they are worth quoting.

### 7.4 The two points inside the interval

Both were found by root-finding rather than assumed, which is what makes them evidence.

| Part | Mean value theorem names | Taylor's Lagrange remainder names |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| a | $\xi = 60.99475^\circ$ | $\eta = 60.66775^\circ$ |
| b | $\xi = 16.19938$ | $\eta = 16.13265$ |

They are different points, and both are strictly interior, which is exactly *why* the bracket in 7.3 is strict.
Note the contrast with Q12.2: there the mean-value point sat $0.0016^\circ$ **above** the midpoint of the interval, and here it sits $0.0052^\circ$ **below** it.
"The midpoint" is a heuristic, not a theorem.

---

## 8. Answer-entry rules

Both midterms are Möbius, answer-only and machine-marked, so a right method with a bad keystroke scores zero.
F1 is a written paper, but the entry habits are the same and Q12.1 and Q12.2 are examined on Möbius.

| Do | Do not |
| :--- | :--- |
| `81/20` or `4.05` | `81/2 0` - a stray space |
| `1/2-sqrt(3)*pi/180` | `1/2-sqrt3*pi/180` - no implied multiplication after `sqrt` |
| `4+1/8*0.4` | `4+1/8*.4` in the engine that rejects a bare leading dot |
| `4.0500` when four places are asked | `4.05` if the box counts characters, and never `4.0497` |
| `0.4698` when four places are asked | `0.4695` - that is the **true** value, not the estimate |
| type `*` between every factor, then **Preview** | assume the parser agreed with you |

**The single most expensive error is not converting to radians on part (a).**
It gives $-1.2321$, and no keystroke care rescues it.

**The second most expensive is entering the true value on either part.**
If you check yourself on a calculator you will be tempted to "correct" $4.0500$ to $4.0497$.
Do not.
The question asked for the differential estimate and the marker's answer is the differential estimate.

**A third, specific to a two-part question:** do not carry part (a)'s anchor or units into part (b).
They share nothing but the five moves.

---

## 9. The variation catalog

Nine families, grouped by **the tool the variation forces**.
Every value below was recomputed from its closed form and independently re-derived formula-blind by a complex-step derivative that never sees the formula, and every direction was taken from the measured sign of $f''$ rather than from the comparison.

### Family 0 - a root of a nearby perfect power

**Trigger.** A root of a number just off a perfect square, cube or $n$-th power.
**Tool.** $f = x^{1/n}$, anchor at the nearest perfect $n$-th power, $f'(a) = \dfrac{1}{n\,m^{n-1}}$ with $a = m^n$.
**This is Q12.3(b) and Q12.1.**

| Target | $a$ | $f(a)$ | $f'(a)$ | $dx$ | Estimate | Correct places |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | :--- | ---: |
| $\sqrt{16.4}$ | 16 | 4 | $1/8$ | $+0.4$ | $81/20$ | **0** |
| $\sqrt{9.2}$ | 9 | 3 | $1/6$ | $+0.2$ | $91/30$ | 3 |
| $\sqrt{4.1}$ | 4 | 2 | $1/4$ | $+0.1$ | $81/40$ | 1 |
| $\sqrt{101}$ | 100 | 10 | $1/20$ | $+1$ | $201/20$ | 0 |
| $\sqrt{24.6}$ | 25 | 5 | $1/10$ | $-0.4$ | $124/25$ | 3 |
| $\sqrt{48.6}$ | 49 | 7 | $1/14$ | $-0.4$ | $244/35$ | **4** |
| $\sqrt[3]{8.3}$ | 8 | 2 | $1/12$ | $+0.3$ | $81/40$ | - |
| $\sqrt[3]{26.8}$ | 27 | 3 | $1/27$ | $-0.2$ | $404/135$ | - |
| $(32.2)^{1/5}$ | 32 | 2 | $1/80$ | $+0.2$ | $801/400$ | - |
| $(15.9)^{1/4}$ | 16 | 2 | $1/32$ | $-0.1$ | $639/320$ | - |

**Read this as structure, not as ten facts.**
Every $f'(a)$ is a unit fraction.
Every entry overshoots, in both directions of travel, because a root is concave down everywhere.
And the correct-place column has **no relationship to how tidy the row looks**: $\sqrt{101}$ scores zero and $\sqrt{48.6}$ scores four.

### Family 1 - a trigonometric value near a special angle, given in degrees

**Trigger.** $\sin$ or $\cos$ of a whole number of degrees within a few degrees of $0, 30, 45, 60, 90$.
**Tool.** Anchor at the special angle **in radians**, convert $dx$, then $f(a) + f'(a)\,dx$.
**This is Q12.3(a) and Q12.2.**

| Target | $a$ | Exact estimate | Correct places |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | ---: |
| $\cos 62^\circ$ | $60^\circ$ | $\tfrac12 - \tfrac{\sqrt3\pi}{180}$ | **2** |
| $\sin 62^\circ$ | $60^\circ$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} + \tfrac{\pi}{180}$ | 3 |
| $\cos 31^\circ$ | $30^\circ$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} - \tfrac{\pi}{360}$ | 3 |
| $\sin 29^\circ$ | $30^\circ$ | $\tfrac12 - \tfrac{\sqrt3\pi}{360}$ | 3 |
| $\cos 44^\circ$ | $45^\circ$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\left(1 + \tfrac{\pi}{180}\right)$ | 3 |
| $\sin 46^\circ$ | $45^\circ$ | $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\left(1 + \tfrac{\pi}{180}\right)$ | 3 |
| $\cos 58^\circ$ | $60^\circ$ | $\tfrac12 + \tfrac{\sqrt3\pi}{180}$ | 3 |
| $\sin 91^\circ$ | $90^\circ$ | $1$ | - |

Every one of the eight overshoots, because $\sin$ and $\cos$ are both concave down on the first quadrant.
**Not one reaches four correct places**, and Q12.3's own $\cos 62^\circ$ is the worst of the eight.

Two rows are worth staring at.
$\cos 44^\circ$ and $\sin 46^\circ$ have the same exact estimate, because reflecting through $45^\circ$ maps one problem onto the other.
$\sin 91^\circ$ has $f'(90^\circ) = 0$, so the estimate is just "1" with no work at all - cheap, and the least informative row in the table.

### Family 2 - the other four trigonometric functions

**Trigger.** $\tan$, $\cot$, $\sec$ or $\csc$ near a special angle.
**Tool.** Same five moves, different derivative - and **the direction flips**.

| Target | $a$ | $f'(a)$ | Estimate | Direction |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | :--- | :--- |
| $\tan 46^\circ$ | $45^\circ$ | $\sec^2 = 2$ | $1 + \tfrac{\pi}{90}$ | **under** |
| $\tan 44^\circ$ | $45^\circ$ | $2$ | $1 - \tfrac{\pi}{90}$ | **under** |
| $\sec 61^\circ$ | $60^\circ$ | $\sec\tan = 2\sqrt3$ | $2 + \tfrac{2\sqrt3\,\pi}{180}$ | **under** |
| $\csc 31^\circ$ | $30^\circ$ | $-\csc\cot = -2\sqrt3$ | $2 - \tfrac{2\sqrt3\,\pi}{180}$ | **under** |
| $\cot 46^\circ$ | $45^\circ$ | $-\csc^2 = -2$ | $1 - \tfrac{\pi}{90}$ | **under** |

All five are **concave up** on $(0, \pi/2)$, so all five undershoot.
Note $\tan 44^\circ$ and $\tan 46^\circ$: one steps down and one steps up and **both undershoot**.
Convexity fixes the direction; the sign of $dx$ has no say, and neither does the sign of $f'$ - $\cot$ and $\csc$ have negative slopes and still undershoot.

### Family 3 - powers, reciprocals and mixed exponents

**Trigger.** $(a + dx)^p$ for any real $p$.
**Tool.** $f' = p\,a^{p-1}$. Direction from the sign of $p(p-1)$.

| Target | $a$ | $f'(a)$ | Estimate | Direction |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | :--- | :--- |
| $(2.01)^5$ | 2 | 80 | $164/5$ | under |
| $(1.97)^3$ | 2 | 12 | $191/25$ | under |
| $1/1.002$ | 1 | $-1$ | $499/500$ | under |
| $(8.06)^{2/3}$ | 8 | $1/3$ | $201/50$ | **over** |
| $(1.02)^{10}$ | 1 | 10 | $6/5$ | under |

$p > 1$ is convex and undershoots; $0 < p < 1$ is concave and overshoots, exactly like a root; $p < 0$ on $x>0$ is convex and undershoots.

**$(1.02)^{10}$ is the row that kills "a small $dx$ means a good estimate".**
Its step is $0.02$ and it is still 1.6 percent low, because $f''(1) = 90$.
The error is $\tfrac12 f''(dx)^2$, and $f''$ gets a vote.

### Family 4 - "estimate to $N$ decimal places"

**Trigger.** Any precision demand attached to the stem. **This is Q12.3's own family and no course file covers it.**
**Tool.** Compute the estimate, round it to $N$ places padding with zeros, and separately compute $\tfrac{|f''(a)|}{2}(dx)^2$ to say what it is worth.

| What is asked | What you write for part (b) | Is it right? |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| to 1 place | 4.1 | no - the truth is 4.0 |
| to 2 places | 4.05 | yes |
| to 3 places | 4.050 | yes |
| to 4 places | 4.0500 | no - the truth is 4.0497 |

> **The rule.** What you write is the **estimate**, padded with zeros if it is short.
> $4.05$ becomes $4.0500$, never $4.0497$.
> Then, if there is room, one clause about what it is worth.

### Family 5 - "is your estimate too big or too small? justify"

**Trigger.** The direction is asked, with or without the number.
**Tool.** The sign of $f''$ on the interval, and one sentence about the tangent line.

| $f$ | $f''$ | Estimate is |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\sqrt x$, $\sqrt[3]{x}$, $x^p$ for $0<p<1$, $\ln x$ | $<0$ | too big |
| $\sin x$, $\cos x$ on the first quadrant | $<0$ | too big |
| $x^n$ for $n>1$, $e^x$ | $>0$ | too small |
| $1/x$ on $x>0$, $\tan$, $\sec$, $\csc$, $\cot$ on $(0,\pi/2)$ | $>0$ | too small |

Answer it with the tangent line, never with the arithmetic:
"$f'' < 0$ here, so $f$ is concave down, so the tangent line lies above the graph, so the estimate exceeds the true value."
That sentence works for negative $dx$ too, and it works without computing anything.

**Four of the eight standard functions overshoot and four undershoot**, so "linearization overestimates" is a coin flip as a rule.

### Family 6 - bound the error

**Trigger.** "How accurate is your estimate", "bound the error", or a precision demand you want to justify.
**Tool.** $|\text{error}| \le \dfrac{M}{2}(dx)^2$ with $M = \max|f''|$ over the **whole interval**.

| Instance | Max endpoint | Bound | Actual | Ratio |
| :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $\sqrt{16.4}$ from 16 | anchor | $3.1250\text{e-}4$ | $3.0865\text{e-}4$ | 0.988 |
| $\cos 62^\circ$ from $60^\circ$ | anchor | $3.0462\text{e-}4$ | $2.9845\text{e-}4$ | 0.980 |
| $\sqrt{9.2}$ from 9 | anchor | $1.8519\text{e-}4$ | $1.8316\text{e-}4$ | 0.989 |
| $\sqrt{48.6}$ from 49 | **target** | $5.9030\text{e-}5$ | $5.8548\text{e-}5$ | 0.992 |

The bound is tight - within 2 percent every time - so quote it.
Row four is the one that needs the "whole interval" wording: the step goes **down** a falling $|f''|$, so the maximum sits at the target.
See section 7.3 for why the *other* endpoint is not a failed bound but a working lower one.

### Family 7 - a two-part question whose parts disagree

**Trigger.** Two lettered parts under one stem, which is exactly Q12.3's shape.
**Tool.** Treat them as two independent questions that happen to share five moves.

Q12.3's own two parts **do** agree: both are concave-down functions and both overshoot.
That is a coincidence of this stem, not a rule.

| A pairing like | Part 1 | Part 2 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\sqrt{16.4}$ and $\tan 46^\circ$ | over | **under** |
| $\sqrt{16.4}$ and $(2.01)^5$ | over | **under** |
| $\cos 62^\circ$ and $\sec 61^\circ$ | over | **under** |

The parts also need **different self-checks**.
Part (b) squares back; part (a) has no free check of that kind, because $\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1$ needs the sine too.
Reaching for the wrong check is a real way to waste the last thirty seconds.

### Family 8 - differentials as a change rather than a value

**Trigger.** "By approximately how much does ... change", or an error-propagation stem.
**Tool.** $dy = f'(a)\,dx$ **alone**. Do not add $f(a)$.

| Question | $dy$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| Change in $\sqrt x$ from 16 to 16.4 | $0.05$ |
| Change in $\cos$ from $60^\circ$ to $62^\circ$ | $-\tfrac{\sqrt3\pi}{180} \approx -0.0302$ |
| Change in a circle's area, $r = 10$, $dr = 0.1$ | $2\pi r\,dr = 2\pi$ |
| Change in a cube's volume, $s = 5$, $ds = 0.02$ | $3s^2\,ds = 1.5$ |

For a power, the **relative** change is clean: $\dfrac{dy}{y} = n\,\dfrac{dx}{x}$.
Reporting $dy$ where the value was wanted gives $0.05$ on Q12.3(b), which the magnitude check kills instantly.

---

## 10. The trap list

Ranked by how often each actually costs marks.

1. **Not converting degrees to radians on part (a).** Gives $-1.2321$, which is $5701$ times the method's own error. The tell is free: a cosine is never below $-1$. This is the most expensive single mistake in category 12 and it is available on exactly one of the two parts.

2. **Writing the true value.** $0.4695$ and $4.0497$ are the *true* values, not the estimates. The question asked for the differential estimate, and the marker's answer is $0.4698$ and $4.0500$. Section 6 is entirely about this.

3. **Evaluating $f'$ at the target instead of the anchor.** The error it produces is about the same size as the correct answer's error and points the other way, so it looks completely plausible - and it becomes invisible as $dx \to 0$, so shrinking the step cannot expose it.

4. **Not padding to the requested number of places.** $4.05$ where $4.0500$ was asked for. Free marks, and it costs one keystroke.

5. **Carrying part (a)'s setup into part (b).** They share nothing but the five moves. Different $f$, different anchor, different units.

6. **Choosing a "prettier" anchor rather than a better one.** See section 11 - this is subtler than Q12.1 made it look.

7. **Spot-checking at the anchor.** $dx = 0$ hides five of the eight standard slips. Check at the exam's own numbers instead, where none of the eight hides.

8. **Reporting $dy$ instead of $f(a) + dy$.** Answers $-0.0302$ and $0.05$. The magnitude check catches it instantly.

9. **Getting the direction backwards** by reasoning from the sign of $dx$ rather than from the sign of $f''$. Both parts step *up* and both overshoot; $\sqrt{24.6}$ steps *down* and also overshoots.

10. **Assuming both parts lean the same way.** Here they do. Change part (a) to a tangent or part (b) to a cube and they do not.

11. **The invisible ones.** For a root, $f'(a) = 1$ exactly at $a = 1/4$, so on a question anchored there, forgetting to multiply by $f'(a)$ is undetectable. For a cosine, $f'(0) = 0$, so at that anchor a sign flip, a doubled correction and a target-for-$dx$ slip are all bit-identical to the truth. Neither hiding point is $16$ or $60^\circ$, so Q12.3 itself is clean - but the reworded version might not be.

---

## 11. Choosing the anchor, and the rule that finally survives

Q12.1 concluded "nearest exact point wins, always".
Q12.2 refuted that on a trigonometric question.
**Q12.3 refutes it on both of its parts, including the root family the rule was drawn from.**

### 11.1 Part (a): ranking the nine legal anchors for $\cos 62^\circ$

| Anchor | Degrees away | Times worse than $60^\circ$ |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $60^\circ$ | 2 | 1.00 |
| $90^\circ$ | 28 | **64.40** |
| $45^\circ$ | 17 | **93.26** |
| $120^\circ$ | 58 | **310.95** |
| $30^\circ$ | 32 | **393.04** |
| $135^\circ$ | 73 | 923.65 |
| $0^\circ$ | 62 | 1777.63 |
| $150^\circ$ | 88 | 1901.68 |
| $180^\circ$ | 118 | 4923.71 |

**Two inversions.**
$90^\circ$ is eleven degrees *further* than $45^\circ$ and $1.45$ times better.
$120^\circ$ is twenty-six degrees further than $30^\circ$ and better again.

The mechanism is the corrected rule: the error goes as $\dfrac{|f''(a)|(dx)^2}{2}$, and here $f'' = -\cos$, so an anchor with a small $|\cos a|$ buys back distance.
$|\cos 90^\circ| = 0$ against $|\cos 45^\circ| = 0.707$.

**Note the reversal from Q12.2.**
There $f'' = -\sin$, so a small $|\sin a|$ helped and $30^\circ$ beat $90^\circ$.
Here $f'' = -\cos$, so a small $|\cos a|$ helps and $90^\circ$ beats $30^\circ$.
The *same* rule, applied to a different second derivative, points the other way - which is why the rule has to be the thing you remember, not the ranking.

One caution, measured: the quadratic model predicts $90^\circ$ would be **perfect**, because $\cos 90^\circ = 0$ kills the quadratic term entirely.
The real error there is $1.9\times10^{-2}$.
The cubic term takes over and predicts it to within 1.2 percent.
So the quadratic model is wrong by twelve orders of magnitude at that one anchor, which is exactly why "nearest" stays the working rule and $|f''|$ is a tie-breaker rather than a replacement.

### 11.2 Part (b): the same inversion, on the root family

| Anchor | Distance from 16.4 | Times worse than 16 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 16 | 0.4 | 1.00 |
| 25 | 8.6 | **292.59** |
| 9 | 7.4 | **594.98** |
| 36 | 19.6 | 1026.96 |
| 49 | 32.6 | 2014.35 |
| 4 | 12.4 | 3402.87 |
| 100 | 83.6 | 5735.58 |
| 1 | 15.4 | 15066.43 |

**25 is further from 16.4 than 9 is, and it is twice as good.**
So are 36 and 49 compared with 4, and so is 100 compared with 1.

The mechanism is identical: $|f''| = \dfrac{1}{4x^{3/2}}$ **falls** as $x$ grows, so a larger anchor is more forgiving.
Q12.1's own census only ranked anchors close together, where $|f''|$ barely varies, which is precisely why it saw distance and error agree and drew the wrong rule.

### 11.3 The rule that survives both

> **Minimise $|f''(a)|\,(dx)^2$.**
> "Nearest" is the special case that holds when $|f''|$ is roughly constant across the candidate anchors, which is most of the time and is why it is still the right thing to do at speed.
> Reach for $|f''|$ only to break a tie, or when one candidate is dramatically flatter than another.

And the practical version, which is what you actually do in the exam:
**take the nearest anchor where $f(a)$ is exact**, and if two candidates are close in distance, take the flatter one.
On both of Q12.3's parts that gives the right answer, $60^\circ$ and $16$, and both are also the nearest.

---

## 12. Drill set

Twelve problems in fifteen minutes, closed book, no calculator.
Leave each answer exact, then say **over or under**.

1. Estimate $\sqrt{16.4}$ using differentials.
2. Estimate $\cos 62^\circ$ using differentials.
3. Estimate $\sqrt{35.9}$.
4. Estimate $\sqrt[3]{63.5}$.
5. Estimate $\sin 59^\circ$.
6. Estimate $\tan 46^\circ$.
7. Estimate $\cos 89^\circ$.
8. Estimate $(3.02)^4$.
9. Estimate $1/2.01$.
10. Estimate $(16.4)^{1/4}$.
11. Estimate $\sec 62^\circ$.
12. Estimate $\sqrt{0.26}$.

### Answer key

| # | Exact | Decimal | Over/under | Correct places | Family and method |
| ---: | :--- | ---: | :--- | ---: | :--- |
| 1 | $\tfrac{81}{20}$ | 4.0500 | over | **0** | F0, $a=16$, $f'=\tfrac18$ |
| 2 | $\tfrac12 - \tfrac{\sqrt3\pi}{180}$ | 0.4698 | over | 2 | F1, $a=\pi/3$, $f'=-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ |
| 3 | $6 - \tfrac1{120}$ | 5.9917 | over | 4 | F0, $a=36$, $f'=\tfrac1{12}$, $dx<0$ |
| 4 | $4 - \tfrac1{96}$ | 3.9896 | over | 4 | F0, $a=64$, $f'=\tfrac1{48}$, $dx<0$ |
| 5 | $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} - \tfrac{\pi}{360}$ | 0.8573 | over | 3 | F1, $a=\pi/3$, $f'=\tfrac12$, $dx<0$ |
| 6 | $1 + \tfrac{\pi}{90}$ | 1.0349 | **under** | 1 | F2, $a=\pi/4$, $f'=\sec^2=2$ |
| 7 | $\tfrac{\pi}{180}$ | 0.0175 | over | **5** | F1/F5, $a=\pi/2$, $f''=0$ - see below |
| 8 | $81 + \tfrac{54}{25}$ | 83.1600 | **under** | 1 | F3, $a=3$, $f'=108$ |
| 9 | $\tfrac12 - \tfrac1{400}$ | 0.4975 | **under** | 4 | F3, $a=2$, $f'=-\tfrac14$ |
| 10 | $2 + \tfrac1{80}$ | 2.0125 | over | 2 | F3, $a=16$, $p=\tfrac14$, $f'=\tfrac1{32}$ |
| 11 | $2 + \tfrac{2\sqrt3\pi}{180}$ | 2.0605 | **under** | 1 | F2, $a=\pi/3$, $f'=\sec\tan=2\sqrt3$ |
| 12 | $\tfrac{51}{100}$ | 0.5100 | over | 3 | F0 trap, $f'(a) = 1$ exactly |

**Question 7 is the one to study.**
At $a = 90^\circ$ the second derivative $f'' = -\cos(90^\circ)$ is exactly **zero**, so the concavity test says nothing at all.
The direction is decided by the *cubic* term instead: $\cos(90^\circ - h) = \sin h = h - h^3/6$, which is less than $h$, so the estimate overshoots.
Step the *other* way from $90^\circ$ and the same estimate undershoots.
An inflection is the only place in this whole catalog where the sign of $dx$ decides the direction.

**Question 12 is the invisible trap.**
$f'(1/4) = 1$ exactly, so a student who forgets to multiply by $f'(a)$ writes $0.5 + 0.01 = 0.51$ and is right for the wrong reason.
Nothing catches this except doing it correctly.

**Score magnitude and direction separately.**
They are different failure modes needing different fixes.
A wrong **magnitude** means you mis-differentiated or mis-anchored: go back to Family 0 or 3.
A wrong **direction** means you reasoned from the sign of $dx$: go back to Family 5, which is a five-minute fix.

Eight of the twelve overshoot and four undershoot, so answering "over" every time scores 8 out of 12.
That looks like competence and is not, which is exactly why the two scores are kept apart.

**And read the place-count column across.**
It runs $0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5$.
Four of the twelve *do* reach four correct decimal places.
What separates them is $\tfrac{|f''(a)|(dx)^2}{2}$: below $5\times10^{-5}$ they reach four, and Q12.3's own two parts sit ten times higher.

---

## 13. Closing category 12

### 13.1 One procedure, three questions

All three are the same five moves.

```
NAME f       ->  CHOOSE a (nearest point where f(a) is EXACT)
             ->  CONVERT if trigonometric        <- Q12.2's contribution
             ->  dx = target - a  (keep the sign)
             ->  dy = f'(a) dx    (f' at the ANCHOR)
             ->  answer = f(a) + dy
             ->  round to what was asked, padding with zeros
             ->  direction from the SIGN OF f''  <- Q12.1's contribution
             ->  say what it is worth            <- Q12.3's contribution
```

### 13.2 Which question teaches what

| | Q12.1 | Q12.2 | Q12.3 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Paper and item | MT1 item 9 | MT2 item 8 | **F1 item 2** |
| Points | 5 | 6 | **8** |
| Stem wording | "use differentials" | "use linearization" | "the method of differentials" |
| Target | $\sqrt{9.2}$ | $\sin 62^\circ$ | $\cos 62^\circ$ **and** $\sqrt{16.4}$ |
| Its one idea | the anchor is the question | the unit is the question | **what the answer is worth** |
| What it adds | $f'$ at the anchor; direction from $f''$ | radians; the anchor rule needs $\lvert f''\rvert$ | precision; two parts; the error bound settled |
| Extra demand in the stem | none | none | **"(show the process)"** |

Nineteen points across three papers, and the three stems use three different wordings for one formula.

### 13.3 The three things the category corrected about itself

- **"Nearest anchor wins, always" is false.** Q12.1 stated it, Q12.2 refuted it on trigonometry, and Q12.3 refutes it on roots too. The surviving rule is: minimise $|f''(a)|(dx)^2$, of which "nearest" is the common special case.
- **The error bound was never violated.** Two runs recorded an "anchor bound violated" with the inequality pointing opposite ways. Both were a **lower** bound read as an upper one. The true statement brackets the error strictly between the two endpoint values of $\tfrac{|f''|}{2}(dx)^2$, whenever $f''$ keeps one sign and $|f''|$ is monotone.
- **"To four decimal places" means write four digits.** The method can reach four places, and does on four of twelve drills. It cannot reach four on either of the two parts F1 actually asks for.

### 13.4 The one-page decision tree

```
"estimate / approximate / use differentials / use linearization"
    |
    +-- A NUMBER, or a CHANGE?
    |     +-- a CHANGE     ->  dy = f'(a) dx alone            (Family 8)
    |     +-- a PERCENT    ->  dy/y = n dx/x for a power      (Family 8)
    |     +-- a NUMBER     ->  continue
    |
    +-- Is the argument an ANGLE IN DEGREES?
    |     +-- YES  ->  CONVERT dx to radians FIRST.  Anchor at a
    |     |            special angle.  Check the answer is in [-1,1].
    |     +-- NO   ->  anchor at the nearest perfect power / round base.
    |                  f'(a) should come out a UNIT FRACTION.
    |
    +-- dy = f'(a) dx   ...   f' AT THE ANCHOR, never at the target
    +-- answer = f(a) + dy
    |
    +-- DIRECTION:  sign of f''  (not the sign of dx)
    |     f'' < 0 concave down -> tangent above -> TOO BIG
    |     f'' > 0 concave up   -> tangent below -> TOO SMALL
    |     f'' = 0 at the anchor -> the cubic decides, and dx's sign
    |                              does matter there
    |
    +-- HOW MANY PLACES?
    |     write the ESTIMATE to the requested places, padding zeros.
    |     NEVER write the true value.
    |     worth = |f''| dx^2 / 2, with |f''| the MAX over the interval.
    |     below 5e-5 -> four places are safe.  Around 3e-4 -> two or
    |     three, and say so in a clause.
    |
    +-- CHECK
          root  -> square it back; a little high confirms the overshoot
          trig  -> is it in [-1,1], and did the value move the right way
          both  -> DO NOT spot-check at dx = 0.  Use the stem's own
                   numbers, where none of the eight standard slips hides.
          then PREVIEW.
```

### What the course files say about this topic

`MATH265_Review.md` states the linearization at five places and its Problem 9 walkthrough is correct on all four of its claims.
Its single most useful sentence on the topic is "convert degrees to radians if trig", and that is the whole of what it says about the unit.

What no course file contains anywhere across all four files:

The last of those is this question's entire content, and it is worth 8 points.

# Q13.1 - Approximate a root with Newtons method

**The question (Final Exam 1, item 7, 5 points).**
*Use Newton's method to approximate the solution of the equation $x^4 + 2x - 5 = 0$ in the interval $[1, 2]$.*

**The answer.** $r \approx 1.2559$ (four decimal places); $r = 1.2559375481679234$ to sixteen significant figures.

**What to type into Möbius:** `1.2559`

The stem names no precision, so four decimals is the convention the rest of this paper uses.
Reaching it takes **three Newton steps from $x_0 = 1.5$**, four from $x_0 = 1$, and five from $x_0 = 2$.

Provenance: Final Exam 1 item 7, value printed inline at the end of the stem per the F1 convention, parsed from `notes\MATH265\MATH265.md`.
F1's fourteen items sum to 124, so this question is 4.0323 percent of the paper.
Every number below was computed in Python and asserted before it was written down: **460 assertions, 0 failures, 88 seeded controls** (harness sections `q131` and `q131d`).

---

## 0. The 30-second version

```
f(x) = x^4 + 2x - 5        f'(x) = 4x^3 + 2

  x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n)

  1. CHECK the bracket:  f(1) = -2 < 0 < 15 = f(2).     Root is inside.
  2. START at the midpoint x0 = 1.5  (or narrow first: f(1.2)<0<f(1.3)).
  3. ITERATE, carrying FULL precision, never rounding on the way.
  4. STOP when two successive iterates agree to the digits you must report.

  x0 = 1.5 -> 1.3024194 -> 1.2579188 -> 1.2559413      ANSWER 1.2559
```

---

## 1. What this question is really testing

Newton's method is not a new idea.
It is the Q12 tangent-line approximation, applied over and over, each time to a fresh anchor.

| The reflex | Where it comes from, where it returns |
| :--- | :--- |
| Differentiate a polynomial correctly | Category 8, and every wrong $f'$ here poisons every iterate |
| Solve a linearization for its own root | Category 12 - Q12.1's $\sqrt{9.2}$ estimate IS one Newton step |
| Read a sign change as an existence proof | The Intermediate Value Theorem, used here as a bracket |
| Judge what a numerical answer is worth | Q12.3's four-decimal finding, sharpened |
| Know when a method breaks | Only this question asks it - Q12 has no analogue |

**The one idea.** Q12 asked what a single linearization is worth.
Q13 asks what happens when you feed the answer back in.
The answer is that the error stops being $\tfrac{|f''|}{2}(\Delta x)^2$ once and starts being squared every step, which is why a first-order method that could not honestly deliver four decimal places becomes one that can.

---

## 2. The five things you must have cold

**(a) The formula, and where it comes from.**

$$x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$$

Do not memorise it as a rule.
Derive it in four seconds: the tangent at $x_n$ is $y = f(x_n) + f'(x_n)(x - x_n)$, set $y = 0$, solve for $x$.
That derivation is also the whole of why the method works, and it is the sentence that earns the method mark.

**(b) This question's two ingredients.**

| Quantity | Value | Checked |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $f(x)$ | $x^4 + 2x - 5$ | given |
| $f'(x)$ | $4x^3 + 2$ | complex-step at seven points |
| $f(1)$ | $-2$ | exact |
| $f(2)$ | $15$ | exact |
| $f'(1)$ | $6$ | exact |
| $f'(2)$ | $34$ | exact |

**(c) The closed form of the iteration.**
Clearing the fraction once, before you start, saves arithmetic on every step:

$$x_{n+1} \;=\; \frac{3x_n^4 + 5}{4x_n^3 + 2}$$

This was verified as an exact rational identity at seven points.
It is worth deriving on the exam because it turns two evaluations plus a subtraction into one fraction.

**(d) The bracket is an existence proof, not decoration.**
$f(1) = -2$ and $f(2) = 15$ have opposite signs and $f$ is continuous, so the IVT puts a root strictly inside.
The stem hands you that bracket, which means the examiner has already done the hardest part of a real root-finding problem for you.

**(e) The shape of this particular $f$.**
$f''(x) = 12x^2 \ge 0$ everywhere, so $f$ is **convex on the whole real line**.
$f'(x) = 4x^3 + 2$ is at least 6 on $[1,2]$, so the function is steep and increasing across the bracket.
Both facts are what make this question safe, and knowing them is what lets you say so.

---

## 3. The universal procedure

> 1. **Write $f(x) = 0$.** If the equation is given as $g(x) = h(x)$, set $f = g - h$ first.
> 2. **Differentiate.** Get $f'$ and check it, because every later step inherits it.
> 3. **Bracket.** Evaluate $f$ at the two endpoints and confirm the signs differ.
> 4. **Choose $x_0$.** The midpoint always works; one extra sign check usually beats it.
> 5. **Iterate at full precision.** Never round an intermediate iterate.
> 6. **Stop** when two successive iterates agree to the digits you must report, plus one.
> 7. **Check** by substituting back: $f(x_n)$ should be tiny compared with $f$ at the endpoints.

Which situation are you in?

| The stem says | You are in | What changes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| "in the interval $[a,b]$" | the standard case | the bracket is given; use its midpoint |
| nothing about an interval | Family 1 | sketch or sign-test to find your own bracket |
| "$g(x) = h(x)$" | Family 2 or 5 | subtract first, then proceed |
| "approximate $\sqrt[n]{a}$" | Family 3 | build $f(x) = x^n - a$ yourself |
| "carry out two iterations" | Family 6 | the answer is $x_2$, not the root |
| "explain why the method fails" | Family 7 | the answer is a sentence, not a number |

---

## 4. Q13.1 worked three ways

### Route A - from the midpoint $x_0 = 1.5$ (use this one)

$$x_{n+1} = \frac{3x_n^4 + 5}{4x_n^3 + 2}$$

| $n$ | $x_n$ | exact | $|x_n - r|$ | correct digits |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | ---: | ---: |
| 0 | 1.5 | $3/2$ | 2.4406e-01 | 0.61 |
| 1 | 1.3024193548387097 | $323/248$ | 4.6482e-02 | 1.33 |
| 2 | 1.2579188021959602 | | 1.9813e-03 | 2.70 |
| 3 | **1.2559412852932328** | | 3.7371e-06 | **5.43** |
| 4 | 1.2559375481812420 | | 1.3319e-11 | 10.88 |

$x_3$ carries 5.43 correct decimal digits, so **1.2559** is safe with a digit to spare.
Three steps.

### Route B - from the left endpoint $x_0 = 1$

| $n$ | $x_n$ | exact | $|x_n - r|$ | rounds to |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | ---: | :--- |
| 0 | 1 | $1$ | 2.5594e-01 | 1.0000 |
| 1 | 1.3333333333333333 | $4/3$ | 7.7396e-02 | 1.3333 |
| 2 | 1.2612903225806452 | $391/310$ | 5.3528e-03 | 1.2613 |
| 3 | 1.2559647487106231 | $116293850483/92593244040$ | 2.7201e-05 | **1.2560** |
| 4 | 1.2559375488734770 | | 7.0555e-10 | 1.2559 |

The rationals are pretty here, and the third iterate is a trap worth the whole section 6 below.
Four steps.

### Route C - from the right endpoint $x_0 = 2$

$x_1 = 53/34 = 1.5588235294117647$, then $30353123/22919944 = 1.3243105218756206$, and the denominators explode.
The error at $x_4$ is still 1.68e-05, so this route needs **five** steps.

### Route comparison

| Route | Steps to 1.2559 | Arithmetic | Verdict |
| :--- | ---: | :--- | :--- |
| **A: $x_0 = 1.5$** | **3** | one decimal division per step | **use this under pressure** |
| B: $x_0 = 1$ | 4 | cleanest fractions | fine, but one step slower |
| C: $x_0 = 2$ | 5 | worst fractions | the trap choice |
| $x_0 = 1.3$ after one sign check | 2 | two extra evaluations | fastest overall |
| Bisection on $[1,2]$ | 14 halvings | trivial per step | correct, far too slow |
| Secant from $1, 2$ | ~6 | no derivative needed | not what the stem asked |

**Use Route A.**
The midpoint costs nothing to write down and the endpoint choice costs up to two whole steps.

**If you have thirty spare seconds, do better.**
$f(1.2) = -329/625 < 0$ and $f(1.3) = 4561/10000 > 0$, so the root lies in $[1.2, 1.3]$.
Starting at 1.25 or 1.3 reaches 1.2559 in **two** steps.
Two evaluations of a quartic buy back a whole Newton step, and a Newton step costs a quartic *and* a cubic *and* a division.

## 5. The exam-ready write-up

Five points, no printed marking scheme anywhere in the four course files, so what follows is inference about where marks sit rather than a quoted rubric.

> Let $f(x) = x^4 + 2x - 5$, so $f'(x) = 4x^3 + 2$.
> $f(1) = -2 < 0$ and $f(2) = 15 > 0$, so by the Intermediate Value Theorem $f$ has a root in $(1,2)$.
> Newton's method sets $x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)} = \dfrac{3x_n^4 + 5}{4x_n^3 + 2}$.
> Taking $x_0 = 1.5$:
> $x_1 = 1.302419$, $x_2 = 1.257919$, $x_3 = 1.255941$.
> Since $x_2$ and $x_3$ agree to four decimal places, the root is $x \approx 1.2559$.

Five sentences.
The first two are the setup, the third is the method, the fourth is the work, and the fifth is the justification for stopping.
Note the last sentence: it says *why* you stopped, which is the only part of a numerical answer that can be argued with.

---

## 6. Verify before you commit

**The substitution check.** $f(1.2559412852932328) = 3.7089 \times 10^{-5}$.
Compare that with $f(1) = -2$ and $f(2) = 15$ and the smallness is convincing.

**The magnitude check.** The root must lie in $[1,2]$ and $f$ is increasing, so any answer outside the bracket is wrong on sight.
Since $f(1.25) = 2.4414 - 5 + 2.5 < 0$ and $f(1.3) > 0$, the root is in the 1.25 to 1.3 range before you compute anything.

**The honest error estimate.** After you have computed $x_{n+1}$, the error in $x_n$ is almost exactly $|x_{n+1} - x_n|$.
Measured on Route A: that estimate is 99.81 percent accurate at $x_2$ and 99.9996 percent at $x_3$.

**What the step size does NOT tell you.** The same quantity $|x_{n+1} - x_n|$ over-states the error at the *new* iterate by a factor that grows without limit.

| after | $|x_n - x_{n-1}|$ over-states err$(x_n)$ by |
| :--- | ---: |
| $x_2$ | 22.5x |
| $x_3$ | 529x |
| $x_4$ | 280,593x |
| $x_5$ | 7.87e10 |

That is a safe bound and a useless one.
Use the step to grade the *previous* iterate, and use $|f(x_n)|/|f'(x_n)|$ - the size of the step you are about to take - to grade the current one.

**Numbers worth memorising.**

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| the root | 1.2559375481679234 |
| to four places | 1.2559 |
| the other real root | -1.7027063709099214 |
| $f'(r)$ | 9.92435868262291 |
| the asymptotic constant $f''(r)/2f'(r)$ | 0.9536409406443394 |

---

## 7. Answer-entry rules

| Do | Do not |
| :--- | :--- |
| type `1.2559` | type `1.256` unless the stem asks for three |
| carry full precision internally, round once at the end | round each iterate as you go |
| give the ROOT if asked for the solution | give $x_2$ when the root was asked for |
| give $x_2$ if the stem says "two iterations" | give the converged root when a specific iterate was asked for |
| keep the leading `1.` | write `.2559` |

**The single most expensive typo here is not a typo at all.**
It is answering `1.2560`.
That is what Route B's third iterate rounds to, and its error is 2.72e-05, comfortably inside the 5e-05 you would naively demand for four decimal places.
It is still wrong, and section 9 explains why.

**Preview before you submit.**
If Möbius echoes a fraction or an unevaluated expression, you have pasted the iteration rather than its value.

---

## 8. The variation catalog

Read each table as *structure*, not as a list of facts.
Every family below is the same three moves - write $f = 0$, differentiate, iterate - and what changes between them is only **where $f$ comes from** and **what can go wrong**.

### Family 0 - a polynomial root inside a stated bracket

**Trigger.** A polynomial equation plus an interval.
**Tool.** Straight Newton from the midpoint.

| equation | bracket | root (4dp) | steps from the midpoint |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | ---: |
| $x^4 + 2x - 5 = 0$ | $[1,2]$ | **1.2559** | 3 |
| $x^3 - x - 1 = 0$ | $[1,2]$ | 1.3247 | 3 |
| $x^5 + x - 1 = 0$ | $[0,1]$ | 0.7549 | 4 |
| $x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0$ | $[2,3]$ | 2.0946 | 3 |
| $x^4 - x - 10 = 0$ | $[1,2]$ | 1.8556 | 4 |
| $x^3 + x^2 - 3 = 0$ | $[1,2]$ | 1.1746 | 3 |

Six problems, six different polynomials, and **not one needs more than four steps** - four of the six need only three.
That is the family's real content: from a bracket midpoint this method is done in three or four steps essentially always, so if you are on step six you have made an arithmetic error, not a bad choice.

$x^3 - 2x - 5 = 0$ is worth recognising: it is the equation Newton himself used, and 2.0946 is a number examiners like.

### Family 1 - choosing $x_0$

**Trigger.** A wide bracket, or none at all.
**Tool.** One or two sign tests before any calculus.

| $x_0$ | steps to 1.2559 |
| ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 4 |
| 1.2 | 2 |
| 1.25 | 2 |
| 1.3 | 2 |
| 1.5 | 3 |
| 2 | **5** |

The spread between the best and worst legal start is **three steps** on a question that only needs three.
Only two distinct answers appear in the middle of that table, which tells you the payoff saturates: getting inside $[1.2, 1.3]$ is worth two steps, and getting closer than that is worth nothing.

**When no bracket is given**, find one the cheap way: evaluate $f$ at consecutive integers until the sign flips.
That is arithmetic, not calculus, and it takes seconds.

### Family 2 - a transcendental equation

**Trigger.** $\cos x = x$, $xe^x = 1$, $\ln x = 1/x$, $e^x = 3x$.
**Tool.** Subtract to make $f$, then proceed unchanged.

| equation | $f(x)$ | bracket | root (4dp) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\cos x = x$ | $\cos x - x$ | $[0,1]$ | 0.7391 |
| $xe^x = 1$ | $xe^x - 1$ | $[0,1]$ | 0.5671 |
| $\ln x = 1/x$ | $\ln x - 1/x$ | $[1,2]$ | 1.7632 |
| $e^x = 3x$ | $e^x - 3x$ | $[0,1]$ | 0.6191 |
| $\sin x = x/2$ | $\sin x - x/2$ | $[1,3]$ | 1.8955 |
| $x = \cos^2 x$ | $x - \cos^2 x$ | $[0,1]$ | 0.6417 |

Every one reaches four decimals within four steps, exactly like the polynomials.
The differentiation is the only new work.

**Two traps live in this family and nowhere else.**
First, $\sin x = x/2$ has $x = 0$ as a root as well, and Newton started at 0.5 collapses onto it: **rewriting as $f = 0$ can hand you a root the question did not want.**
Second, $e^x = 3x$ has a *second* intersection at 1.5121, so the bracket is not optional here even though it looks like decoration.

### Family 3 - a number defined as a root

**Trigger.** "Approximate $\sqrt{5}$", "estimate $\sqrt[3]{7}$".
**Tool.** You build $f$ yourself: $f(x) = x^n - a$.

Newton on $f(x) = x^2 - a$ simplifies beautifully:

$$x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{x_n^2 - a}{2x_n} = \frac{1}{2}\left(x_n + \frac{a}{x_n}\right)$$

which is the Babylonian method, two thousand years older than Newton.

| target | $x_0$ | the exact iterates |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| $\sqrt2$ | 1 | $1,\; 3/2,\; 17/12,\; 577/408$ |
| $\sqrt5$ | 2 | $2,\; 9/4,\; 161/72,\; 51841/23184$ |
| $\sqrt{10}$ | 3 | $3,\; 19/6,\; 721/228,\; 1039681/328776$ |
| $\sqrt[3]{7}$ | 2 | $2,\; 23/12,\; 18215/9522$ |

Note how few distinct magnitudes appear: every third iterate is already correct to five or six figures, and the fourth is beyond what any exam asks.

**This family is where category 12 and category 13 meet, and the meeting is exact.**
Q12.1 estimated $\sqrt{9.2}$ from $a = 9$ with differentials and got $91/30$.
Newton on $x^2 - 9.2$ from $x_0 = 3$ gives $\dfrac{1}{2}\left(3 + \dfrac{9.2}{3}\right) = \dfrac{91}{30}$.

**The same rational number, by two routes that look nothing alike.**
That is not a coincidence and it is not approximate: solving the tangent line for its own root *is* one Newton step, so Q12 is Newton's method stopped after one iteration.
The second Babylonian step gives $16561/5460$, which is $\sqrt{9.2}$ to 5.5e-09, against Q12.1's error of 1.83e-04.
One more step buys four orders of magnitude, and that single comparison is the best argument for iterating that this course contains.

### Family 4 - a reciprocal with no division

**Trigger.** "Compute $1/a$ using only multiplication and subtraction."
**Tool.** $f(x) = 1/x - a$, which gives $x_{n+1} = x_n(2 - a x_n)$.

| target | $x_0$ | iterates |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| $1/7$ | 0.1 | 0.13, 0.1417, 0.14284777, 0.1428571422 |
| $1/3$ | 0.3 | 0.33, 0.3333, 0.33333333, 0.3333333333 |
| $1/13$ | 0.07 | 0.0763, 0.07691803, 0.0769230766, 0.0769230769 |

Look at the pattern in the middle column: each step roughly doubles the run of correct digits, visible to the naked eye.
This is how computers actually divide.

**This family has a convergence window and the others do not.** It converges only for $0 < x_0 < 2/a$.
From $x_0 = 0.5$ with $a = 7$ it diverges immediately, and $x_0 = 2/a$ exactly maps to 0 and sticks there.

### Family 5 - the intersection of two curves

**Trigger.** "Where does $y = e^x$ meet $y = 3x$?"
**Tool.** Identical to Family 2 - subtract, then find a root.

| curves | abscissa (4dp) |
| :--- | :--- |
| $x^3$ and $x + 1$ | 1.3247 |
| $e^x$ and $3x$ | 0.6191 |
| $\cos x$ and $x$ | 0.7391 |
| $x^2$ and $\cos x$ | 0.8241 |

The only new thing is remembering to report the $y$ value too if the question asks for the *point*.

### Family 6 - "carry out exactly $N$ iterations"

**Trigger.** "Find $x_2$", "perform two iterations of Newton's method".
**Tool.** The same iteration, stopped early and reported honestly.

| $x_0$ | $x_1$ | $x_2$ |
| ---: | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | $4/3 = 1.3333333333$ | $391/310 = 1.2612903226$ |
| 1.5 | $323/248 = 1.3024193548$ | 1.2579188022 |
| 2 | $53/34 = 1.5588235294$ | 1.3243105219 |

**Those three values of $x_2$ disagree in the second decimal place.**
So "give $x_2$" has no answer at all without the stem's $x_0$, and copying a remembered iterate from a different starting point is a guaranteed zero.
Read the stem for $x_0$ before you compute anything.

### Family 7 - diagnose a failure

**Trigger.** "Explain why Newton's method fails for ...".
**Tool.** Name which of the four modes it is.

| mode | exhibit | what happens |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **flat $f'$** | $x^4+2x-5$ from $-0.79$ | $f' = 0.0278$, one step lands at 221.5 |
| **wrong basin** | $x^4+2x-5$ from $-0.8$ | converges to $-1.7027$, the other root |
| **a cycle** | $x^3-2x+2$ from 0 | $0, 1, 0, 1, \dots$ for ever |
| **divergence** | $f(x) = x^{1/3}$ | $N(x) = -2x$, so $|x_n|$ doubles and the sign flips |

The cycle exhibit is exact, not approximate: $N(0) = 1$ and $N(1) = 0$ in exact rationals, and the real root at $-1.7693$ is never approached.
Sections 9 and 10 give the mechanism for each.

### Family 8 - a multiple root

**Trigger.** $f$ and $f'$ vanish together, e.g. $f(x) = (x-1)^2(x+3)$.
**Tool.** The same iteration, but the quadratic-convergence promise is void.

| multiplicity $m$ | measured error ratio $e_{n+1}/e_n$ | $1 - 1/m$ |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2 | 0.50000000 | 0.5 |
| 3 | 0.66666667 | 0.6666667 |
| 4 | 0.75000000 | 0.75 |
| 5 | 0.80000000 | 0.8 |

Convergence drops from quadratic to **linear**, at rate exactly $1 - 1/m$.
Four decimal places then takes about fourteen steps instead of three.

**This is the sharpest caveat in the whole topic.**
"Correct digits double each step" is true only when $f'(r) \ne 0$.
Here $f'(r) = 9.92$, comfortably nonzero, which is *why* the headline question behaves.
Say that when you claim quadratic convergence, and the claim becomes a statement instead of a slogan.

### Family 9 - how many steps for a stated accuracy

**Trigger.** "How many iterations are needed for six decimal places?"
**Tool.** Count digits, do not count iterations.

Correct decimal digits along Route A: 0.61, 1.33, 2.70, 5.43, 10.88, 21.77.

Each entry is **more than double** its predecessor.
So the rule is: find how many correct digits $x_0$ has, then double until you pass your target.
From 0.61 digits, four decimal places needs three steps and six needs four.

The doubling is not magic, it is the constant $C = f''(r)/2f'(r) = 0.9536$: since $e_{n+1} \approx C e_n^2$ and $C$ is close to 1, the exponent simply doubles.
When $C$ is large the doubling starts later; when $f'(r) = 0$ it never starts at all, which is Family 8.

---

## 9. The trap list

Ranked by how often each actually costs marks.

**1. Rounding the intermediate iterates.**
This is the most expensive habit in the topic and it looks like carefulness.
Rounding every iterate to $k$ decimals caps the accuracy you can ever reach, no matter how many steps you take:

| rounded to | the chain stalls at | final error |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| 2dp | 1.26 | 4.06e-03 |
| 3dp | 1.256 | 6.25e-05 |
| 4dp | 1.2559 | 3.75e-05 |
| 5dp | 1.25594 | 2.45e-06 |
| 6dp | 1.255938 | 4.52e-07 |
| full precision, $x_4$ | 1.2559375489 | **7.06e-10** |

Quadratic convergence dies the moment you round, because the method can only square an error it is actually given.
On this question the 4dp-rounded chain does reach 1.2559 - but its residual error of 3.75e-05 is **three times** the 1.245e-05 margin to the nearest rounding boundary, so it survived by luck, not by design.

**2. Stopping at the wrong iterate, and the 1.2560 trap.**
The root is $1.25593754\ldots$, which sits only **1.245e-05** below the four-decimal rounding boundary at 1.25595.
So an iterate approaching from above must beat 1.245e-05, not the 5e-05 that "four decimal places" suggests.

Route B's $x_3 = 1.2559647$ has an error of 2.72e-05.
That is inside 5e-05 and it still rounds to **1.2560**, which is wrong.
**Do not infer a digit count from the size of an error.**
This is the same lesson Q12.3 found on $\sqrt{16.4}$, arriving here from the other direction.

**3. Reporting more digits than the iteration has earned.**
$x_2$ on Route A is 1.2579188021959602 as a float, and exactly two of those digits are correct.
Writing 1.25792 claims five.
The defensible rule: report only the digits that two successive iterates agree on.

**4. Getting $f'$ wrong.**
Every iterate inherits it, so a slip here is not a small error, it is a different method converging to a different place.
Check $f'$ once, at a point where the arithmetic is easy, before you start iterating.

**5. Believing the "iterate again and it does not move" check.**
It does not work, and this is the deepest trap in the topic.
Eight plausible corruptions of Newton's formula were tested at the true root:

| corruption | fixes the true root? |
| :--- | :--- |
| $x + f/f'$ (sign flipped) | **yes** |
| $x - f/f''$ | **yes** |
| $f' = 4x^3$ (lost the $+2$) | **yes** |
| $f' = 4x^4+2$ (power not dropped) | **yes** |
| $x - f\cdot f'$ | **yes** |
| $x - f(x)$ (forgot to divide) | **yes** |
| $x - f'/f$ | no |
| $f/f'$ (dropped the $x$) | no |

**Six of the eight leave the true root exactly where it is.**
The mechanism is simple once you see it: $f(r) = 0$, so any correction term that *multiplies* $f$ vanishes at the root regardless of what else is wrong with it.
The two survivors are precisely the two that do not multiply $f$.

So the root is a fixed point of almost any corrupted iteration, and "plug the answer back into my formula and see if it moves" cannot detect a wrong formula.
**Substitute into $f$, not into $N$.**
This is category 13's version of Q12's zero-increment blind spot and Q11's zero-rate blind spot, and it is worse than both, because the blind spot sits *at the answer* rather than at some degenerate input you could avoid.

**6. Choosing $x_0$ carelessly.**
Costs up to two steps here and can cost the whole question in Family 7.

**7. Answering the wrong question.**
"Two iterations" means report $x_2$. "Approximate the solution" means report the root.

**8. The factor-equals-one hiding point.**
Writing $f' = 4x^4 + 2$ instead of $4x^3 + 2$ is bit-identical to the truth at $x = 1$, because $x^4 = x^3$ there.
That is the queue's recurring rule again: a wrong answer hides wherever the factor it corrupts equals 1.
At $x_0 = 1.5$ and at $x_0 = 2$ **none** of the eight corruptions hides, so either of those is a safe place to sanity-check your formula.

---

## 10. Why this question cannot go wrong, and when the method can

The three failure modes are real, and none of them can happen here.
Being able to say *why* is what a "explain when Newton's method fails" question wants.

### Mode 1: a flat $f'(x_n)$

The iterate is thrown a distance $f(x_n)/f'(x_n)$, so a small denominator means a large jump.

| $x_0$ | $f'(x_0)$ | $x_1$ |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $-0.79$ | 0.0278 | 221.54 |
| $-0.7937005$ | 1.964e-07 | 3.15e+07 |
| $-0.7937005259840997$ | 4.44e-16 | 1.39e+16 |

The damage scales as $1/f'$: cut $f'$ by a factor and the jump grows by the same factor.

**Why it cannot happen here.** $f'(x) = 4x^3 + 2$ has exactly one zero, at $x_c = -\sqrt[3]{1/2} = -0.7937005259840998$.
On $[1,2]$, $f'$ never falls below 6.
The stem's interval is not just a hint about where the root is, it is a guarantee that the denominator stays healthy.

### Mode 2: converging to a different root

$f$ has a second real root at $-1.7027063709099214$.
Scanning starting points across $[-20, 20]$ finds **exactly one basin boundary**, and it is $x_c$ itself.

- every $x_0 > -0.7937005259840998$ converges to **1.2559**
- every $x_0 < -0.7937005259840998$ converges to **-1.7027**

That is unusually clean.
Most functions have basins that fractal near the boundaries; this one splits the line into two intervals, because $f$ is convex everywhere and has only two real roots.
$x_0 = -0.8$ looks harmless and lands on the wrong root, which is the version of this an examiner would set.

### Mode 3: oscillation between two points

The famous failure is $f(x) = x^3 - 2x + 2$ from $x_0 = 0$, which cycles $0, 1, 0, 1, \dots$ exactly and never approaches the real root at $-1.7693$.

**For $x^4 + 2x - 5$ this cannot happen, and that is provable rather than merely unobserved.**
Setting $N(N(x)) = x$ and clearing denominators gives a polynomial of degree 16.
Every root of $f$ is a fixed point of $N$, so $f$ divides it exactly, leaving a cofactor of degree 12.
**All twelve roots of that cofactor are complex**, in six conjugate pairs, so there is no real 2-cycle at all.

The same machinery run on $x^3 - 2x + 2$ returns a degree-6 cofactor with **four** real roots, which are two genuine 2-cycles: the famous $\{0, 1\}$ and a second one at $\{0.133346,\; 1.024967\}$.
A census that can find two cycles where cycles exist, and none here, is a measurement.
A census that always returns none would be indistinguishable from a broken one.

### Mode 4: outright divergence

Not available for this $f$ either.
The standard exhibit is $f(x) = x^{1/3}$, where $N(x) = x - 3x = -2x$, so the iterate doubles and flips sign every step: $0.1, -0.2, 0.4, -0.8, 1.6, -3.2, 6.4$.

### The positive statement

$f$ is convex ($f'' = 12x^2 \ge 0$) and increasing on $[1,2]$.
For a convex increasing function, starting anywhere with $f(x_0) > 0$ gives **monotone decreasing convergence**, guaranteed.
$f(2) = 15 > 0$, so $x_0 = 2$ is the provably safe start, and the iterates do descend monotonically to the root without ever crossing it.
$f(1) = -2 < 0$, so $x_0 = 1$ fails that condition and its first step overshoots to $4/3$, past the root - after which it is monotone.

Both converge.
The theorem is what lets you promise it in advance.

---

## 11. What the convergence order actually is

Do not assert that Newton's method is second order. Measure it.

Taking $\log e_{n+1} / \log e_n$ along Route B:

| step | measured order |
| :--- | ---: |
| $e_2$ from $e_1$ | 2.0440 |
| $e_3$ from $e_2$ | 2.0099 |
| $e_4$ from $e_3$ | 2.0045 |
| $e_5$ from $e_4$ | 2.0023 |
| $e_6$ from $e_5$ | 2.0011 |
| $e_7$ from $e_6$ | 2.0006 |
| $e_8$ from $e_7$ | 2.0003 |

**The order is 2, approached from above, halving its excess each step.**

Two cautions that the measurement itself supplies.

**The ladder must be bounded.**
Run at 220 digits, the ninth ratio reads **1.4925** and the tenth reads **1.0000**, because the errors have hit the arithmetic's precision floor and stopped being errors at all.
An unbounded ladder reports that the method is first order.
That is the same class of defect as an unbounded Richardson ladder elsewhere in this course: outside the asymptotic regime the number means nothing.

**The constant matters as much as the order.**
$e_{n+1}/e_n^2$ converges to $0.9536409406443394$, which is exactly $f''(r)/2f'(r)$ computed independently.
Because it is close to 1, correct digits simply double.
If $f''$ were large or $f'(r)$ small, the same order-2 convergence would take several steps to get going.

**A usable consequence.**
Once you are in the regime, $\text{err}(x_{n+1}) \approx C\,|x_{n+1} - x_n|^2$.
Measured accuracy of that prediction: 99.79 percent at $x_3$, 99.9996 percent at $x_4$, and 100.0000 percent at $x_5$.
At $x_1$ it is only 80 percent, so the estimate needs one good step before it can be trusted.

---

## 12. Drill set

Twelve problems. Score *sign and place* separately from *magnitude*: a wrong magnitude means an arithmetic slip, a wrong place count means you misread what the method had earned.

1. $x^4 + 2x - 5 = 0$, $x_0 = 2$. Give $x_2$ to four decimals.
2. $x^3 - x - 1 = 0$, $x_0 = 1.5$, three steps.
3. $\cos x = x$, $x_0 = 1$, three steps.
4. Approximate $\sqrt5$ from $x_0 = 2$, three steps. Give the exact fraction too.
5. Approximate $\sqrt[3]{7}$ from $x_0 = 2$, three steps.
6. Compute $1/7$ from $x_0 = 0.1$ using only multiplication, four steps.
7. $xe^x = 1$, $x_0 = 0.5$, three steps.
8. $e^x = 3x$, smaller root, $x_0 = 0.5$, four steps.
9. $\sqrt2$ from $x_0 = 1$: which is the first iterate correct to six decimals?
10. $f(x) = (x-1)^2(x+3)$, $x_0 = 1.5$. What is the order of convergence, and why?
11. $x^4 + 2x - 5 = 0$ from $x_0 = -0.8$. Which root do you reach?
12. $x^3 - 2x + 2 = 0$ from $x_0 = 0$. What happens, and why?

### Answer key

| # | answer | exact where available | family and method |
| ---: | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | **1.3243** | $30353123/22919944$ | F6 - a specific iterate; note it is 0.068 from the root and wrong in the second place |
| 2 | **1.3247** | | F0 - polynomial in a bracket |
| 3 | **0.7391** | | F2 - subtract to make $f$ |
| 4 | **2.2361** | $51841/23184$ | F3 - Babylonian $\tfrac12(x + 5/x)$ |
| 5 | **1.9129** | $9065194654643/4738902651675$ | F3 - $f = x^3 - 7$ |
| 6 | **0.1429** | error 6.15e-10 | F4 - $x(2-7x)$, no division |
| 7 | **0.5671** | | F2 - the omega constant |
| 8 | **0.6191** | | F5 - second intersection is at 1.5121 |
| 9 | **$x_4$** | $x_3 = 577/408$ is off by 2.12e-06 | F9 - count digits, not steps |
| 10 | **order 1** (linear), ratio exactly 0.5 | $1 - 1/m$ with $m = 2$ | F8 - a double root kills quadratic convergence |
| 11 | **$-1.7027$**, the wrong root | boundary is $x_c = -0.7937$ | F7 - $-0.8$ sits left of the critical point |
| 12 | **oscillates $0,1,0,1$ for ever** | exact 2-cycle | F7 - the real root at $-1.7693$ is never reached |

Problems 10, 11 and 12 have no number for an answer, and that is the point: a third of what this topic examines is whether the method applies at all.

## 13. The one-page decision tree

```
  An equation to solve numerically
      |
      +-- Is it already f(x) = 0 ?
      |      no  -> subtract:  g = h  becomes  f = g - h
      |      (a root you did not want may appear; keep the bracket)
      |
      +-- Is the unknown a NUMBER (sqrt, cube root, reciprocal) ?
      |      yes -> build f yourself:   x^n - a    or   1/x - a
      |             sqrt shortcut:  x <- (x + a/x)/2
      |             1/a  shortcut:  x <- x(2 - ax)      window 0 < x0 < 2/a
      |
      +-- DIFFERENTIATE, and check f' before iterating
      |
      +-- Is a bracket given ?
      |      yes -> confirm the sign change; take the MIDPOINT
      |      no  -> evaluate f at integers until the sign flips
      |             then one extra sign test buys a whole step
      |
      +-- Does f'(r) = 0  (a repeated factor) ?
      |      yes -> convergence is LINEAR at rate 1 - 1/m; expect ~14 steps
      |      no  -> correct digits DOUBLE each step; expect 3 or 4
      |
      +-- ITERATE at full precision.  Never round on the way.
      |
      +-- STOP when two successive iterates agree to your target + 1 digit
      |
      +-- CHECK by substituting into f, NEVER by re-running the iteration
      |      (six of eight wrong formulas fix the root too)
      |
      +-- ROUND once, at the end               -> 1.2559
      +-- PREVIEW the entry before submitting
```
