# Q19.1 - Area between a line and a parabola

**The question (Final Exam 1, item 10, 8 points).** Find the area between the curves $y = x$ and $y = 2 - x^2$.

**The answer.** $\dfrac{9}{2} = 4.5000$

**What to type into Möbius:** `9/2`

Provenance: parsed out of `notes\MATH265\MATH265.md`, Final Exam 1 block, where the value is printed inline at the end of the stem in that paper's convention.
Final Exam 1 prints 14 values summing to 124, so this item is 6.45 percent of that paper.
Every number below was recomputed in Python before it was written: 18 wrong-answer candidates, five independent routes to the area, and a root census controlled in both directions.

---

## 0. The 30-second version

```
1. SET THE CURVES EQUAL      x = 2 - x^2   ->   x^2 + x - 2 = 0   ->   x = -2, x = 1
2. PICK A POINT BETWEEN      at x = -1/2 : parabola 1.7500 , line -0.5000 -> parabola on top
3. INTEGRATE (TOP - BOTTOM)  A = int_{-2}^{1} ( (2 - x^2) - x ) dx
4. EVALUATE                  [ 2x - x^3/3 - x^2/2 ]_{-2}^{1} = 7/6 - (-10/3) = 9/2
```

Four lines, and none of them needs a lookup.
Step 2 is the one students skip, and it is the one that costs the sign.

---

## 1. What this question is really testing

This question **opens the applications-of-integration block**, which is the largest category in the whole bank at nine questions (Q19.1 through Q19.9).
Everything in section 3 below is the foundation those other eight sit on, so it is worth over-learning here rather than re-learning eight times.

| The reflex it wants | Where it comes back |
| :--- | :--- |
| An integral of a *difference* measures the region between two graphs | Q19.2, and every area question ever set |
| Find the interval yourself when the question does not give one | Q19.1 and Q19.7 (where you solve for the endpoint) |
| Decide which curve is on top by evaluating, not by squinting | Q19.2, where the answer changes three times across the interval |
| An integral of a rate gives an accumulated amount | Q19.3, Q19.8, Q19.9 |
| Set up an integral from a physical description | Q19.4, Q19.5 |
| Divide an integral by the length of the interval | Q19.6, Q19.7 |
| Antidifferentiate a polynomial and evaluate | all nine |

The single sentence about its purpose: **the examiner is checking that you can turn a picture into a definite integral, in that order, and not the other way round.**
The integration itself is a two-term polynomial and is the easy part.

At 8 points it is one of the heavier items on Final Exam 1 (4 of the 14 items carry more, and the heaviest carries 20).
That weight is almost certainly for the setup rather than for the arithmetic, though no marking scheme exists anywhere in the course files, so treat that as inference and not as fact.

---

## 2. The five things you must have cold

**(a) Solving a quadratic, exactly.**

| Form | Method | Worked here |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $x^2 + bx + c = 0$ with integer roots | factor | $x^2 + x - 2 = (x+2)(x-1)$ |
| anything else | quadratic formula | $x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}$ |
| check | Vieta | sum of roots $= -b$, product $= c$ |

Here the sum is $-2 + 1 = -1 = -b$ and the product is $-2 \times 1 = -2 = c$, both correct.
That check costs three seconds and catches a sign slip in the factoring.

**(b) The three antiderivatives this question needs.**

| $f(x)$ | $\int f\,dx$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| $k$ (a constant) | $kx$ |
| $x$ | $x^2/2$ |
| $x^2$ | $x^3/3$ |

**(c) The Fundamental Theorem, part 2.** $\int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)$, upper minus lower, in that order.
Reversing it flips the sign, and section 6 shows that on this question a flipped sign still has the right magnitude.

**(d) What "the area between the curves" means when no interval is given.**
It means the *bounded* region the two curves enclose between themselves.
The endpoints are therefore the intersection points, and finding them is part of the question.

**(e) The sign convention.**
$\int_a^b (\text{top} - \text{bottom})\,dx$ is positive.
$\int_a^b (\text{bottom} - \text{top})\,dx$ is the negative of it.
Area is a positive number, so if your integral comes out negative you have the order backwards, not a wrong area.

---

## 3. The universal procedure - the foundation for all nine Q19 questions

> **1. Sketch, roughly.** You are not being marked on the picture; you are using it to see how many pieces the region has.
>
> **2. Find the intersections exactly.** Set the two expressions equal and solve algebraically. Never read them off the sketch.
>
> **3. Decide which curve is on top, by evaluating both at one point strictly between consecutive intersections.** Write the comparison down.
>
> **4. Write the definite integral before you evaluate it.** $A = \int_a^b (\text{top} - \text{bottom})\,dx$.
>
> **5. Antidifferentiate and evaluate**, upper limit minus lower limit.
>
> **6. Check the sign and the magnitude.** A negative answer means step 3 went the wrong way.

### 3.1 Why it is (top minus bottom), and never a careless absolute value

A vertical strip at position $x$ has height $\text{top}(x) - \text{bottom}(x)$ and width $dx$.
Adding up the strips is exactly $\int (\text{top} - \text{bottom})\,dx$.
The height of a strip is a length, so it must be positive, which is the whole reason the order matters.

The textbook formula is often written $A = \int_a^b |f(x) - g(x)|\,dx$, and that is correct.
It is also useless as written, because you cannot antidifferentiate an absolute value directly.
What the absolute value is really telling you is: **find where $f - g$ changes sign, and split the integral there.**

On Q19.1 there is nothing to split.
The difference $D(x) = (2 - x^2) - x = -(x+2)(x-1)$ has its only two zeros at the endpoints $-2$ and $1$, and it is strictly positive at every one of the 20,000 interior points tested.
So $\int_{-2}^{1} |D| = \int_{-2}^{1} D$ here, and the absolute value is invisible.

**That is exactly why the absolute value is dangerous on this question.** It is a rule you are told, that you never see fire, on the question that introduces the topic. Q19.2 is where it fires, and section 3.5 shows what it costs there.

**The rule to carry:** the absolute value matters *only* when the curves cross **strictly inside** the interval.
Two intersection points that are the interval's own endpoints never need a split.
So the split test is one question: **are there any crossings strictly between $a$ and $b$?**

### 3.2 Finding the intersections exactly rather than reading them off a graph

Set the expressions equal and solve.

$$x = 2 - x^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^2 + x - 2 = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (x+2)(x-1) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x = -2,\ 1$$

Three reasons never to read them off the sketch:

1. **A slightly wrong endpoint is almost free, and that is the trap.** This document's first draft claimed a 1.5 percent endpoint error becomes a 4.5 percent area error; the verification refuted it outright. Integrating from $-1.97$ instead of $-2$, a 1.5 percent endpoint error, changes the area by **0.0298 percent**. The reason is worth knowing: $\dfrac{dA}{da} = -D(a)$, and $D$ *vanishes* at a true intersection, so the area is **stationary** in the endpoint and the error is second order. The measured order in the offset is 1.9870, 1.9935, 1.9968, 1.9984. So a sketch-read endpoint that is nearly right gives an answer that is nearly right, you never notice the method was wrong, and you carry it to Q19.2 where the endpoints are $\pm\pi/4$ and there is nothing to nearly-read.
2. **Irrational intersections exist and look like nothing.** Family 1 in section 8 has a pair whose intersections are $\dfrac{-1 \pm \sqrt{33}}{4}$, which no sketch will ever hand you.
3. **A tangency looks like a crossing.** Two curves that touch without crossing produce a *repeated* root, which the algebra shows and the picture does not. See family 4.

**The independent check, and a warning about it.** A numerical root census that hunts for sign changes was run on this difference over $[-6, 6]$ and returned exactly two roots, $-2$ and $1$.
That census was proved honest in both directions before its verdict was trusted: it returns **zero** on $y = x$ against $y = -2 - x^2$ (no real intersections), **three** on $y = x$ against $y = x^3$, and **four** on $y = 0$ against $y = x^4 - 5x^2 + 4$.
It also returns **zero** on a tangency, $y = 2x - 1$ against $y = x^2$, which is the honest failure of the method: a curve that touches without crossing has no sign change to find.
Worse, whether such a touch is found at all depends on the arithmetic of the grid.
On $y = x^2$ against $y = x^4$ the same census reported **three** roots on an even grid, which happens to land on $x = 0$, and **two** on an odd grid, which does not.
**A sign-change census is not a root-finder at a tangency**, and the algebra is what settles it.

### 3.3 Vertical strips versus horizontal strips

| | Vertical strips ($dx$) | Horizontal strips ($dy$) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Strip height / width | $\text{top}(x) - \text{bottom}(x)$ | $\text{right}(y) - \text{left}(y)$ |
| You need | both curves as $y = f(x)$ | both curves as $x = g(y)$ |
| Limits are | the $x$ of the intersections | the $y$ of the intersections |
| Reach for it when | the top and bottom boundaries each stay the same curve all the way across | the left and right boundaries each stay the same curve all the way up |

**The decision is not about taste, it is about how many pieces each choice needs.**
Count the pieces, and pick the smaller count.

On Q19.1, vertical wins **1 integral to 2**:

- **Vertical.** The top is the parabola for the whole span $-2 \le x \le 1$ and the bottom is the line for the whole span. One integral.
- **Horizontal.** Solving gives $x = \pm\sqrt{2 - y}$ for the parabola and $x = y$ for the line. For $-2 \le y \le 1$ the region runs from the parabola's left branch across to the line. For $1 \le y \le 2$ it runs from the parabola's left branch across to its right branch. The right-hand boundary **changes curve at $y = 1$**, so that is two integrals.

Section 4 works the horizontal route anyway, because doing it once is how you learn to recognise the questions where it is the *shorter* count.
Family 5 in section 8 has one: $x = y^2$ against $x = y + 2$ is one integral in $y$ and two in $x$, exactly the mirror image of this question.

**The cue.** Write both curves as $y = f(x)$ and ask whether the top boundary is a single formula across the whole span. Then write them as $x = g(y)$ and ask the same about the right boundary. Whichever gives a single formula, use that variable. If a sideways-opening parabola or a curve like $x = y^2$ appears, that is the strongest single hint that $y$ is the easier variable.

### 3.4 What a marker expects to see written down

No marking scheme exists anywhere in the four course files, so this is **inference from the question's wording and its point value**, not a quoted rubric.
On that basis, three things should appear on the page before the number does:

| Write this down | Because |
| :--- | :--- |
| **The intersection work.** $x = 2 - x^2 \Rightarrow x^2 + x - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow x = -2, 1$ | The question gave no interval, so producing one is part of the answer |
| **The orientation decision.** "At $x = -1/2$ the parabola is at $1.7500$ and the line is at $-0.5000$, so the parabola is above." | It is the only step that determines the sign, and it is one line |
| **The definite integral, before its value.** $A = \int_{-2}^{1} (2 - x^2 - x)\,dx$ | It is the sentence that says you understood the geometry |

Then the antiderivative, then the evaluation, then the number.
Möbius marks the number only, but writing these three lines is what makes you get the number right, which is the practical argument for them regardless of what any rubric says.

### 3.5 What generalises to Q19.2, and what each later sub-family adds

Q19.1 and Q19.2 are the same question shape.
The whole of section 3 transfers unchanged.
Three things change:

1. **The interval is given** on Q19.2 (it is $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$), so step 2 stops being "find the endpoints" and becomes "find the crossings *inside* the given endpoints".
2. **The curves are transcendental**, so the intersections come from $\cos x = 1/\sqrt 2$ rather than from a quadratic, and there are two of them at $\pm\pi/4$.
3. **The split fires.** Both crossings are strictly interior, so the region is three pieces, and the top curve alternates.

That third point is the one worth measuring.
Integrating Q19.2 in one go over $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ without splitting gives **-0.2214414691**, which is *negative* and therefore obviously not an area.
Splitting at $\pm\pi/4$ and adding the three magnitudes gives **0.8284271247**, which is exactly $2\sqrt 2 - 2 = 0.8284271247$ (the $\pi$ terms in the three pieces cancel).
So on Q19.2 the mistake is loud. On Q19.1 it does not exist. Learn the rule here where it is quiet, so it is already a habit there.

The rest of the category adds one new idea each:

| Question | What it adds on top of section 3 |
| :--- | :--- |
| Q19.2 area, cosine vs a horizontal line | the interval is given, and the split fires |
| Q19.3 net change | the integrand is a **rate**, and $\int_a^b r(t)\,dt$ is the accumulated amount |
| Q19.4, Q19.5 work | you must **build** the integrand from a physical description; the strip is a slice of chain or a stretch of spring |
| Q19.6, Q19.7 average value | $\dfrac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f$; Q19.7 inverts it and solves for the endpoint |
| Q19.8, Q19.9 displacement and distance | **displacement is $\int v$, distance is $\int \lvert v \rvert$** - which is section 3.1's split rule in physics clothing |

Note the last row. Displacement against distance is exactly the difference between $\int (f-g)$ and $\int |f-g|$, so Q19.8 is Q19.1's absolute-value question asked again with velocity instead of curves. That is the single strongest reason to get section 3.1 solid here.

---

## 4. Q19.1 worked five ways

### Route A - vertical strips, the exact antiderivative (use this one)

Intersections: $x = 2 - x^2$, so $x^2 + x - 2 = 0$, so $(x+2)(x-1) = 0$, giving $x = -2$ and $x = 1$.

Orientation at $x = -\tfrac12$: the parabola gives $2 - \tfrac14 = 1.7500$, the line gives $-0.5000$.
The parabola is above, by $2.2500$.

$$A = \int_{-2}^{1}\Big( (2 - x^2) - x \Big)\,dx = \int_{-2}^{1} (2 - x - x^2)\,dx$$

$$= \Big[\, 2x - \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3} \,\Big]_{-2}^{1}
= \Big( 2 - \tfrac12 - \tfrac13 \Big) - \Big( -4 - 2 + \tfrac83 \Big)
= \frac{7}{6} - \left(-\frac{10}{3}\right) = \frac{27}{6} = \frac{9}{2}$$

### Route B - the parabola shortcut

When the difference of the two curves is a quadratic $D(x) = a(x - x_1)(x - x_2)$, the enclosed area is

$$A = \frac{|a| \, (x_2 - x_1)^3}{6}$$

Here $D(x) = -(x+2)(x-1)$, so $a = -1$, $x_2 - x_1 = 3$, and $A = \dfrac{1 \cdot 27}{6} = \dfrac92$.
Computed: **4.5000000000**.

This is worth knowing as a **check**, not as a method to show.
It was verified against quadrature on the 114 two-root quadratics in a 196-triple coefficient sweep (the other 82 have no two real roots and were skipped), and on a second pair ($y = 3x+1$ against $y = x^2 - 2x + 5$) where it also holds.

**Its trap is live here and invisible.** The $|a|$ is $1$ on Q19.1, so a student who forgets it entirely still gets $9/2$.
On $y = x$ against $y = 4 - 2x^2$ the same omission is wrong by a factor of exactly $2$. See family 1.

### Route C - Archimedes, the two-thirds law

A parabolic segment fills exactly $\tfrac23$ of the parallelogram built on its chord.

$$A = \frac{2}{3} \times (\text{span}) \times (\text{maximum vertical gap})$$

The maximum gap is at the midpoint $x = -\tfrac12$ and equals $2.2500$; the span is $3$.
So $A = \tfrac23 \times 3 \times 2.2500 = $ **4.5000000000**.

This is algebraically identical to route B, since the maximum gap of $a(x-x_1)(x-x_2)$ is $|a|(x_2-x_1)^2/4$.
It is the better one to remember, because it doubles as a **magnitude check on any area question**: the enclosing parallelogram here has area $3 \times 2.2500 = 6.7500000000$, and $9/2$ is two-thirds of that. Note the shape is a parallelogram standing on the chord, not an axis-aligned rectangle; a rectangle of the same width and height would not even contain the region.
It is specific to a parabola, though. On $y = \sqrt x$ against $y = x^2$ the two-thirds law is wrong, and the harness proves it there rather than assuming it.

### Route D - horizontal strips

Solve each curve for $x$: the parabola is $x = \pm\sqrt{2-y}$, the line is $x = y$.
The intersections in $y$ are $y = -2$ and $y = 1$, and the parabola's vertex is at $y = 2$.

$$A = \underbrace{\int_{-2}^{1}\Big( y - \big(-\sqrt{2-y}\big) \Big)dy}_{\text{line on the right}} \; + \; \underbrace{\int_{1}^{2} 2\sqrt{2-y}\;dy}_{\text{both parabola branches}}$$

First piece: $\left[\tfrac{y^2}{2}\right]_{-2}^{1} + \int_{1}^{4}\sqrt u\,du$ with $u = 2-y$, which is $-\tfrac32 + \tfrac{14}{3} = \tfrac{19}{6}$.
Second piece: $2\int_0^1 \sqrt u\,du = \tfrac43$.
Total $\tfrac{19}{6} + \tfrac43 = \tfrac{27}{6} = \tfrac92$.

Computed: **3.1666666667** $+$ **1.3333333333** $=$ **4.5000000000**.

The strip description was not assumed; it was checked by sampling points inside each strip and confirming they satisfy both inequalities, and by sampling points just outside and confirming they do not.

### Route E - numerical quadrature (a check, never an answer)

Tanh-sinh quadrature of $(2 - x^2 - x)$ over $[-2, 1]$ gives **4.5000000000000**, and levels 12 and 13 agree to 1.599e-14.
Composite Simpson at $n = 512$ sits 0.000e+00 from the exact value.

**A digit-lock inherits the precision of the method that produced it, so the method's order was measured rather than assumed.**
On *this* integrand the measurement is degenerate, and that is worth saying plainly: the integrand is a **quadratic**, Simpson's rule is exact on every cubic, so the error is 0.000e+00 at every $n$ from 16 to 512 and **no convergence order can be measured on this question at all**.
The order was therefore measured on a separate curved control, $\sin(t^2)$ over $[0,1]$: **4.0030, 4.0008, 4.0002, 4.0001, 4.0006**, which is 4 as advertised.
The same routine on a cusp integrand, $|t|^{2/3}$ over $[-1,1]$, measures **1.6663, 1.6666, 1.6667, 1.6667, 1.6667**, which proves the measurement can report something other than 4 rather than always printing the answer you hoped for.

One more measured fact, because it reinforces section 3.1 from an unexpected direction.
Integrating $|D|$ over $[-2, 2]$ in one piece, straight through the kink at $x = 1$, is wrong by 4.790e-07.
Splitting at the kink first brings that to 1.243e-14.
**Even the numerics want you to split at the crossing.**

### Route comparison

| Route | Time under pressure | Risk | Verdict |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **A - vertical strips** | ~2 min | a sign slip in orientation, or an arithmetic slip at $x=-2$ | **use this one** |
| B - the $\lvert a\rvert s^3/6$ shortcut | ~20 s | forgetting $\lvert a\rvert$; only works when the difference is a quadratic | check with it |
| C - Archimedes two-thirds | ~20 s | same as B; parabolas only | best magnitude check |
| D - horizontal strips | ~5 min | two integrals, a square root, and a boundary change at $y=1$ | wrong tool here |
| E - quadrature | not available | no calculator does this in Möbius | verification only |

**Under exam pressure, do route A and check with route C.**
Route C is twenty seconds and it catches a wrong interval, a wrong orientation and a dropped term at once, because all three change the magnitude away from two-thirds of the box.

---

## 5. The exam-ready write-up

The version to reproduce on paper, in six sentences:

> The curves meet where $x = 2 - x^2$, that is where $x^2 + x - 2 = 0$, so $(x+2)(x-1) = 0$ and $x = -2$ or $x = 1$.
> Between those values, at $x = -\tfrac12$, the parabola is at $1.7500$ and the line is at $-0.5000$, so the parabola is the upper curve throughout.
> There are no other intersections, so no split is needed.
> Therefore $A = \displaystyle\int_{-2}^{1}\big( (2-x^2) - x \big)\,dx$.
> An antiderivative is $F(x) = 2x - \dfrac{x^2}{2} - \dfrac{x^3}{3}$, so $A = F(1) - F(-2) = \dfrac76 - \left(-\dfrac{10}{3}\right)$.
> $A = \dfrac{27}{6} = \dfrac92$.

The three sentences that carry the reasoning are the first, the second and the fourth: the interval, the orientation, and the integral written before it is evaluated.
This is the same discipline `Q16.1 - Five integrals.md` sets for choosing a technique: name what you are doing before you do it, so the check has something to check against.

---

## 6. Verify before you commit

### 6.1 The three-way agreement, measured

| Route | Value | Agreement with the exact $9/2$ |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Exact antiderivative, in exact rational arithmetic | 4.5000000000 | exact, no tolerance needed |
| Tanh-sinh quadrature of (top $-$ bottom) | 4.5000000000000 | within 1.599e-14 |
| Horizontal strips, two pieces in $y$ | 4.5000000000 | within 2.1e-14 |
| Shortcut $\lvert a\rvert s^3/6$ | 4.5000000000 | exact |
| Archimedes $\tfrac23 \cdot s \cdot h$ | 4.5000000000 | exact |

**All five agree to 2.1e-14.**
That tolerance is the honest one: it is what the floating-point routes actually achieved, not a round number chosen to make the table look tidy.

### 6.2 Three checks worth eight seconds each

**The box check.** The region sits inside the parallelogram on the chord, width $3$ (the span) and height 2.2500 (the largest gap), area 6.7500000000. Your answer must be smaller than that, and for a parabolic segment it should be exactly two-thirds of it. $9/2$ is.

**The sign check.** If the integral came out negative, you subtracted in the wrong order. The magnitude is still right, so **do not redo the integral** - just drop the minus sign and understand why.

**The endpoint check.** Put each intersection back into *both* original equations. At $x = 1$: the line gives $1$, the parabola gives $2 - 1 = 1$. At $x = -2$: the line gives $-2$, the parabola gives $2 - 4 = -2$. Both match, so the interval is right. This is `Q16.1`'s differentiate-back check in its algebraic form: undo the step and see whether you land where you started.

### 6.3 The wrong-answer census

18 plausible mistakes, every one evaluated, none excluded as too silly to matter.
14 of them change the answer and are caught.
4 do not.

| The mistake | What it gives | Verdict |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| Reverse the orientation: integrate (line - parabola) | -4.5000000000 | **HIDES in magnitude** |
| Drop the absolute value in the shortcut: a(span)^3/6 with a = -1 | -4.5000000000 | **HIDES in magnitude** |
| Evaluate F(a) - F(b) instead of F(b) - F(a) | -4.5000000000 | **HIDES in magnitude** |
| Split at x = 0 for no reason and add the two pieces | 4.5000000000 | **identical, signed** |
| Use the parabola's own roots as the interval: [-sqrt 2, sqrt 2] | 3.7712361663 | caught |
| Use [-2, 2], reading 2 as an intersection | 2.6666666667 | caught |
| Sign-flip both roots and integrate over [-1, 2] | 1.5000000000 | caught |
| Keep only the positive part of the interval: [0, 1] | 1.1666666667 | caught |
| Forget to subtract the line: integrate (2 - x^2) | 3.0000000000 | caught |
| Forget to subtract the parabola: integrate x | -1.5000000000 | caught |
| Integrate the absolute value of (top minus bottom) over [-2, 2] | 6.3333333333 | caught |
| Split at x = 0 and subtract the two pieces | 2.1666666667 | caught |
| Antiderivative slip: +x^2/2 where -x^2/2 belongs | 1.5000000000 | caught |
| Antiderivative slip: x^3 where x^3/3 belongs | -1.5000000000 | caught |
| Shortcut with span misread as 1 (roots taken as -1 and 0) | 0.1666666667 | caught |
| Shortcut with /3 instead of /6 | 9.0000000000 | caught |
| Integrate in y but stop at y = 1, forgetting the cap | 3.1666666667 | caught |
| Integrate in y with the line as the left boundary throughout | 6.1666666667 | caught |

**The headline: a sign error on this question keeps the correct magnitude.**
Three different mistakes all land on exactly $-9/2$ - reversing the orientation, dropping the absolute value in the shortcut, and evaluating $F(a) - F(b)$ instead of $F(b) - F(a)$.
Every one of them produces $4.5$ the moment the student writes "area, so it is positive" and drops the sign.
**So the sign error hides completely here, and there is no arithmetic check that can find it.** The only defence is the one-line orientation statement in section 3.4, which fixes the order before the integration rather than after it.

A fourth candidate is identical even in sign: splitting at $x = 0$ for no reason and adding the pieces gives $9/2$ exactly, because there is no sign change at $0$ to be wrong about. An unnecessary split is harmless. A missing necessary one is not.

Of the 14 caught mistakes, the closest miss is off by 0.7287638337, which is 16 percent of the answer.
So **any** mistake that actually changes the region is loud, and every quiet one is a sign.
That is a clean partition and it tells you exactly where to spend your checking time.

## 7. Answer-entry rules

Both exams are Möbius: answer-only, machine-marked, and a correct method with a bad keystroke scores zero.

| Do | Do not |
| :--- | :--- |
| `9/2` | `9\2` (wrong slash) |
| `4.5` (if a decimal is accepted) | `4.5 units^2` - units are not part of a numeric answer |
| `27/6` will usually be accepted as equal | leaving it as `27/6` when the box wants lowest terms |
| Preview the rendered answer before submitting | assuming the parser read `2-x^2` the way you meant |

**The single most expensive typo on this question is a leading minus.** `-9/2` is a different number, and the grader has no way to know you meant the area.
If your working produced a negative, fix the reasoning, then type the positive.

If the box asks for the *setup* rather than the value, the integral is `int(2-x^2-x, x=-2..1)` in Möbius syntax. Preview it: an unbracketed `2-x^2-x` is fine, but `2-x^2-x` typed as `2-x**2-x` is not universally accepted.

## 8. The variation catalog

Read each table as **structure**, not as a list of facts.
Every row is the same four steps from section 3; what changes between families is only **which step becomes the hard one**.

### Family 1 - polynomial against polynomial, interval not given

**Trigger.** Two polynomial curves, no interval stated.
**The hard step is step 2**, finding the intersections.
**Tool.** Factor or the quadratic formula. If the difference is a quadratic, route B and route C both apply as checks.

| Curves | Area | Notes |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| $y = x$, $y = 2 - x^2$ (the question) | 4.5000000000 | roots $-2, 1$; $\lvert a\rvert = 1$ |
| $y = 2x$, $y = x^2$ | 1.3333333333 | roots $0, 2$; $\lvert a\rvert = 1$ |
| $y = x + 6$, $y = x^2$ | 20.8333333333 | roots $-2, 3$; $\lvert a\rvert = 1$ |
| $y = 4 - x^2$, $y = x^2 - 4$ | 21.3333333333 | roots $-2, 2$; $\lvert a\rvert = 2$ |
| $y = x$, $y = 4 - 2x^2$ | 7.8987736390 | irrational roots; $\lvert a\rvert = 2$ |
| $y = \sqrt{x}$, $y = x^2$ | 0.3333333333 | not a quadratic; no shortcut |

Read the structure: five of the six have integer intersections and one does not, and the two rows with $|a| = 2$ are the ones where forgetting the $|a|$ in the shortcut costs you a factor of exactly $2$.
On Q19.1 itself $|a| = 1$, so that error is invisible - which is why the row with $|a| = 2$ is in the table.

### Family 2 - the curves cross inside the interval, so the region splits

**Trigger.** An interval is given, and solving $f = g$ produces a solution **strictly between** the endpoints.
**The hard step is step 3**, because the answer to "which is on top" changes partway across.
**Tool.** Find every interior crossing, then integrate $(top - bottom)$ separately on each sub-interval, choosing the orientation afresh on each one. Equivalently, take the absolute value of each piece and add.

| Curves and interval | Area | Notes |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| $y = x^3$, $y = x$ on $[-1,1]$ | 0.5000000000 | crosses at $0$; unsplit gives $0$ |
| $y = \cos x$, $y = 1/\sqrt 2$ on $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ (Q19.2) | 0.8284271247 | crosses at $\pm\pi/4$; unsplit gives -0.2214414691 |
| $y = \sin x$, $y = \cos x$ on $[0,\pi]$ | 2.8284271247 | crosses at $\pi/4$ |

Read the structure: in every row the unsplit integral is smaller than the true area, and in two of the three it is *negative* or *zero*, which is a free tell. **A negative or suspiciously small "area" is almost always a missed split.**

### Family 3 - the interval is given and there is no interior crossing

**Trigger.** An interval is given and $f - g$ has no zero strictly inside it.
**This is the easiest family and it is the one that lulls you**, because it looks exactly like family 2 until you check.
**Tool.** Check for interior crossings, find none, then integrate straight through.

| Curves and interval | Area | Notes |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| $y = e^x$, $y = 1$ on $[0,1]$ | 0.7182818285 | no interior crossing |
| $y = 1$, $y = 1/x$ on $[1,2]$ | 0.3068528194 | no interior crossing |
| $y = \cos x$, $y = \sin x$ on $[0,\pi/4]$ | 0.4142135624 | crossing sits ON the right endpoint |

The third row is the instructive one: the crossing sits exactly *on* the right endpoint, which needs no split. **On the boundary is not inside.**

### Family 4 - a tangency

**Trigger.** Setting the curves equal produces a **repeated** root.
**The hard step is step 2 again**, but for a different reason: the algebra shows a double root and the sketch shows what looks like a crossing.
**Tool.** Factor fully and count multiplicities. A double root is a touch, and a touch is **not** a crossing, so it needs no split.

| Curves | Area | Notes |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| $y = x^2$, $y = x^4$ | 0.2666666667 | touch at $0$; no split needed |
| $y = x^2$, $y = 2x - 1$ | 0.0000000000 | tangent: the region is a single point, area $0$ |

The second row is the degenerate case worth having seen once: a line tangent to a parabola encloses no region at all, and the correct answer is $0$.

### Family 5 - horizontal strips are the shorter route

**Trigger.** One or both curves is naturally $x$ as a function of $y$ (a sideways parabola, $x = y^2$, $x = \sqrt y$), or the region's top boundary changes curve while its right boundary does not.
**The hard step is step 1**, seeing which variable to use.
**Tool.** Solve both for $x$, find the intersections in $y$, integrate $(\text{right} - \text{left})\,dy$.

| Setup | Area | Notes |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| $x = y^2$, $x = y + 2$ in $y$ | 4.5000000000 | one integral in $y$, two in $x$ |
| the same region in $x$: $[0,1]$ piece | 1.3333333333 | lower boundary is $-\sqrt x$ |
| the same region in $x$: $[1,4]$ piece | 3.1666666667 | lower boundary is the line |

Read the structure: the same region costs one integral in $y$ and two in $x$, and the two $x$-pieces are $4/3$ and $19/6$ - the very same two numbers that appeared in Q19.1's own horizontal route, with the roles swapped. **The two routes are mirror images, and the count of pieces is the only thing that should decide between them.**

### Family 6 - solve for a parameter from a required area

**Trigger.** The area is given and a constant in one of the curves is not.
**The hard step is step 5 run backwards.**
**Tool.** Do the integration with the letter in place, set the result equal to the given area, solve.

| Setup | Value | Notes |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| $y = k - x^2$ over $y = 0$, area $= 36$ | 36.0000000000 | $k = 9$ |
| the same with $k = 4$ | 10.6666666667 | $32/3$, so $k=4$ is refuted |

$\int_{-\sqrt k}^{\sqrt k}(k - x^2)\,dx = \tfrac43 k^{3/2}$, so $\tfrac43 k^{3/2} = 36$ gives $k^{3/2} = 27$ and $k = 9$.
**This is the family Q19.7 belongs to**, with an average value in place of an area, so it is worth doing once here.

---

## 9. The trap list

Ranked by how often each one actually costs a mark, worst first.

1. **Reading the intersections off the sketch instead of solving.** Not because a nearly-right endpoint is costly - measured above, it is nearly free, at 0.0298 percent for a 1.5 percent endpoint error. Because the habit is what fails, and it fails loudly the moment the intersections are not integers: mistaking them for $\pm\sqrt 2$ here is 16.1948 percent off, over 543 times worse.
2. **Getting the orientation backwards, and then hiding it.** Verified above: three separate versions of this mistake all give exactly $-9/2$, and all three become the correct $4.5$ the moment the minus sign is dropped as "obviously area is positive". Decide the orientation by *evaluating at an interior point*, in writing, before integrating.
3. **Using the parabola's own roots as the interval.** $2 - x^2 = 0$ gives $x = \pm\sqrt2$, which are where the parabola meets the *$x$-axis*, not where it meets the line. That gives 0.7287638337 too much. The line is not the $x$-axis.
4. **Not splitting when the curves cross inside a given interval.** Latent on Q19.1, fatal on Q19.2, where the unsplit answer is -0.2214414691 against a true 0.8284271247.
5. **Splitting when nothing crosses.** Harmless arithmetically, as verified, but it burns two minutes you do not have and doubles the chance of an evaluation slip.
6. **Sign errors evaluating at a negative limit.** $F(-2) = 2(-2) - \frac{(-2)^2}{2} - \frac{(-2)^3}{3} = -4 - 2 + \frac83 = -\frac{10}{3}$. The $-x^3/3$ term becomes **positive** at a negative $x$. This is where most of the arithmetic marks are lost on this specific question.
7. **Dropping the $|a|$ in the shortcut.** Invisible here because $|a| = 1$; a factor-of-2 error on the family-1 row where $|a| = 2$.
8. **Forgetting that "area between curves" with no interval means the enclosed region.** Integrating over some interval you invented gives a number that is not the answer to any question.
9. **Reporting a negative number.** Area is a magnitude. If the arithmetic gives $-9/2$, the area is $9/2$.

## 11. The one-page decision tree

```
Q: "area between/enclosed by ..." ?
 |
 +-- Is an INTERVAL given?
 |     |
 |     NO  -> the endpoints ARE the intersections. Solve f(x) = g(x) exactly.        [F1]
 |     |     Two solutions -> that is your interval.
 |     |     Repeated root -> tangency; check whether a region exists at all.        [F4]
 |     |
 |     YES -> solve f(x) = g(x) anyway, and ask: any solution STRICTLY inside?
 |             NO  -> one integral, straight through.                                [F3]
 |             YES -> SPLIT at every interior crossing.                              [F2]
 |
 +-- Which variable?
 |     Top boundary one formula all the way across?   -> vertical strips, dx
 |     Right boundary one formula all the way up?     -> horizontal strips, dy       [F5]
 |     Both work? -> count the pieces each needs, take the smaller count.
 |
 +-- ORIENTATION: evaluate BOTH curves at one point strictly between
 |     consecutive intersections. Write the comparison down. Do not squint at a sketch.
 |
 +-- SET UP:  A = int_a^b (TOP - BOTTOM) dx      <- write this line before evaluating
 |
 +-- EVALUATE: F(b) - F(a), upper minus lower.
 |
 +-- CHECK:  sign positive?                       (negative = orientation reversed)
 |           smaller than span x max-gap?         (box check)
 |           about 2/3 of the box, if a parabola? (Archimedes)
 |           endpoints satisfy BOTH equations?
 |
 +-- PREVIEW the Möbius entry before submitting.
```

# Q19.2 - Area between a cosine and a horizontal line

**The question (Final Exam 2, item 8, 4 points).** Find the area between the curves $\cos x$ and the horizontal line $y = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ in the interval $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$.

**The answer.** $2\sqrt{2} - 2 \approx 0.8284271247$

**What to type into Möbius:** `2*sqrt(2)-2`

*Provenance: parsed from `C:\Users\mnguyen\notes\MATH265\MATH265.md`, Final Exam 2 block, item 8. Final Exam 2 prints twelve point values summing to 81, and 4 is the joint-lightest value on that paper. Every number on this page was computed in `math265-answer-verification.py` sections `q192`, `q192d` and `q192s` before it was written down: 291 assertions, 0 failures, 37 seeded controls.*

---

## 0. The 30-second version

```
cos x = 1/sqrt2   ->  x = +- pi/4          both INSIDE [-pi/2, pi/2]
so the region is THREE pieces, and the top curve alternates
|D| is EVEN                                ->  do [0, pi/2] and double
A = 2 * [ int_0^(pi/4) (cos x - 1/sqrt2) + int_(pi/4)^(pi/2) (1/sqrt2 - cos x) ]
  = 2 * (sqrt2 - 1) = 2 sqrt2 - 2 = 0.8284
```

The whole question is four decisions: solve for the crossings, notice both are interior, split there, and decide the orientation separately on each piece.
Everything else is one antiderivative you already know.

---

## 1. What this question is really testing

| The reflex being tested | Where it comes back |
| :--- | :--- |
| Solve $\cos x = c$ and pick the branch the interval asks for | every trig equation on both papers |
| Notice that a crossing is *strictly inside* the interval | Q19.8, where $\int v$ and $\int \lvert v \rvert$ differ for the same reason |
| Split the integral at the crossing and decide orientation per piece | the definition of $\int \lvert f - g \rvert$ |
| Use evenness to halve the work on purpose, not by accident | any symmetric-interval integral |
| Antidifferentiate $\cos x$ and a constant, and evaluate | Q16.x, Q17.x, Q18.1 |

Q19.1 is the same question with a parabola.
The whole of its section 3 transfers here unchanged, and this page cites it rather than repeating it: see `notes\Q19.1 - Area between a line and a parabola.md`.

**What Q19.2 adds is that the boundary curve is transcendental and periodic**, and that changes exactly three things.

1. **The intersections are solutions of $\cos x = c$, so there are infinitely many.** The interval is what selects which pair you use, and choosing the wrong pair is an error species Q19.1 cannot have.
2. **The curves genuinely cross inside the interval**, so the region splits and the $\lvert \text{top} - \text{bottom} \rvert$ question becomes live rather than theoretical. Q19.1's own page says the absolute value is "a rule you are told, that you never see fire". This is where it fires.
3. **The region is symmetric**, so half the work is free if you take it deliberately.

---

## 2. The four things you must have cold

**Two antiderivatives.**

| $f(x)$ | $\int f\,dx$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| $\cos x$ | $\sin x$ |
| $c$ (a constant) | $cx$ |

That is the entire integration content of this question.
The difficulty is all in the setup.

**Four cosine values, and the angles that produce them.**

| $x$ | $\cos x$ | $x$ | $\cos x$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $\pi/3$ | $1/2$ |
| $\pi/6$ | $\sqrt3/2$ | $\pi/2$ | $0$ |
| $\pi/4$ | $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} = \dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ | | |

**The general solution of $\cos x = c$.**

$$\cos x = c \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x = \pm\arccos(c) + 2k\pi, \quad k \in \mathbb{Z}$$

The $\pm$ is because cosine is even, and the $2k\pi$ is because it is $2\pi$-periodic.
Verified: all fourteen members of the family $\pm\pi/4 + 2k\pi$ for $k = -3 \ldots 3$ satisfy $\cos x = 1/\sqrt2$ to $10^{-14}$, and exactly **two** of them lie in $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$.

**Which functions are even.**
$\cos x$ is even, and a constant is even, so $D(x) = \cos x - 1/\sqrt2$ is even, and so is $\lvert D \rvert$.
Measured directly at 41 sample points across the interval, agreement to $10^{-15}$.

---

## 3. The universal procedure

> **1. Sketch, roughly.** You are using it to count pieces, not to read numbers off it.
>
> **2. Find the crossings exactly**, by solving $f(x) = g(x)$ algebraically.
>
> **3. Keep only the crossings strictly inside the given interval.** This step does not exist on Q19.1 and it is the whole of the new content here.
>
> **4. Decide which curve is on top on each sub-interval**, by evaluating both at one point strictly between consecutive knots.
>
> **5. Write each definite integral before evaluating it**, as $\int (\text{top} - \text{bottom})\,dx$.
>
> **6. Add the pieces.** They are all positive by construction, so there is nothing to repair.

Steps 1, 2, 4, 5 are Q19.1's procedure verbatim.
Steps 3 and 6 are what a periodic boundary adds.

### 3.1 Step 2 in detail - solving $\cos x = 1/\sqrt2$ without losing a branch

$$\cos x = \frac{1}{\sqrt2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x = \pm\frac{\pi}{4} + 2k\pi$$

Three separate mistakes live in this one line, and each produces a different wrong area.

| The slip | What you get | Why it happens |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Taking $x = \pm 3\pi/4$ | area $1.9179486412$ | $3\pi/4$ solves $\cos x = -1/\sqrt2$, not $+1/\sqrt2$. Verified: no member of the $\pm3\pi/4$ family lies in $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ at all. |
| Taking the "standard" pair $\pi/4$ and $7\pi/4$ | area $4.7463757660$ | That is the pair a $[0, 2\pi]$ habit produces. $7\pi/4$ is outside the given interval. |
| Taking only $x = \pi/4$ and forgetting $-\pi/4$ | half an answer | The $\pm$ in $\arccos$ is the easiest symbol in mathematics to drop. |

**The habit that prevents all three: write the general solution first, then intersect it with the interval.**
Do not solve "the" equation; solve the family and then filter.

### 3.2 Step 3 - the periodic trap, measured

A numerical root census was run over the difference $D(x) = \cos x - 1/\sqrt2$.
It was controlled in both directions before its verdict was trusted.

| Window | Roots found | What it shows |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ (the question) | **2** | $\pm\pi/4$, both to $10^{-10}$ |
| $[-\pi/8, \pi/8]$ | **0** | the routine can return zero |
| $[0, \pi/2]$ | **1** | the routine can return one |
| $[-2\pi, 2\pi]$ | **4** | the same equation, a wider window |
| $[-3\pi, 3\pi]$ | **6** | and the count keeps growing |
| $\cos x = 2$, anywhere | **0** | no solutions at all |

**Read the fourth row carefully.**
Two of those four roots, at $\pm 7\pi/4$, are not in the region and contribute nothing.
A periodic boundary makes "how many intersections are there" a question with no answer until you say *where*.
On Q19.1 you could search $[-6, 6]$ and be safe; here that would find extra roots and split the integral in places the question never asked about.

**The census has an honest failure, and grid parity decides whether you see it.**
On a tangency it finds nothing, because a curve that touches without crossing has no sign change.
Tested on $\cos x = 1$: an **even** grid, which happens to land exactly on $x = 0$, reports **1 root**, and an **odd** grid, which does not, reports **0**.
Same routine, same function, different answer.
This reproduces on a cosine what Q19.1 measured on $x^2$ against $x^4$, and the conclusion is the same: **a sign-change census is not a root-finder at a tangency, and the algebra is what settles it.**

A third instance turned up while building this page.
A grid point that lands *exactly* on a root makes the product $D(x_i) \cdot D(x_{i+1})$ equal to zero rather than negative, so the sign-change test misses the root entirely and the region silently loses a split.
It cost a wrong drill answer before it was caught.
**If you write such a census yourself, test `== 0` separately.**

### 3.3 Step 4 - orientation is decided per piece, and never at a knot

Three pieces, three separate decisions.

| Piece | Test point | $\cos x$ | $1/\sqrt2$ | On top |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $[-\pi/2, -\pi/4]$ | $x = -3\pi/8$ | $0.3827$ | $0.7071$ | the **line** |
| $[-\pi/4, \pi/4]$ | $x = 0$ | $1.0000$ | $0.7071$ | the **cosine** |
| $[\pi/4, \pi/2]$ | $x = 3\pi/8$ | $0.3827$ | $0.7071$ | the **line** |

The sign of $D$ genuinely alternates $-, +, -$, which is what "the curves cross" means.
At all three test points $\lvert D \rvert > 10^{-3}$, and each test point is strictly interior to its own piece.

**Never test at a knot.** At $x = \pm\pi/4$, $D$ is exactly zero and the comparison decides nothing.
This is not a pedantic point.
The generic router written to check this page's catalog used the midpoint of each piece, and on the tangency case $y = 1$ against $\cos x$ that midpoint *is* the touch point $x = 0$, where $D = 0$ and "$D > 0$" is false.
It returned $-1.1415926536$ for an area of $\pi - 2$: the sign of the whole answer flipped, from one badly-chosen probe point.
The fix is to probe where $\lvert D \rvert$ is largest, not where the piece happens to be widest.

### 3.4 Step 6 - use the symmetry on purpose

$D$ is even, so $\lvert D \rvert$ is even, so

$$A = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \lvert D \rvert \, dx = 2\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \lvert D \rvert \, dx$$

Verified numerically: the half-interval integral is $0.4142135624 = \sqrt2 - 1$, exactly half the answer.

That turns three integrals into two, and it removes the third piece, which was the one most likely to be added with the wrong sign.
**Take the symmetry deliberately.**
A student who computes the half and forgets to double gets $\sqrt2 - 1 \approx 0.4142$, a positive, plausible-looking number that no check based on sign or magnitude will reject.

### 3.5 What generalises, and what is specific to a periodic boundary

| Generalises to the whole Q19 category | Specific to a periodic boundary |
| :--- | :--- |
| Sketch, solve exactly, decide orientation strictly between, integrate top minus bottom | The intersections are an infinite family, so you must filter by the interval |
| A crossing strictly inside the interval forces a split | A wider search window finds real roots that are not in the region |
| A negative answer means the orientation went the wrong way | The answer's $\pi$ terms may cancel, so "no $\pi$ in the answer" is not evidence of an error |
| Symmetry halves the work when the region is symmetric | Symmetry is nearly always available, because $\sin$ and $\cos$ are even or odd about the natural points |
| Horizontal strips are the alternative when the boundary changes curve | Horizontal strips bring $\arccos$, whose derivative is infinite at the endpoint |

The next questions in the category go elsewhere.
Q19.3, Q19.8 and Q19.9 integrate a rate; Q19.4 and Q19.5 build the integrand from a physical description; Q19.6 and Q19.7 divide by the interval length.
**Q19.8 is this page's split rule in physics clothing**: displacement is $\int v$, distance is $\int \lvert v \rvert$, and the split happens where the velocity changes sign.

---

## 4. Q19.2 worked five ways

Write $D(x) = \cos x - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ and $F(x) = \sin x - \dfrac{x}{\sqrt2}$, so $F' = D$.

### Route A - three pieces, the exact antiderivative (use this one)

**Piece 2, the middle lobe**, where the cosine is on top:

$$\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\left(\cos x - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)dx = \Big[\sin x - \tfrac{x}{\sqrt2}\Big]_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} = \sqrt2 - \frac{\pi\sqrt2}{4} \approx 0.3034928278$$

**Pieces 1 and 3, the outer lobes**, where the line is on top. By symmetry they are equal:

$$\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} - \cos x\right)dx = \frac{\pi\sqrt2}{8} - 1 + \frac{\sqrt2}{2} \approx 0.2624671485$$

**Add them.**

$$A = \left(\sqrt2 - \frac{\pi\sqrt2}{4}\right) + 2\left(\frac{\pi\sqrt2}{8} - 1 + \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right) = 2\sqrt2 - 2$$

The two $\pi\sqrt2/4$ terms cancel exactly.
Section 6.4 explains why that is not a coincidence.

### Route B - symmetry first, two pieces

$$A = 2\left[\int_0^{\pi/4}\left(\cos x - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)dx + \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} - \cos x\right)dx\right] = 2\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2} - \frac{\pi\sqrt2}{8} + \frac{\pi\sqrt2}{8} - 1 + \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\right) = 2(\sqrt2 - 1)$$

**This is the fastest route on paper** and the cancellation is visible inside the bracket rather than only at the end.
Two integrals instead of three, and one fewer chance to get a sign wrong.

### Route C - horizontal strips in $y$

Solve for $x$: the curve is $x = \pm\arccos y$.

- **The middle lobe**, $1/\sqrt2 \le y \le 1$, has width $2\arccos y$.
- **The outer lobes**, $0 \le y \le 1/\sqrt2$, each run from $x = \arccos y$ out to $x = \pi/2$, so each has width $\pi/2 - \arccos y$.

Using $\int \arccos y \, dy = y\arccos y - \sqrt{1-y^2}$,

$$\int_{1/\sqrt2}^{1} 2\arccos y \, dy = \sqrt2 - \frac{\pi\sqrt2}{4}, \qquad 2\int_0^{1/\sqrt2}\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \arccos y\right)dy = \frac{\pi\sqrt2}{4} - 2 + \sqrt2$$

Total $2\sqrt2 - 2$, agreeing with route A to $10^{-12}$.
**This is the wrong route to choose under exam pressure**: it needs $\arccos$, an integration by parts, and three integrals rather than two.
It is here because it is a genuinely independent check, and because family F9 in section 8 is a question where it wins.

### Route D - numerical quadrature (a check, never an answer)

Split at $\pm\pi/4$ first, then integrate each piece.
Simpson on the three pieces agrees with the closed form to $10^{-13}$; a double-exponential (tanh-sinh) rule agrees to the same.

### Route E - Archimedes' two-thirds law, and why it does not apply

Q19.1's best memorisable shortcut is $A = \frac23 \times \text{span} \times \text{largest gap}$, which is exact for a parabola against a chord.
**It is not a general law and it is wrong here.**
Applied to the whole interval it is off by more than $0.5$.

Applied to the *middle lobe only* it gives $0.3067170615$ against the true $0.3034928278$, which is **1.0624 percent high**.
That is the dangerous case: a cosine arch looks so much like a parabola that a wrong shortcut lands within one percent, and no mental check will reject it.
**Carry Archimedes as a magnitude check on parabolas only.**

### Route comparison

| Route | Integrals | Where it goes wrong | Verdict |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| A - three pieces | 3 | three orientation decisions, three chances to slip | correct, slightly long |
| **B - symmetry, two pieces** | **2** | you must remember to double | **use this one under pressure** |
| C - horizontal strips | 3 | needs $\arccos$ and parts | good check, bad exam route |
| D - quadrature | n/a | no closed form | verification only |
| E - Archimedes | 0 | it is a parabola law | do not use here |

All four computational routes plus the closed form agree, with a total spread of $6.7 \times 10^{-16}$.

---

## 5. The exam-ready write-up

No marking scheme exists anywhere in the four course files, so what follows is **inference from the wording and the point value**, not a quoted rubric.
Item 8 carries no "no credit will be given" clause, no "show your work", and no "state which rule" instruction; Final Exam 2's single no-credit clause is on item 1.
Möbius marks the number only.

Five lines earn the number:

1. **The crossings.** "$\cos x = 1/\sqrt2 \Rightarrow x = \pm\pi/4 + 2k\pi$; only $x = \pm\pi/4$ lie in $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$."
2. **The split.** "Both are interior, so the region is three pieces."
3. **The orientation.** "At $x = 0$, $\cos 0 = 1 > 1/\sqrt2$, so the cosine is on top in the middle; at $x = 3\pi/8$, $\cos x = 0.383 < 0.707$, so the line is on top outside."
4. **The integral, before its value.** $A = 2\left[\int_0^{\pi/4}(\cos x - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2})dx + \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} - \cos x)dx\right]$
5. **The evaluation.** $A = 2(\sqrt2 - 1) = 2\sqrt2 - 2$.

Line 1 is the one this question exists to test.
Line 3 is the one that determines the sign.

---

## 6. Verify before you commit

### 6.1 The five-way agreement, measured

| Route | Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| Exact antiderivative, three pieces | $0.8284271247461903$ |
| Split Simpson | agrees to $10^{-13}$ |
| Split tanh-sinh | agrees to $10^{-13}$ |
| Symmetry decomposition | agrees to $10^{-12}$ |
| Horizontal strips | agrees to $10^{-12}$ |
| Closed form $2\sqrt2 - 2$ | $0.8284271247461903$ |

Total spread $6.661 \times 10^{-16}$.

### 6.2 Four checks worth eight seconds each

| Check | On this question |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Is it positive?** | $0.828 > 0$. If yours is negative, an orientation is backwards. Do not just drop the minus. |
| **Is it smaller than the bounding box?** | The box is $\pi \times 1 = 3.14$ wide by tall. $0.828$ is comfortably inside. |
| **Is it smaller than the area under the whole arch?** | $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos x\,dx = 2$, and the region is a proper subset. $0.828 < 2$. |
| **Does the middle lobe look like about a third of it?** | Middle $0.303$, outer pair $0.525$. Roughly one-third to two-thirds, which a sketch supports. |

### 6.3 The wrong-answer census

Twelve candidate errors, no point excluded as degenerate.
Eleven of the twelve are **positive**, so a positivity check rejects only one of them.

| # | The mistake | Value | Hides? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | Reversed orientation, straight through | $+0.2214414691$ | **YES** |
| 2 | No split, correct orientation | $-0.2214414691$ | no (negative) |
| 3 | Only the middle lobe | $+0.3034928278$ | partly |
| 4 | Forgot to double the half-region | $+0.4142135624$ | **YES** |
| 5 | Wrong branch, used $\pm3\pi/4$ | $+1.9179486412$ | no |
| 6 | Wrong period, used $\pi/4$ and $7\pi/4$ | $+4.7463757660$ | no |
| 7 | Split at $x = 0$ instead of at the crossings | $+0.2214414691$ | **YES** |
| 8 | Outer lobes only | $+0.5249342969$ | partly |
| 9 | Sign flipped on one outer lobe | $+0.3034928278$ | partly |
| 10 | Calculator in degree mode | $+12.6876615874$ | no |
| 11 | Dropped the constant, integrated $\cos x$ alone | $+2.0000000000$ | no |
| 12 | Treated the region as a rectangle | $+4.4428829382$ | no |

**Two collision groups, and they are the finding.**

**Three errors share the value $0.2214414691$**: reversing the orientation, integrating straight through with no split, and splitting at $x = 0$ rather than at the crossings.
Row 2 is negative, and **the moment a student writes "an area is positive" and drops the minus, it becomes row 1 exactly.**
That is the identical mechanism Q19.1 found, where three errors all evaluated to $-4.5$ and all repaired to $4.5$.

**But the consequence is the opposite way round, and this is what a periodic boundary changes.**
On Q19.1 the sign error hid *in magnitude* and was caught *in sign*, because the magnitude was right.
Here the magnitude is wrong ($0.221$ against $0.828$) and the *sign* is what the repair fixes, so the student ends up with a positive, confident, wrong number.
**On Q19.1 "make it positive" accidentally rescues you. On Q19.2 it hides the error and loses the mark.**
This is why the orientation must be settled before the integration, not repaired after it.

**Two errors share $0.3034928278$**: computing only the middle lobe, and adding one outer lobe with the wrong sign (the two outer lobes are equal, so a sign flip on one cancels the other exactly).

Row 4 is the second genuine hider: half the answer, positive, and sitting exactly on the edge of the half-to-double plausibility band.
Only one of the twelve sits strictly inside that band (row 8).

**What catches the hiders.** Not arithmetic. A sketch with the three pieces marked, and an explicit statement of which curve is on top in each, catches rows 1, 2, 3, 7, 8 and 9. Rows 5 and 6 are caught by writing the general solution before filtering. Row 4 is caught by writing the factor of 2 down at the moment you use the symmetry, not after.

### 6.4 Why the $\pi$ cancels - the result worth carrying

Replace the height $1/\sqrt2$ with a general $c$ in $[0,1]$ and let $a = \arccos c$.
The same three-piece calculation gives a master formula for the whole family:

$$A(c) = 4\sqrt{1-c^2} - 4c\arccos(c) + \pi c - 2$$

Checked against the catalog at 51 values of $c$ and at every named instance.
Differentiating, and using $\cos a = c$ so the two $\arccos'$ terms cancel:

$$\frac{dA}{dc} = \pi - 4\arccos(c)$$

This vanishes exactly when $\arccos c = \pi/4$, that is at $c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, and $\dfrac{d^2A}{dc^2} = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{1-c^2}} > 0$.

**So the question's own line height is precisely the one that minimises the area.**
The minimum value is $2\sqrt2 - 2$, confirmed as the smallest over a half-million-point sweep of $c$.

And the $\pi$ in $A(c)$ appears only inside $\pi c - 4c\arccos c = c(\pi - 4\arccos c)$, which is $c$ times the derivative.
At the stationary height that bracket is zero, so **no $\pi$ survives**.
The $\pi$ terms cancel for a reason, and the reason is that $1/\sqrt2$ was chosen, not picked at random.

Two consequences worth having.

- **"There is no $\pi$ in my answer" is not evidence of a dropped term** on this particular question. At $c = 1/2$ the answer is $2\sqrt3 - 2 - \pi/6$ and the $\pi$ is genuinely there.
- **A "find $c$ so the area is $A$" question has two answers, not one.** $A(c)$ falls to its minimum at $1/\sqrt2$ and rises again, so $A(c) = 1$ is solved by both $c = 0.4488842358$ and $c = 0.9349464147$. Family F7 in section 8 is that question, and answering it with one root is the mistake it is designed to catch.

### 6.5 Two numerical warnings, because both look like health

**A near-miss split point costs almost nothing.** Moving the split from $\pi/4$ to $\pi/4 + 0.0025$ changes the area by **0.000534 percent**, and the measured order of the error in the offset is $2.0094, 2.0047, 2.0024, 2.0012$ - second order, because $D$ vanishes at a true crossing. A *mis-identified* split at $3\pi/8$ costs **14.70 percent**. Q19.1 measured the same thing on its endpoints. **The answer cannot tell you that a nearly-right crossing was guessed rather than solved.**

**Whether unsplit quadrature looks wrong depends on the grid, not on the mathematics.** Integrating $\lvert D \rvert$ straight through both kinks with Simpson at $n = 4000$ has error $8.9 \times 10^{-16}$, which looks exact. At $n = 4002$ the same routine on the same function has error $7.3 \times 10^{-8}$. The kinks sit at one quarter and three quarters of the span, so any $n$ divisible by 8 places them on panel boundaries and the kink becomes invisible. Measured convergence orders across the kink: **4.02, 4.01, 4.00, 4.00** on an aligned ladder, and **1.78, 1.89, 1.94, 1.97, 1.99** on a mis-aligned one. A lucky grid is not a correct method.

### 6.6 What the quadrature order actually is here

Q19.1 could not measure this: its integrand was a quadratic, Simpson is exact on every cubic, and the error was zero at every $n$.
**Here it is measurable**, because the integrand is a cosine.

| Integrand | Measured Simpson order |
| :--- | :--- |
| $\cos x - 1/\sqrt2$ on the middle lobe (this question) | $4.0050,\ 4.0012,\ 4.0003,\ 4.0001,\ 4.0000$ |
| $t^{2/3}$ on $[0,1]$ (control, must not read 4) | $1.6663,\ 1.6666,\ 1.6667,\ 1.6667,\ 1.6667$ |
| $2\arccos y$ on $[1/\sqrt2, 1]$ (route C's integrand) | $1.4999,\ 1.5000,\ 1.5000,\ 1.5000$ |
| $\lvert D \rvert$ across the kink, mis-aligned grid | $1.78 \rightarrow 1.99$ |

The third row is why route C used a double-exponential rule instead: $\arccos$ has an infinite slope at $y = 1$, so Simpson loses two and a half orders on the horizontal integrand even though it is a clean fourth-order method on the vertical one.
Simpson's error on that piece was $1.29 \times 10^{-8}$; tanh-sinh's was $6.1 \times 10^{-16}$.
**The digits quoted in section 6.1 inherit the precision of tanh-sinh, not of Simpson.**

## 7. Answer-entry rules

Both exams are Möbius: answer-only, machine-marked, so a correct method with a bad keystroke scores zero.

| Do | Do not |
| :--- | :--- |
| `2*sqrt(2)-2` | `2sqrt(2)-2` - implicit multiplication is not universally parsed |
| `sqrt(8)-2` and `2*(sqrt(2)-1)` are the same number | `2*sqrt(2-2)`, which is $0$ - watch the bracket |
| `0.8284271247` if a decimal is wanted | `0.83` - three significant figures is off by more than $5 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| Preview the rendered answer | assuming the parser read `sqrt` the way you meant |

**The single most expensive typo on this question is a bracket around the wrong thing.**
`2*sqrt(2)-2` and `2*sqrt(2-2)` differ by one character and by the whole answer.

**The second most expensive is a leading minus.**
If your working produced $-0.2214$, the fix is not to delete the sign.
The fix is that you never split, and the number is wrong by a factor of nearly four.

Units are not part of a numeric answer; do not type `units^2`.

---

## 8. The variation catalog

Read each table as **structure**, not as a list of facts.
Every row is the same six steps from section 3.
What changes between families is only **which step becomes the hard one**.

Fifteen rows, eight families, plus family F7 which has no closed form at all.
Every value below was verified against a formula-blind router that splits at every sign change it finds and never sees the claimed answer.

### Family F1 - a cosine against a horizontal line, interval given

**Trigger.** A trig curve and a constant, with an interval, and the constant is between the curve's minimum and maximum on that interval.
**Tool.** The master formula of section 6.4, or the three-piece split.

| Question | Answer | Decimal |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\cos x$ vs $y = 1/\sqrt2$ on $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ **(the question)** | $2\sqrt2 - 2$ | $0.8284271247$ |
| $\cos x$ vs $y = 1/2$ on $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ | $2\sqrt3 - 2 - \pi/6$ | $0.9405028395$ |
| $\cos x$ vs $y = \sqrt3/2$ on $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ | $\pi\sqrt3/6$ | $0.9068996821$ |

**The structure to see.** Only three distinct answers appear, and all three come from one formula with $c = 1/\sqrt2, 1/2, \sqrt3/2$.
The third one is a bare multiple of $\pi$ with no algebraic part, which happens because at $c = \sqrt3/2$ the $4\sqrt{1-c^2} = 2$ exactly cancels the $-2$.
**Nothing in a well-formed answer to this family is predictable from its shape** - the $\pi$ can vanish, dominate, or sit alongside a surd.

### Family F2 - a sine instead of a cosine, interval shifted

**Trigger.** $\sin x$ against a constant.
**Tool.** Identical, with $x = \arcsin c$ and $\pi - \arcsin c$ as the crossings. Note the second crossing is **not** $-\arcsin c$; the reflection is about $\pi/2$, not about $0$.

| Question | Answer | Decimal |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\sin x$ vs $y = 1/2$ on $[0, \pi]$ | $2\sqrt3 - 2 - \pi/6$ | $0.9405028395$ |
| $\sin x$ vs $y = 0$ on $[0, 2\pi]$ | $4$ | $4.0000000000$ |

The first row is **the same number as F1's second row**, because $\sin x$ on $[0,\pi]$ is $\cos x$ on $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ shifted.
The second row is the classic: $\int_0^{2\pi}\sin x \, dx = 0$ and $\int_0^{2\pi}\lvert \sin x\rvert dx = 4$, which is the cleanest possible demonstration of why the absolute value is not decoration.

### Family F3 - no crossing at all, so no split

**Trigger.** The line is above the curve's maximum or below its minimum on the whole interval.
**Tool.** One integral. Check the orientation once, at any interior point.

| Question | Answer | Decimal |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $y = 2$ vs $\cos x$ on $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ | $2\pi - 2$ | $4.2831853072$ |
| $\cos x$ vs $y = -1$ on $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ | $2 + \pi$ | $5.1415926536$ |

**The cue that puts you in this family:** compare the constant with $\max$ and $\min$ of the curve on the interval *before* solving anything.
If it is outside that range, there is nothing to solve.

### Family F4 - two trig curves crossing each other

**Trigger.** Neither boundary is constant.
**Tool.** Same procedure. $\sin x = \cos x \Rightarrow \tan x = 1 \Rightarrow x = \pi/4 + k\pi$.

| Question | Answer | Decimal |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\sin x$ vs $\cos x$ on $[0, \pi/2]$ | $2\sqrt2 - 2$ | $0.8284271247$ |
| $\sin x$ vs $\cos x$ on $[0, \pi]$ | $2\sqrt2$ | $2.8284271247$ |

**The first row is numerically identical to the exam question**, from an entirely different geometry.
That is worth noticing: if you meet $2\sqrt2 - 2$ on a paper, it does not tell you which question you solved.

### Family F5 - the interval is not given, so the crossings are the limits

**Trigger.** "Find the area enclosed by" with no interval.
**Tool.** Consecutive crossings become $a$ and $b$, and there is then no interior split by construction.

| Question | Answer | Decimal |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\cos x$ vs $y = 1/\sqrt2$ between consecutive crossings | $\sqrt2 - \pi\sqrt2/4$ | $0.3034928278$ |
| $\sin x$ vs $y = 0$ over one arch $[0, \pi]$ | $2$ | $2.0000000000$ |
| $\cos x$ vs $y = 0$ over one arch $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ | $2$ | $2.0000000000$ |

**On a periodic curve this family is ambiguous unless you say which pair of consecutive crossings**, and by periodicity every choice gives the same answer.
That is the one place where the infinitude of intersections costs you nothing.

### Family F6 - many periods

**Trigger.** The interval is longer than one period, or is an exact multiple of one.
**Tool.** Compute one period, multiply, then handle the leftover.

| Question | Answer | Decimal |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\lvert \cos x - 1/\sqrt2 \rvert$ over one full period $[0, 2\pi]$ | $2\sqrt2 + \pi\sqrt2/2$ | $5.0498685938$ |
| the same over $[-\pi/2, 3\pi/2]$, also a full period | $2\sqrt2 + \pi\sqrt2/2$ | $5.0498685938$ |
| $\sin x$ vs $y = 0$ on $[0, 3\pi/2]$ | $3$ | $3.0000000000$ |

The first two rows are equal because both windows have length $2\pi$, verified rather than assumed.
**Any window of length $2\pi$ gives the same total, wherever it starts.**

### Family F7 - solve for the line height from a required area

**Trigger.** "Find $c$ such that the area between $\cos x$ and $y = c$ on $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ is $A$."
**Tool.** The master formula $A(c) = 4\sqrt{1-c^2} - 4c\arccos c + \pi c - 2$, then solve numerically.

| Target area | Solutions | Note |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $A = 1$ | $c = 0.4488842358$ **and** $c = 0.9349464147$ | two answers |
| $A = 2\sqrt2 - 2$ | $c = 1/\sqrt2$ only | the minimum, so exactly one |
| $A < 2\sqrt2 - 2$ | none | below the minimum |

**This family is the reason section 6.4 is on this page.**
$A(c)$ is not monotone, so "find $c$" has two answers, one answer, or none, and which case you are in is decided by comparing the target with $2\sqrt2 - 2$.
A student who bisects blindly finds one root and stops.

### Family F8 - a tangency, where the curves touch without crossing

**Trigger.** The constant equals the curve's extreme value on the interval.
**Tool.** No split. The difference has a repeated root and never changes sign.

| Question | Answer | Decimal |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $y = 1$ vs $\cos x$ on $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ (touch at $x = 0$) | $\pi - 2$ | $1.1415926536$ |
| $\sec^2 x$ vs $y = 2$ on $[-\pi/4, \pi/4]$ (touch at both endpoints) | $\pi - 2$ | $1.1415926536$ |

**A tangency is invisible to a numerical search and obvious to the algebra**, which is section 3.2's measured result.
It is also where a midpoint orientation probe can land exactly on $D = 0$ and flip the sign of the answer.

### Family F9 - horizontal strips are the shorter route

**Trigger.** The region's left and right boundaries are each a single curve, but the top and bottom are not.
**Tool.** Solve for $x$ in terms of $y$, integrate in $y$.

| Question | Answer | Decimal |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Middle lobe as $\int_{1/\sqrt2}^{1} 2\arccos y \, dy$ | $\sqrt2 - \pi\sqrt2/4$ | $0.3034928278$ |

The general antiderivative to have: $\int \arccos y \, dy = y\arccos y - \sqrt{1-y^2}$.
It is a by-parts, and it is the only new integration technique the whole category needs.

---

## 9. The trap list

Ranked by how often it actually costs the mark.

1. **Not splitting at the crossings.** Gives $-0.2214$, and then "make it positive" gives $+0.2214$, which is confidently, quietly wrong. This is the whole question.
2. **Losing the $\pm$ in $x = \pm\arccos c$.** Half the crossings, half the region, or a region in the wrong place.
3. **Forgetting to double after using the symmetry.** Gives $\sqrt2 - 1 = 0.4142$, positive and plausible.
4. **Taking the wrong branch.** $3\pi/4$ solves $\cos x = -1/\sqrt2$. Check your branch against the sign of $c$.
5. **Taking the wrong period.** $7\pi/4$ is a real solution and is not in the interval.
6. **Deciding orientation at a crossing.** $D = 0$ there and the comparison decides nothing. Test strictly between.
7. **Deciding orientation once for the whole interval** when the curves cross. Three pieces, three decisions.
8. **Splitting somewhere that is not a crossing.** Splitting at $x = 0$ changes nothing; the sign does not turn there. An unnecessary split is harmless only when there is no sign change at it - here $x=0$ is inside a piece, so the two halves still carry the same wrong sign.
9. **Degree mode.** Gives $12.69$, which at least announces itself.
10. **Reading the crossings off a sketch.** A near-miss crossing costs 0.0005 percent, so you will never be told you were guessing.
11. **Assuming a missing $\pi$ means a dropped term.** On this specific $c$ the $\pi$ cancels for a reason.

---

## 10. Drill set

Score **sign** separately from **magnitude**.
A wrong sign means the orientation procedure is not automatic yet; a wrong magnitude means the split or the antiderivative is.

Find the area between the given curves on the given interval.

1. $\cos x$ and $y = 1/\sqrt2$ on $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$
2. $\cos x$ and $y = 1/\sqrt2$ on $[-\pi/4, \pi/4]$
3. $\cos x$ and $y = 1/\sqrt2$ on $[0, \pi/2]$
4. $\sin x$ and $y = 1/2$ on $[0, \pi/2]$
5. $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ on $[0, \pi/2]$
6. $\cos x$ and $y = 0$ on $[0, \pi]$
7. $\sin x$ and $y = 0$ on $[0, 3\pi/2]$
8. $\cos x$ and $y = 1/2$ on $[0, \pi]$
9. $\cos x$ and $y = -1/\sqrt2$ on $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$
10. $y = 2\cos x$ and $y = 1$ on $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$
11. $\cos(2x)$ and $y = 1/\sqrt2$ on $[-\pi/4, \pi/4]$
12. $\sec^2 x$ and $y = 2$ on $[-\pi/4, \pi/4]$

### Answer key

| # | Exact | Decimal | Family and method |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | $2\sqrt2 - 2$ | $0.8284271247$ | F1 - the question; three pieces or symmetry |
| 2 | $\sqrt2 - \pi\sqrt2/4$ | $0.3034928278$ | F5 - interval *is* the crossings, no split |
| 3 | $\sqrt2 - 1$ | $0.4142135624$ | F1 with symmetry; exactly half of #1 |
| 4 | $\sqrt3 - 1 - \pi/12$ | $0.4702514198$ | F2 - crossing at $\pi/6$, two pieces |
| 5 | $2\sqrt2 - 2$ | $0.8284271247$ | F4 - crossing at $\pi/4$; same value as #1 |
| 6 | $2$ | $2.0000000000$ | F5 - one arch, crossings at $\pi/2$ only |
| 7 | $3$ | $3.0000000000$ | F6 - one and a half arches, split at $\pi$ |
| 8 | $\sqrt3 + \pi/6$ | $2.2556495832$ | F1 - crossing at $\pi/3$, asymmetric interval |
| 9 | $2 + \pi\sqrt2/2$ | $4.2214414691$ | F3 - line below the minimum, no split |
| 10 | $4\sqrt3 - 4 - \pi/3$ | $1.8810056791$ | F1 scaled; exactly twice F1's $c = 1/2$ row |
| 11 | $\sqrt2 - 1$ | $0.4142135624$ | F1 with $u = 2x$; exactly half of #1 |
| 12 | $\pi - 2$ | $1.1415926536$ | F8 - endpoints touch, no interior split |

**The structure of this key.** Twelve drills, **ten distinct values**, because #1 and #5 coincide and #3 and #11 coincide.
Three of the twelve are exactly half of #1, and #10 is exactly twice a catalog row.
**The halving pattern is not universal** - #8 is not twice #4 - so recognise it, do not assume it.

## 11. The one-page decision tree

```
Area between two curves, one of them periodic?
|
+- Is an interval given?
|    NO  -> the consecutive crossings ARE the interval    [F5]
|    YES -> keep going
|
+- Solve f(x) = g(x).  Write the GENERAL solution first:
|        cos x = c  ->  x = +- arccos(c) + 2k*pi
|        sin x = c  ->  x = arcsin(c) + 2k*pi  and  pi - arcsin(c) + 2k*pi
|        tan x = c  ->  x = arctan(c) + k*pi
|   then INTERSECT that family with the given interval.
|   (Do not search a wider window - it finds real roots that are not in the region.)
|
+- How many crossings are STRICTLY INSIDE (a, b)?
|    0  -> ONE integral.  Orientation checked once.        [F3, F8]
|    1  -> TWO integrals, split there.
|    n  -> n+1 integrals.                                  [F1, F2, F4]
|
+- Is the region symmetric about a point or a line?
|    YES -> do half and DOUBLE.  Write the 2 down NOW.     [saves a piece]
|
+- On EACH piece: pick a point strictly between the knots,
|   where |f - g| is not small, and see which is larger.
|   Integrate (top - bottom).  Never test AT a knot.
|
+- Add the pieces.  All positive by construction.
|
+- CHECK: positive?  smaller than the bounding box?
|          middle lobe about a third?
+- PREVIEW the Moebius string before submitting.
```
