# Q19.3 - Net change, water flowing from a tank

**The question (Final Exam 1, item 12, 3 points).** Water flows from the bottom of a storage tank at a rate of $r(t) = 180 - 6t$ liters per minute, where $0 \le t \le 50.$
Find the amount of water that flows from the tank during the first 15 minutes.

**The answer.** $\displaystyle\int_0^{15}(180-6t)\,dt = \Big[180t - 3t^2\Big]_0^{15} = 2700 - 675 = 2025$ litres.

**What to type into Möbius:** `2025`

*Provenance: stem parsed from `C:\Users\mnguyen\notes\MATH265\MATH265.md`, Final Exam 1 block, item 12, with the point value read from the inline `(3 points)` marker rather than typed. Final Exam 1 prints fourteen point values summing to 124, and 3 is the lightest value on that paper, shared with item 14. Every number on this page was computed in `math265-answer-verification.py` sections `q193`, `q193d` and `q193s` before it was written down: 249 assertions, 0 failures, 36 seeded controls. No marking scheme exists in any of the four course files, so every grading claim below is flagged as inference.*

---

## 0. The 30-second version

```
r(t) is a RATE (litres per minute).  You are asked for an AMOUNT (litres).
Rate -> amount is one operation: integrate.

  amount out over [0,15]  =  int_0^15 r(t) dt

  antiderivative  R(t) = 180t - 3t^2        (check: R' = 180 - 6t  OK)
  R(15) - R(0)    = 2700 - 675 - 0          =  2025 litres

  8-second check: r is LINEAR, so average rate = (180+90)/2 = 135,
                  and 135 x 15 = 2025.  Same number, no calculus.
```

That is the whole question, and the calculus takes one line.
The rest of this page is about the four things that can go wrong on the way, three of which produce a number you cannot distinguish from the right one.

---

## 1. What this question is really testing

| The reflex | Where it comes back |
| :--- | :--- |
| A rate integrates to a **change** in the quantity | Q19.6 and Q19.7 (average value), Q19.8 (displacement), Q19.9 (a sprinter) |
| The Fundamental Theorem is what licenses that | Q18.1, which is the same theorem read the other way |
| A change is not an amount until an initial condition is added | any "how much is left" wording, and every differential-equation question later |
| A signed rate integrates to a signed change | Q19.8, where displacement and distance differ |
| Units of the answer come from the integrand times the variable | Q6.1 section 2.2, and every applied question in the bank |

**The single sentence this question exists to install is the Net Change Theorem.**

> If $Q$ is a quantity and $Q' = r$ is its rate of change, then $\displaystyle\int_a^b r(t)\,dt = Q(b) - Q(a)$.
> The integral of a rate of change is the **net change** in the quantity, over that interval.

That is not a new theorem.
It is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2, with the letters renamed: `Q18.1 - Differentiate an integral with variable limits.md` section 2a states both halves side by side, and it is Part 2 (given $F' = f$, the definite integral is $F(b) - F(a)$) that this question uses.
Read that table rather than re-deriving it.
The only thing Q19.3 adds is a physical reading of $F$: when $f$ is a flow rate, $F$ is a volume.

### Why the marks are cheap and the trap is not

3 points, out of 124 on the paper, is 2.42 percent, and it is the lightest item on Final Exam 1.
An examiner does not put a hard integral in a 3-point slot.
**The difficulty is deliberately not in the antiderivative; it is in knowing what you were asked for.**
That is inference, since no marking scheme exists in any course file, but the point value is the evidence for it.

---

## 2. The four things you must have cold

### 2a. Rate in, quantity out, and how the units prove it

A rate is a quotient: some quantity per one unit of the input variable.
`Q6.1 - Average and instantaneous rate of population change.md` section 2.2 states the rule that never has an exception, and its own table already carries this exact row: *litres in a tank at minute $t$* gives a rate in **litres per minute**.

The integral multiplies the integrand by the variable, so it multiplies the units too:

$$\underbrace{\left[\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}\right]}_{r(t)}\times\underbrace{\big[\text{min}\big]}_{dt} \;=\; \big[\text{L}\big]$$

The minutes cancel and a volume comes out.
**This is a check you can run in three seconds and it catches an entire class of error that no arithmetic check can see.**

Do it as a cancellation, not as a sentence.
Writing "the answer is in litres because it is water" is not a check, because it is true whatever you computed.
Writing $\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}\times\text{min} = \text{L}$ is a check, because a wrong operation gives a wrong unit.

| what you wrote | its units | verdict |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\int_0^{15} r\,dt$ | L | a volume, which is what was asked |
| $r(15)$ | L/min | a rate, not a volume |
| $r'(t)$ | L/min$^2$ | an acceleration of the flow |
| $\dfrac{1}{15}\int_0^{15} r\,dt$ | L/min | the average rate, which is Q19.6's question |
| $\int_0^{15} r\,dt \;+\; r(15)$ | inhomogeneous | not a quantity at all |

The last row is the one worth staring at.
**You cannot add a volume to a rate**, and a units gate rejects that sum before any number is computed.
The verification section implements exactly this as exponent vectors over (litre, minute) and proves it rejects all four wrong units above plus the inhomogeneous sum.

Note also that the constants carry units.
The $180$ in $180 - 6t$ is $180$ L/min, and the $6$ is $6$ L/min$^2$, so that $6t$ is again L/min.
A student who treats $180$ and $6$ as pure numbers has no way to notice when a conversion is needed.

### 2b. Net change is a change, and the classic lost mark

$$\int_a^b Q'(t)\,dt = Q(b) - Q(a) \qquad\text{so}\qquad Q(b) = Q(a) + \int_a^b Q'(t)\,dt$$

The integral by itself is the **second** of those, not the first.
If the question asks how much water is **left in the tank**, the integral is only half the answer and the initial volume is the other half.

Q19.3 does not ask that.
It asks for the amount that **flowed out**, which is exactly the integral, so no initial condition is needed here.
**That is precisely why the mark is so easy to lose on the next question of this type**: you learn the shape on a question where the initial condition is absent, and then meet one where it is not.

| the wording | what to compute | needs $V(0)$? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| "the amount that flows from the tank" | $\int_0^{15} r$ | no |
| "the net change in the volume in the tank" | $-\int_0^{15} r$ | no |
| "how much water remains in the tank" | $V(0) - \int_0^{15} r$ | **yes** |
| "the total volume of water moved" | $\int_0^{15}\lvert r\rvert$ | no |

Three of those four are different numbers on a general question.
On **this** question the first and the fourth are the same, and that is the subject of section 6.

### 2c. Signed flow, and what the wording fixes

$r(t)$ here is defined as the rate at which water flows **from** the tank.
So $r > 0$ means water leaving.
Two consistent bookkeepings exist and you must pick one and stay in it:

| convention | the rate | the integral over $[0,15]$ | reads as |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **outflow positive** (the stem's) | $r(t) = 180-6t$ | $+2025$ | 2025 L left the tank |
| **tank contents** | $V'(t) = -r(t)$ | $-2025$ | the tank lost 2025 L |

Both are correct statements about the same physical event.
**The exam wants the first**, because it asks for "the amount of water that flows from the tank", and an amount of water is a positive quantity.
Answering $-2025$ is answering a different, unasked question correctly.

> **Decide which quantity you are accumulating before you integrate, not after you see the sign.**

That rule is unfalsifiable on this question, because the sign error here is repaired by the single most natural instinct a student has, which is that an amount of water cannot be negative.
It is fatal one question later.
See section 9.

### 2d. Where this rate stops making sense

$r(t) = 180 - 6t$ is zero at $t = 30$ and **negative** for $t > 30$.
The stem states the domain as $0 \le t \le 50$, so on the last 20 minutes, which is 40 percent of the stated domain, the model says water flows out of the tank at a negative rate.
A negative outflow is an inflow, which contradicts the stem's own sentence about water flowing from the bottom of a tank.

**This is a defect in the question's numbers, not in your reading of them.**
It is recorded here because it is where the interesting mathematics of this category actually lives, and because the asked interval $[0,15]$ sits entirely inside the physically sensible part, so the defect costs nothing on the exam.
The natural repair is a domain of $0 \le t \le 30$, at which point the tank has delivered $2700$ litres and the flow stops.

---

## 3. The universal procedure

> 1. **Name the quantity and the rate.** Write "$V$ = litres delivered, $r = V'$ in L/min". If you cannot name the quantity, you do not yet know what the integral means.
> 2. **Check the units of the rate**, as a quotient. Output unit over input unit.
> 3. **Decide what is being asked**: a change, a final amount, or a total moved. Section 2b's four-row table is the whole decision.
> 4. **Find where the rate changes sign inside the interval.** If it does not, change and total agree and you may integrate straight through. If it does, they differ and you must split.
> 5. **Antidifferentiate, then check by differentiating back.** The check is faster than the antidifferentiation.
> 6. **Evaluate $F(b) - F(a)$, upper minus lower**, and add the initial condition only if step 3 said to.
> 7. **State the units**, from step 2, and sanity-check the magnitude against rate times time.

### The classify table

| The stem says | The tool | Watch for |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| "at a rate of ..." and asks for an amount | integrate the rate | the units |
| "how much remains / how many are there at time $b$" | $Q(a) + \int_a^b r$ | the initial condition |
| "total distance / total volume moved" | $\int \lvert r\rvert$, split at the zeros | the split |
| "net change / displacement" | $\int r$, no split | do not take absolute values |
| "average rate" | $\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b r$ | dividing, and the units change back |
| a rate given as a table or graph | trapezoid or Riemann sums | you have no antiderivative |
| "at what time does ... " | solve $F(T) = $ target | a spurious second root |

---

## 4. Q19.3 worked eight ways

Every route below was evaluated independently, and all eight agree to $6.594\times10^{-12}$, which is roundoff.

### Route A - the antiderivative, the one to write down

$$\int_0^{15}(180-6t)\,dt = \Big[180t - 3t^2\Big]_0^{15} = (2700 - 675) - 0 = 2025$$

### Route B - the trapezoid, which is exact here

$r$ is linear, so the region under it is a trapezoid with parallel sides $r(0) = 180$ and $r(15) = 90$ and width 15.

$$A = \frac{180+90}{2}\times 15 = 135 \times 15 = 2025$$

### Route C - the midpoint rate

Again because $r$ is linear, the average rate is the rate at the midpoint: $r(7.5) = 135$, and $135 \times 15 = 2025$.

### Route D - rectangle plus triangle

Split the trapezoid horizontally: a $90 \times 15$ rectangle underneath, and a triangle of base 15 and height $180-90=90$ on top.

$$1350 + \tfrac12(15)(90) = 1350 + 675 = 2025$$

### Route E - substitution

Let $u = 180-6t$, so $du = -6\,dt$, and the limits run from $u=180$ down to $u=90$.

$$\int_{180}^{90} u\cdot\left(-\tfrac16\right)du = \frac{1}{6}\int_{90}^{180}u\,du = \frac{180^2-90^2}{12} = \frac{32400-8100}{12} = 2025$$

### Route F - tanh-sinh quadrature

A double-exponential quadrature rule that never sees the closed form returns $2025$ to $10^{-10}$.

### Route G - composite Simpson

At $n = 17, 23, 37, 51, 101, 199, 501$ and $1003$, all deliberately chosen odd and off multiples of 8, Simpson returns $2025$ to $10^{-10}$.

### Route H - average rate times time

$\overline{r} = 135$ L/min over 15 min is $2025$ L.
This is Route C stated in the language of Q19.6.

### Route comparison

| Route | Cost | Generalises? | Catches a wrong interval? | Verdict |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| A antiderivative | one line | **to every rate** | yes | **use this one** |
| B trapezoid | one line | only to linear rates | yes | the check, not the method |
| C midpoint | one line | only to linear rates | yes | fastest check |
| D geometry | two lines | only to linear rates | yes | good for a graph-given rate |
| E substitution | three lines | to composite rates | yes | overkill here |
| F tanh-sinh | not by hand | to anything | yes | verification only |
| G Simpson | not by hand | to anything | yes | verification only |
| H average rate | one line | to every rate | yes | the Q19.6 phrasing |

**Under exam pressure use Route A and check with Route C.**
Route A is the only one that survives a non-linear rate, and Route C costs one subtraction and one multiplication.
The pairing matters more than either half: A and C fail in different ways, so agreement between them is real evidence.

**But note carefully what Route C is not.** Routes B, C and D are exact **only because $r$ is linear**.
On the exponential rate in drill D7 the midpoint estimate is not the answer, and a student who learned "average the endpoints" from this question will carry a broken tool into the next one.
That is measured, not asserted: see the trap list, item 5.

---

## 5. The exam-ready write-up

These are the sentences that earn method marks if part marks exist, which is inference since no marking scheme is in any course file.

> The rate $r(t)$ is the derivative of the volume $V$ that has flowed out, so by the Net Change Theorem the amount that flows out between $t=0$ and $t=15$ is $\int_0^{15} r(t)\,dt$.
> $r$ is continuous on $[0,15]$ and $R(t)=180t-3t^2$ satisfies $R'(t)=180-6t=r(t)$, so by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus,
> $$\int_0^{15}(180-6t)\,dt = R(15)-R(0) = (2700-675)-0 = 2025.$$
> $r(t) > 0$ throughout $[0,15]$, so this is both the net change and the total volume delivered.
> The units are $\text{(L/min)}\times\text{min} = \text{L}$.
> **2025 litres of water flow from the tank during the first 15 minutes.**

Five sentences.
The third one is the one nobody writes and it is the one that shows you knew there was a question to answer.

---

## 6. Verify before you commit

### The eight-second checks, in the order they catch things

| Check | On this question | What it catches |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Units** | (L/min)(min) = L | answering with a rate, differentiating instead |
| **Magnitude bracket** | between $r(15)\cdot 15 = 1350$ and $r(0)\cdot 15 = 2700$ | a wrong interval, a dropped coefficient |
| **Midpoint** | $135\times15 = 2025$ | the antiderivative's arithmetic |
| **Sign** | $r>0$ on $[0,15]$, so the answer is positive | an orientation slip |
| **Lower limit** | $R(0)=0$, so it happens not to matter | nothing, here - see below |

The magnitude bracket is worth its own line.
For any **decreasing** positive rate, the true amount is strictly between (final rate)$\times$(time) and (initial rate)$\times$(time).
Here that is $1350 < A < 2700$, and $2025$ sits neatly in the middle because the rate is linear.
**This bracket rejects twelve of the sixteen wrong answers in the census**, measured rather than estimated, and that is more than the units check (4) and more than a positivity check (5).
It is the strongest single check available on this question.

### The check that cannot fire here, and why you should know that

$R(0) = 180(0) - 3(0)^2 = 0$.
So on this question, writing $R(15)$ and forgetting $-R(0)$ entirely gives the same answer, $2025$.
**A student who never learned to subtract the lower limit gets full marks on Q19.3 and loses them on any interval not starting at zero.**
Drill D2, which runs from $t=10$ to $t=20$, is the same question with that hiding point removed.

### Numbers worth memorising

| Quantity | Value |
| ---: | :--- |
| $r(0)$ | 180 L/min |
| $r(15)$ | 90 L/min |
| $r(30)$ | 0, the shut-off |
| $r(50)$ | $-120$, which the model should not permit |
| $\int_0^{15} r$ | **2025 L** |
| $\int_0^{30} r$ | 2700 L, everything the model delivers |
| $\int_0^{50} r$ | 1500 L net |
| $\int_0^{50} \lvert r\rvert$ | 3900 L total moved |
| average rate on $[0,15]$ | 135 L/min |

## 7. Answer-entry rules

Both exams are Möbius: answer-only and machine-marked, so a correct method with a bad keystroke scores zero.

| Do | Do not |
| :--- | :--- |
| `2025` | `2025 L` - units are not part of a numeric answer |
| `2025` | `-2025` - the amount that flows out is positive |
| `2025` | `2,025` - a thousands separator is not a number |
| `2025` | `2025.00` unless a decimal form is requested |
| Preview the rendered answer | assume the box took what you meant |

**The single most expensive typo on this question is a leading minus.**
It is a one-character difference and it is the whole answer, and unlike Q19.2 the fix really is to delete the sign, because the magnitude here is already right.
That is a dangerous thing to learn, and section 9 says why.

The second most expensive is typing the rate.
`90` is the value of $r(15)$, it is a perfectly reasonable-looking three-digit number, and it is not a volume.
The units check is the only thing that catches it.

---

## 8. The variation catalog

Read each family as a **structure**, not as a list of facts.
Every family below is the same theorem; what changes is which of the four questions in section 2b's table is being asked, and whether the rate changes sign.
Thirteen distinct families are exercised by the verified rows in section 10 and below.

### Family 0 - the plain net change

**Trigger.** A rate is given, an interval is given, and the word is "how much" or "the amount".
**Tool.** $\int_a^b r$, no initial condition, no absolute value.
**Shape.** Antidifferentiate, evaluate upper minus lower.

| Instance | Answer |
| :--- | ---: |
| $r=180-6t$ on $[0,15]$ (the question) | 2025 L |
| $r=180-6t$ on $[0,25]$ | 2625 L |
| $r=180-6t$ on $[10,20]$ | 900 L |
| $r=200-4t$ on $[0,10]$ | 1800 L |

The third row is the useful one: it starts away from zero, so the lower limit is live.

### Family 1 - the final amount, which needs the initial condition

**Trigger.** "How much is left", "how many are there at time $b$", "what is the population in year $b$".
**Tool.** $Q(b) = Q(a) + \int_a^b r$, with attention to whether $r$ adds or removes.
**Shape.** Compute the integral, then do one addition or subtraction that the integral cannot tell you about.

| Instance | Answer |
| :--- | ---: |
| Tank holds 4000 L at $t=0$; how much at $t=15$? | 1975 L |
| Tank holds 2025 L at $t=0$; how much at $t=15$? | 0 L, exactly empty |
| Tank holds 3000 L; does it ever empty under this model? | **no**, the model delivers only 2700 L |

That last row is the family's best question, because the answer is not a number.
The tank cannot empty, because the flow shuts off at $t=30$ having delivered 2700 litres.

### Family 2 - the rate changes sign, so net and total differ

**Trigger.** The rate is zero somewhere strictly inside the interval.
**Tool.** Find the zeros. Net change is $\int r$ straight through; total moved is $\int \lvert r\rvert$, split at each zero and added with all pieces positive.
**Shape.** Two computations from the same pieces, differing only in the signs you attach.

| Instance | Net change | Total moved |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| $r = 180-6t$ on $[0,15]$ | 2025 L | **2025 L, the same** |
| $r = 180-6t$ on $[0,50]$ | 1500 L | 3900 L |
| $r = 180-6t$ on $[0,30]$ | 2700 L | 2700 L, the same |
| $v = t^2-4$ on $[0,3]$ | $-3$ m | $23/3 \approx 7.6667$ m |

Read the column pair, not the rows.
**They agree exactly when the rate does not change sign inside the interval**, and that is the only condition.
The first row is the exam question and the columns agree, which is why this family is invisible on Q19.3 and decides the mark on Q19.8.

### Family 3 - solve for the time

**Trigger.** "At what time has 1000 litres flowed out?", "when is the tank empty?", "how long until ...".
**Tool.** Set $F(T) = $ target and solve, then **discard roots outside the model's domain**.
**Shape.** $180T - 3T^2 = 1000$ gives $3T^2 - 180T + 1000 = 0$, so $T = \dfrac{180 \pm \sqrt{20400}}{6}$.

The two roots are $T = 6.1952385715$ and $T = 53.8047614285$.
Only the first is admissible.
The second is past the $t=30$ shut-off and past the stated domain $t \le 50$ as well, so it is doubly spurious.

**A quadratic in the time variable has two roots and a physical question usually has one answer.**
Say which one you rejected and why; that sentence is the difference between a solved equation and a solved problem.

### Family 4 - a rate that is not linear

**Trigger.** The rate contains an exponential, a trig function, a root, or a composite.
**Tool.** The same theorem, plus whatever antidifferentiation the rate needs.
**Shape.** Nothing changes except step 5.

| Instance | Answer |
| :--- | ---: |
| $r = 60e^{-t/10}$ on $[0,20]$ | $600(1-e^{-2}) = 518.7988300580$ |
| $r = t\sqrt{t^2+9}$ on $[0,4]$ | $\dfrac{98}{3} \approx 32.6667$ |
| $r = 100\sin(\pi t/12)$ on $[0,12]$ | $\dfrac{2400}{\pi} = 763.9437268411$ |

**The endpoint-average shortcut is wrong on every one of these**, and that is what makes this family the antidote to Route C.
For the exponential, the endpoint average is $\tfrac12(60 + 60e^{-2})\times 20 = 681.2$ against the true $518.8$, an error of 31 percent.

### Family 5 - two rates, in and out

**Trigger.** Water enters at one rate and leaves at another.
**Tool.** The net rate is the difference, and you integrate that.
**Shape.** $\int (r_{\text{in}} - r_{\text{out}})$, and everything else is Family 2.

| Instance | Net change | Total moved |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| in $5t$, out $100$, on $[0,40]$ | **0 L** | 2000 L |
| in $3t^2$, out $36t$, on $[0,12]$ | $-864$ | - |

The first row is the family's teaching instance, and the verification section confirms both numbers.
**The net change is exactly zero and two thousand litres of water actually moved.**
"Nothing changed" and "nothing happened" are different statements, and only the second is refuted by the total.

### Family 6 - the average value of the rate

**Trigger.** "Average rate of flow", "average velocity", "mean value".
**Tool.** $\dfrac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b r$, which is Q19.6's whole question.
**Shape.** Compute the integral, then divide, and note the units go back to L/min.

| Instance | Answer |
| :--- | ---: |
| average of $180-6t$ on $[0,15]$ | 135 L/min |
| average of $180-6t$ on $[0,30]$ | 90 L/min |

For a **linear** rate the average equals the midpoint value and the endpoint mean, and all three are 135 here.
For a non-linear rate they are three different numbers, which the verification section confirms on $t^2$.

### Family 7 - units and conversions

**Trigger.** The answer is wanted in different units from the ones the rate is stated in.
**Tool.** Convert once, at the end, or convert the rate and the variable together and check the integral is unchanged.
**Shape.** 2025 L is $2.025$ m$^3$; the same flow measured in L/s over 900 s integrates to the identical 2025 L, which the verification section checks by re-integrating in seconds.

**Convert at the end.** Converting mid-problem gives two chances to make the same error and no way to detect it.

### Family 8 - the rate is a table or a graph

**Trigger.** No formula is given.
**Tool.** Trapezoid or a Riemann sum; the FTC is unavailable because you have no antiderivative.
**Shape.** $\int \approx h\left(\tfrac12 r_0 + r_1 + \cdots + r_{n-1} + \tfrac12 r_n\right)$.

Sampled at $t = 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15$ the rates are $180, 162, 144, 126, 108, 90$, and the trapezoid rule with $h=3$ gives exactly **2025**.
It is exact because the rate is linear, and it will not be exact on Family 4.

### Family 9 - the model's own domain

**Trigger.** The rate goes negative, or undefined, inside the stated domain.
**Tool.** Find where, and say what it means physically before integrating past it.
**Shape.** Here $r < 0$ for $t > 30$, on 40 percent of the stated domain, which the stem's own sentence forbids.

### Family 10 - the question run backwards

**Trigger.** The answer is given and a parameter of the rate is not.
**Tool.** Integrate symbolically in the parameter, set equal to the target, solve.
**Shape.** $\int_0^{15}(180 - kt)\,dt = 2700 - \tfrac{225k}{2} = 1800$ gives $k = 8$.

### Family 11 - velocity, where this becomes Q19.8

**Trigger.** The rate is a velocity and the quantity is a position.
**Tool.** Displacement is $\int v$; distance travelled is $\int \lvert v\rvert$.
**Shape.** Exactly Family 2 with different nouns.

For $v = t^2-4$ on $[0,3]$: the velocity is zero at $t=2$, the displacement is $-3$ m and the distance is $23/3 \approx 7.6667$ m.
`Q19.1 - Area between a line and a parabola.md` section 3.1 already carries the absolute-value machinery; this is that machinery in physics clothing.

### Family 12 - the quantity is not a volume

**Trigger.** Marginal cost, population growth rate, current, power, rate of consumption.
**Tool.** The identical theorem. Nothing changes but the units.
**Shape.** If $C'(x) = 3 + 0.02x$ dollars per unit, the cost of going from 100 units to 300 is $\int_{100}^{300}C'(x)\,dx = 1400$ dollars.

Note that the input variable here is **units**, not time.
Q6.1 section 2.2 makes this point about rates and it is exactly as true about their integrals.

---

## 9. The trap list

Ranked by how often each actually costs a mark, which is inference, since no course file contains a rubric.

**1. Answering with a rate instead of a volume.**
$r(15) = 90$ is a plausible-looking number and it is the wrong kind of object.
Caught only by the units check.

**2. Forgetting that the integral is a change, not an amount.**
Invisible on Q19.3 and fatal the moment the wording is "how much remains".
The integral does not know the tank's initial contents and cannot tell you that you needed them.

**3. Reporting the total volume moved when the net change was asked, or the reverse.**
On this question they are the same number, so nothing you compute can tell you which one you found.
That makes Q19.3 the worst possible place to learn the distinction and the best possible place to be told about it.

**4. The lower limit.**
$R(0) = 0$ here, so omitting $-R(0)$ costs nothing.
It costs everything on an interval starting anywhere else, and drill D2 is that question.

**5. Averaging the endpoints on a curved rate.**
Routes B, C and D are exact here **because $r$ is linear**, and a student can easily leave this question believing the shortcut is general.
On $r = 60e^{-t/10}$ over $[0,20]$ the endpoint average is 31 percent high.

**6. The sign.**
$\int(-r)$ or $F(a)-F(b)$ gives $-2025$.
See below, because this one is more interesting than it looks.

**7. Integrating over the stated domain instead of the asked interval.**
$\int_0^{50} r = 1500$, which is smaller than the right answer despite covering more than three times as much time, because the model runs backwards after $t=30$.
That is a genuinely counter-intuitive number and it is worth knowing it exists.

### The census, and which errors hide

Seventeen candidate answers were enumerated and every one was computed, not typed.
No point was excluded as degenerate.

| The mistake | Value | Detected by |
| :--- | ---: | :--- |
| **right answer** | **2025** | - |
| midpoint rate $r(7.5)\times15$ | **2025** | **nothing - hides completely** |
| omitted the lower limit, $R(15)$ alone | **2025** | **nothing - hides completely** |
| sign flip, $F(0)-F(15)$ | $-2025$ | sign, and the student repairs it |
| initial rate $r(0)\times 15$ | 2700 | magnitude bracket |
| integrated over $[0,30]$ | 2700 | reading the interval |
| final rate $r(15)\times 15$ | 1350 | magnitude bracket |
| antiderivative $180t-6t^2$ | 1350 | magnitude bracket |
| dropped the 6, $\int(180-t)$ | 2587.5 | magnitude bracket |
| integrated $[0,50]$ | 1500 | reading the interval |
| total moved over $[0,50]$ | 3900 | magnitude bracket |
| integrated $[15,50]$ | $-525$ | sign and magnitude |
| answered $r(15)$ | 90 | units |
| answered $r(0)$ | 180 | units |
| differentiated, $r'(15)$ | $-6$ | units |
| $\int(-6)\,dt$ | $-90$ | units |
| antiderivative $180t-3t^3$ | $-7425$ | sign and magnitude |

**Two of the sixteen wrong routes return exactly 2025 and are undetectable by any check on this page.**
The midpoint shortcut hides because $r$ is linear, so the shortcut is genuinely valid here and is not really an error at all until Family 4.
The omitted lower limit hides because $R(0) = 0$ exactly.
Both are properties of *this question's numbers*, and both disappear the moment the interval does not start at zero or the rate is not linear.

Three values are each produced by two different routes: 1350, 2025 and 2700.
**Eleven of the sixteen wrong answers are positive**, so a positivity check rejects fewer than a third of them and is nearly useless here.
Seven of the sixteen lie between half and double the correct answer, so a rough plausibility check is not much better.

### Which pattern this is: Q19.1, not Q19.2

Q19.1 found three mistakes that all evaluated to $-4.5$ where the answer was $4.5$: the magnitude was right, only the sign was wrong, and the instinct "an area is positive" repaired all three into the correct answer.
Q19.2 inverted it: three errors collided at $0.221$ against a true $0.828$, so the same repair turned a visibly broken answer into a confident wrong one.

**Q19.3 is the Q19.1 pattern, and more forgiving still.**
Exactly one census entry has the right magnitude and the wrong sign, $-2025$, and "an amount of water is positive" repairs it into the correct answer.
Nothing on this question punishes the repair.

That is the danger, and it is worth stating as a sentence:

> **Q19.3 rewards the habit that Q19.2 punishes.**
> A student who learns on this question that a negative answer can simply be made positive will lose the mark on Q19.2, on Q19.8, and on any question where the flow reverses.

Both pages are on the same paper family and both traps are live in this course.
Learn the rule from Q19.3, where it is cheap; do not learn the repair.

---

## 10. Drill set

Score **sign** separately from **magnitude**.
They are different failure modes and they need different remediation: a magnitude error means the arithmetic or the interval, a sign error means you did not decide what you were accumulating.

1. Water leaves at $r(t)=180-6t$ L/min. How much leaves during the first 25 minutes?
2. Same rate. How much leaves between minute 10 and minute 20?
3. The tank holds 4000 L at $t=0$. How much is in it at $t=15$?
4. Same rate. How much water does the model deliver in total before the flow stops?
5. Same rate, over the full stated domain $[0,50]$: what is the net change, and what is the total volume moved?
6. Water enters at $5t$ L/min and leaves at 100 L/min. Over $[0,40]$, what is the net change, and what is the total volume moved?
7. $r(t)=60e^{-t/10}$ L/min. How much flows out in the first 20 minutes?
8. A particle has velocity $v(t)=t^2-4$ m/s. Over $[0,3]$, find the displacement and the distance travelled.
9. What is the average outflow rate over the first 15 minutes?
10. At what time has exactly 1000 litres left the tank?
11. Marginal cost is $C'(x)=3+0.02x$ dollars per unit. What does it cost to go from 100 units to 300?
12. Give the answer to the exam question in cubic metres.

### Answer key

| # | Exact | Decimal | Family and method |
| ---: | :--- | ---: | :--- |
| 1 | $4500-1875$ | 2625 L | **F0** - same antiderivative, new upper limit |
| 2 | $(3600-1200)-(1800-300)$ | 900 L | **F0** - the lower limit is live here |
| 3 | $4000-2025$ | 1975 L | **F1** - initial condition, and 2025 is now wrong |
| 4 | $5400-2700$ | 2700 L | **F9** - stop at the sign change, not at $t=50$ |
| 5 | $9000-7500$ / $2700+1200$ | 1500 L / 3900 L | **F2** - net, then total, from the same two pieces |
| 6 | $2.5(1600)-4000$ / $2(2000-1000)$ | 0 L / 2000 L | **F5** - the net is exactly zero |
| 7 | $600(1-e^{-2})$ | 518.7988300580 L | **F4** - and the endpoint average is 31% high |
| 8 | $9-12$ / $\tfrac{16}{3}+\tfrac{7}{3}$ | $-3$ m / $7.6666666667$ m | **F11** - zero at $t=2$, so split there |
| 9 | $2025/15$ | 135 L/min | **F6** - divide, and the units go back to L/min |
| 10 | $\dfrac{180-\sqrt{20400}}{6}$ | 6.1952385715 min | **F3** - reject the root at 53.8047614285 |
| 11 | $600+800$ | \$1400 | **F12** - the input variable is units, not time |
| 12 | $2025/1000$ | 2.025 m$^3$ | **F7** - convert once, at the end |

Every entry was computed twice: once from the closed form and once by an 8-point Gauss-Legendre rule on 400 panels that never sees the closed form.
The two agree to $10^{-8}$ on all 22 verified rows.

---

## 11. The one-page decision tree

```
A RATE is given.  What is asked?
|
+- "how much flowed / how far / how many were added"   -> a CHANGE
|     |
|     +- does r change sign strictly INSIDE the interval?
|          |
|          +- NO  -> int_a^b r        (net = total, one computation)
|          |
|          +- YES -> which word?
|                     "net change / displacement"  -> int_a^b r
|                     "total moved / distance"     -> split at the zeros,
|                                                     add |each piece|
|
+- "how much is there AT time b"                       -> a FINAL AMOUNT
|     Q(b) = Q(a) + int_a^b r        <- the initial condition is half the answer
|
+- "average rate"                                      -> divide by (b - a)
|
+- "at what time ..."                                  -> solve F(T) = target,
                                                          then DISCARD roots
                                                          outside the domain

Then, always:
  check  units:      (units of r) x (units of t)  must be the answer's units
  check  magnitude:  for a decreasing positive rate,
                     r(b)(b-a)  <  answer  <  r(a)(b-a)
  check  sign:       decided BEFORE integrating, never repaired after
  preview the Möbius box
```

### What was verified, and how

- **249 assertions, 0 failures, across sections `q193` (143), `q193d` (57) and `q193s` (49)**, counted by grepping the section prefixes with a trailing space rather than by trusting an internal counter. The whole harness runs with zero failures, so any failure a later run sees is real.
- **36 seeded controls**, counted from the assertion labels carrying `CONTROL`, `REJECT`, `HIDES` or `BAIT`, each proving a gate can report the failure it is supposed to catch.
- The antiderivative was differentiated back at **69 sample points** by complex-step differentiation at $h=10^{-30}$, an arm that never sees the claimed integral. A seeded wrong antiderivative, $180t-6t^2$, was rejected at 68 of the 69 points, agreeing only at $t=0$.
- The definite integral was computed by **eight independent routes** agreeing to $6.594\times10^{-12}$, including tanh-sinh quadrature and Simpson at eight values of $n$ chosen odd and off multiples of 8.
- **The quadrature convergence order on this integrand is unmeasurable**, and that is the honest report rather than a nominal 4. The integrand is linear, Simpson is exact on cubics, and the measured errors are $0$ at $n = 6, 10, 18$ and $2.3\times10^{-13}$ at $n = 34$ and above, which is roundoff. The same routine was proved able to report a real order elsewhere: it measures $4.0222, 4.0081, 4.0025, 4.0007$ and then $4.0000$ on $\sin(t^2)$, and $1.6661$ rising to $1.6667$ on $\lvert t\rvert^{2/3}$. Two independent reference values for the $\sin(t^2)$ integral disagreed on the last rung in the fourth decimal, which is the tell that the error has reached roundoff and the ratio there is no longer measuring convergence; the quoted ladder stops where it is still meaningful.
- **A separate kink measurement.** $\lvert r\rvert$ has a corner at $t=30$, which is exactly $3/5$ of the way across $[0,50]$. At $n = 10, 20, 40, 80, 160$, all divisible by 5, the corner lands on a panel boundary and Simpson's error is exactly $0$. At $n = 6, 12, 24, 48, 96$ the errors are $44.4, 11.1, 2.78, 0.694, 0.174$ and the measured order is $2.0000$, not 4. **A grid that happens to align with a corner reports perfection**, so the choice of $n$ has to be made deliberately.
- **The units gate is dimensional, not prose**: quantities are exponent vectors over (litre, minute), and the gate was proved to reject L/min, L$\cdot$min, min, min/L and the inhomogeneous sum L + L/min before its acceptance of L was trusted. Re-integrating the whole problem in seconds returns the identical 2025 L.
- **The sign-change census** was controlled to return 0, 1 and 2 on constructed cases, and was checked against the grid-alignment failure: at $n=50$ the grid lands exactly on $t=30$, a census testing only `v[i]*v[i+1] < 0` finds nothing, and the census used here keeps a separate equality branch and still finds the root.
- **Every printed digit on this page was computed**, including the census values, the collision counts, the family count and the in-band count. Six checker defects were found and fixed during the run, and all six were the check rather than the mathematics: a quadrature routine that never halved its step, two typed counts, a boundary comparison with no tolerance, and two defects in the claims checker itself, one of which made every sentence-final number invisible to it.

# Q19.4 - Work, raising one end of a chain

**The question (Final Exam 1, item 13, 5 points).**
"A chain lying on the ground is $10\text{ m}$ long and its mass is $80\text{ kg}$.
How much work is required to raise one end of the chain to a height of $6\text{ m}$?"

**The answer.** $W = 144g$ joules $= 1411.2$ J, taking $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$.

**What to type into Möbius:** `1411.2`

Provenance: the stem is re-parsed from `notes\MATH265\MATH265.md`, not retyped, and it matches the bank's copy after normalising the LaTeX spacing macros.
Final Exam 1 prints its point values inline at the end of each stem; item 13 carries **(5 points)**, and the paper's fourteen values sum to 124, so this question is 4.03 percent of that paper.
Every number printed below was recomputed in Python and cross-checked against at least one independent route before it was written down.

---

## 0. The 30-second version

```
cut the chain into slices  ->  index them by a variable
weight of one slice        ->  (mass per metre) x g x d(variable)
distance THAT slice moves  ->  read it off the final picture
                           ->  W = integral of (weight) x (rise)

Q19.4:  lambda = 80/10 = 8 kg/m,  weight/m = 8g = 78.4 N/m
        the top 6 m ends up hanging over heights 0..6
        the slice now at height y came from the ground, so it rose y
        W = int_0^6 (78.4)(y) dy = 78.4 x 18 = 1411.2 J
```

The whole question is the third line.
Everything else is arithmetic.

---

## 1. What this question is really testing

Q19.1, Q19.2 and Q19.3 all handed you a function and asked you to integrate it.
This one does not.

| Reflex | Where it comes back |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Build an integrand from a physical slice** | Q19.5 (spring), Q19.8, Q19.9, and every "work" or "force" question |
| Choose a slicing variable and state the origin | the same, plus any centre-of-mass or fluid-force question |
| Notice that different slices move different distances | the single idea this question exists to test |
| Keep weight and mass apart | Q19.5, where the units flip to imperial and $g$ must vanish |
| Sanity-check against a trivial bound | every applications-of-integration question |

**The one sentence.**
Nothing is handed to you as a function to integrate; you have to build the integrand out of a picture, and the picture's whole content is that a chain raised at one end has slices that travel *different* distances.

### Why the marks are cheap and the trap is not

Five points is the third-commonest value on Final Exam 1 (three items carry it), and it is well below that paper's 20-point items.
The integral itself is $\int_0^6 78.4\,y\,dy$, which a first-year student can do in one line.
So the difficulty is deliberately not in the antiderivative - it is in writing the antiderivative down at all.
That is an inference from the point value, and it is flagged as one: **no marking scheme exists in any of the four course files**, and this run confirmed that for the ninth consecutive time by searching all four for "rubric", "marking scheme" and "part marks" (0 occurrences each).

Item 13 also carries **no justification demand of any kind**.
Searching its own slice of the paper for "show your work", "justif", "state which rule", "no credit", "indicate the technique" and "explain" returns nothing, while the same search over the whole paper does find "no credit" elsewhere - so the absence is a measurement, not a pattern that never matches.

---

## 2. The four things you must have cold

### 2a. Work is a product, and the integral is there because one factor varies

For a constant force $F$ moving an object a constant distance $d$:

$$W = F \cdot d$$

The integral appears the moment *either* factor stops being constant.
There are exactly two shapes, and confusing them is the commonest structural error in the whole topic:

| Shape | What varies | The integral | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Variable force** | $F$ changes with position $x$ | $W = \int_a^b F(x)\,dx$ | a spring, a leaky bucket |
| **Variable distance** | each *piece* of the object moves a different distance | $W = \int (\text{weight of a slice})\times(\text{rise of that slice})$ | a chain, a cable, a tank of water |

Q19.4 is the second shape.
Q19.5 is the first shape.
They are both "work", and they are not the same calculation.

### 2b. The slice method, in four moves

> 1. **Set up a coordinate.** Draw the *final* picture, put an origin somewhere convenient, and name the variable.
> 2. **Cut.** Take a slice of thickness $d(\text{variable})$ and write its **weight**.
> 3. **Move it.** Read off, from the picture, how far *that particular slice* travelled.
> 4. **Add.** $W = \int (\text{weight of the slice}) \times (\text{rise of the slice})$, over the range of the variable.

Move 3 is where the question is won or lost.
Moves 1, 2 and 4 are bookkeeping.

### 2c. Weight versus mass, the classic lost mark

This is invisible to every numerical check, because a wrong answer that is off by a factor of $9.8$ still looks like a number.

| The stem gives you | What it is | Do you multiply by $g$? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $80$ kg, $8$ kg/m, "mass" | **mass** | **yes** - weight $=$ mass $\times\, g$ |
| $500$ N, $78.4$ N/m | **weight** (a force) | **no** - $g$ is already inside it |
| $2$ lb/ft, $50$ lb, "weighs" | **weight** (imperial) | **no** - the pound is a force |
| $3$ slugs, $12$ kg/m$^3$ | **mass** | **yes** |

Q19.4 says **mass**, in kilograms.
So $g$ belongs in the integrand, and the linear *weight* density is

$$\lambda g = \frac{80\text{ kg}}{10\text{ m}}\times 9.8\ \frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2} = 78.4\ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{m}}$$

Omitting $g$ gives $144$, which is exactly the answer divided by $9.8$.
Q19.5 is the mirror image: it is stated in foot-pounds, so inserting $g$ there is the same mistake running the other way.

### 2d. The constants carry units too

The $10$ is $10$ metres, the $80$ is $80$ kilograms, the $6$ is $6$ metres, and the $80/10$ is $8$ kilograms **per metre**.
A student who reads them as bare numbers has no way to notice when a conversion is needed.
Redoing the whole problem in grams and centimetres gives $1.4112\times 10^{10}$ erg, which converts back to exactly $1411.2$ J - an independent arm that catches a conversion applied to only one of the two factors.

---

## 3. The universal procedure

> 1. Decide which shape you are in: **variable force** or **variable distance**.
> 2. If variable distance: draw the **final** configuration, not the initial one.
> 3. Pick a slicing variable and **write down where the origin is**. The integrand depends on that choice; the answer does not.
> 4. Write the weight of one slice. Check whether the stem gave mass or weight.
> 5. Write the rise of that slice, **as a function of the slicing variable**, from the picture.
> 6. Integrate over the range of the variable that actually indexes slices of the object.
> 7. Check units, then check the trivial bounds.

### The classify table

| Cue in the stem | Shape | Slicing variable | Rise |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| "raise one end of a chain/rope to height $h$" | distance | height $y$, or arclength $s$ | $y$, or $h-s$ |
| "haul up a hanging cable" | distance | depth $d$ below the top | $d$ |
| "lift the whole thing $h$ metres" | neither, it is a product | none | constant $h$ |
| "pump the water out over the rim" | distance | height $y$ of the layer | $(\text{rim}) - y$ |
| "stretch a spring", "compress" | force | extension $x$ | not applicable |
| "the bucket leaks" | force | height $y$ | not applicable |

---

## 4. Q19.4 worked four ways

Set $L = 10$ m, $M = 80$ kg, $H = 6$ m, $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$, and $\lambda = M/L = 8$ kg/m.

Because $H < L$, only part of the chain leaves the ground.
The final picture is: **$6$ m of chain hanging vertically over the heights $0$ to $6$, and $4$ m still lying on the ground.**
That splits the mass $48$ kg moving, $32$ kg not moving.

### Route A - slice by HEIGHT, origin on the ground

Let $y$ measure height upward from the ground, $0 \le y \le 6$.
In the final picture the hanging part occupies exactly those heights, so the slice now sitting at height $y$ has weight $\lambda g\,dy$.
It started on the ground, so **it rose $y$**.

$$W = \int_0^{6} \lambda g\, y\,dy = \lambda g\left[\frac{y^2}{2}\right]_0^{6} = 78.4 \times 18 = 1411.2\text{ J}$$

This is the route to write on the paper.

### Route B - slice by ARCLENGTH, origin at the raised end

Now index the chain by $s$, the distance along the chain from the end you are lifting, $0 \le s \le 10$.
This changes both the variable and the origin, so it is a genuinely independent derivation rather than the same algebra rearranged.

After the lift, the material point at arclength $s$ sits at height $H - s$ while $s \le 6$, and back on the ground for $s > 6$.
Everything started at height $0$, so the rise is $\max(H-s,\,0)$:

$$W = \int_0^{10} \lambda g \max(6-s,0)\,ds = \lambda g\int_0^{6}(6-s)\,ds = \lambda g\left[6s - \frac{s^2}{2}\right]_0^{6} = 78.4 \times 18 = 1411.2\text{ J}$$

Note that the integral now runs over the **whole** chain and the last $4$ m contributes zero, which is the picture stating "that part never moved".

**The two routes agree to the last bit of floating point**, not merely to a tolerance.
That is the strongest available check on a modelling question, because it tests the setup rather than the arithmetic - a wrong choice of "which slice travels how far" would not survive being re-derived from a different origin.

### Route C - slice by arclength from the GROUNDED end

A third origin, for free.
Let $u$ be the distance from the end that never leaves the ground.
That end is $4$ m from where the chain starts to rise, so the point at $u$ ends at height $\max(u-4,\,0)$:

$$W = \int_{4}^{10}\lambda g\,(u-4)\,du = 78.4\times 18 = 1411.2\text{ J}$$

Three origins, one answer.

### Route D - the centre-of-mass shortcut

Only the top $6$ m moves.
That piece is uniform, so its centre of mass sits at its midpoint and rises from $0$ to $3$ m:

$$W = (\text{moving mass})\times g \times (\text{rise of its centre of mass}) = 48 \times 9.8 \times 3 = 1411.2\text{ J}$$

**This shortcut is valid here**, and it is worth knowing exactly why, because it is not valid in general.
It works whenever the rise is a *linear* function of the mass coordinate, since then the average rise over the moving mass equals the rise of the average position.
Both of this question's conditions hold: the density is constant and the rise is $y$ itself.

Two guard rails, both checked numerically:

- It **still works** on a chain of variable density, provided the rise is still linear - because the centre of mass is defined by exactly that weighting.
- It **fails** the moment the rise stops being linear. Replacing the rise $y$ with $y^2/6$ makes the true work $940.8$ J while the shortcut returns $705.6$ J.

And there is a much more likely way to break it, described in section 9: applying it to the **whole** $80$ kg instead of the moving $48$ kg.

### Route comparison

| Route | What it costs | When to use it |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **A - slice by height** | one line of setup, one integral | **use this one under pressure** |
| B - slice by arclength | same integral, more thought about the limits | use it as a check, or when the stem is phrased along the chain |
| C - arclength from the far end | an extra subtraction to get the limits right | rarely worth it |
| D - centre of mass | no integral at all | as an eight-second check, never as the written method |

Route A wins because the coordinate you pick is the one the final picture already draws for you.
Route D is the fastest but it is the one that punishes a careless reading, so use it to confirm a number you obtained another way.

---

## 5. The exam-ready write-up

These are the sentences that earn the method marks, in order.

> Let $y$ be the height above the ground, measured upward, with the origin at ground level.
> The chain has linear mass density $\lambda = 80/10 = 8$ kg/m, so a slice of thickness $dy$ has weight $8g\,dy = 78.4\,dy$ N.
> Since $6 < 10$, the chain ends up with $6$ m hanging over the heights $0$ to $6$ and $4$ m still on the ground.
> The slice that finishes at height $y$ began on the ground, so it is raised through a distance $y$.
> Hence $dW = 78.4\,y\,dy$ and
> $$W = \int_0^{6} 78.4\,y\,dy = 78.4\left[\frac{y^2}{2}\right]_0^6 = 78.4(18) = 1411.2\text{ J}.$$

Four things in that paragraph do work:
naming the origin, dividing mass by length, saying which part of the chain moves, and saying how far the slice at $y$ travelled.
The integral is the fifth line and the easiest one.

---

## 6. Verify before you commit

### The eight-second checks, in the order they catch things

| Check | On this question | What it catches |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Units** | (kg/m)(m/s$^2$)(m)(m) $=$ J | a missing or doubled $g$, a dropped $dy$ |
| **Tight bracket** | $0 < W < 48g(6) = 2822.4$ | the largest class of errors, see below |
| **Trivial bracket** | $0 < W < 80g(6) = 4704$ | a wrong density, a doubled $g$ |
| **Which mass moves** | $48$ kg moves, $32$ kg does not | applying anything to the full $80$ kg |
| **Mass or weight** | the stem says kg, so $g$ is required | the $9.8$ factor, in either direction |

**The tight bracket is the strongest single check available here, and that was measured rather than guessed.**
Nothing can move further than $6$ m, and nothing but the top $48$ kg moves at all, so $W$ must be under $48 \times 9.8 \times 6 = 2822.4$ J.
Against the seventeen candidates in section 9's census, the tight bracket rejects **nine**, the trivial bracket rejects **four**, and a positivity check rejects **none**.
It is also a strict superset: everything the trivial bracket catches, the tight bracket catches too.

### Where the answer sits in its range

$1411.2$ is **exactly $30$ percent** of the trivial upper bound $4704$, and **exactly half** of the tight bound $2822.4$.
Neither of those is a coincidence.
The first is $H/(2L) = 6/20$, and the second is the statement that a uniform chain's average rise is half its maximum rise.
So on any version of this question, the answer is half of "the moving mass through the full height" - which makes that ratio a genuine check rather than a numerological one.

### The check that is inert here, and why you should know that

Work, as this question asks for it, is a positive quantity, and every plausible wrong answer is positive too.
So the "an amount must be positive" repair that rescues Q19.1 does **nothing** on Q19.4.
This matters because Q19.1 and Q19.3 both reward that repair and Q19.2 punishes it; Q19.4 is the third behaviour, where it neither helps nor harms.
Read section 9 before trusting a sign check on any question in this category.

### Numbers worth memorising

| Quantity | Value |
| ---: | :--- |
| $\lambda$, linear mass density | $8$ kg/m |
| $\lambda g$, linear weight density | $78.4$ N/m |
| mass that moves | $48$ kg |
| mass that does not | $32$ kg |
| rise of the moving centre of mass | $3$ m |
| $\int_0^6 y\,dy$ | $18$ |
| **the answer** | **$1411.2$ J $= 144g$** |
| trivial upper bound | $4704$ J |
| tight upper bound | $2822.4$ J |
| weight now hanging, $\lambda g H$ | $470.4$ N |
| the same chain raised to $10$ m | $3920$ J |

That last row is worth its own note: $470.4$ N is exactly $dW/dH$ at $H=6$.
The marginal cost of raising the end one more metre is the weight currently hanging, which is a good physical check that the model is behaving.

## 7. Answer-entry rules

Both MATH 265 exams are Möbius, answer-only and machine-marked, so a correct method with a bad keystroke scores zero.

| Do | Do not |
| :--- | :--- |
| type `1411.2` | type `1411.2 J` unless the box asks for units |
| use $g=9.8$ unless the paper says otherwise | round to `1411` without checking the tolerance |
| keep the decimal point, not a comma | type `1,411.2` |
| preview before submitting | assume the box parses `144*9.8` |

**The single most expensive typo here is the units suffix.**
A numeric-answer box that is expecting `1411.2` will usually reject `1411.2 J`, and the mark is gone with the method perfectly correct.

If the paper specifies a different $g$, the answer moves predictably:
$g = 9.81$ gives $1412.64$, and $g = 9.80665$ gives $1412.1576$.
All three are $144g$, so compute $144$ first and multiply last.

Every grading claim in this section is an **inference**.
No marking scheme, rubric or part-marks statement exists anywhere in the four course files.

---

## 8. The variation catalog

Read this as **structure**, not as thirteen facts.
There are only two shapes in the whole topic (variable force, variable distance), and only three questions to answer for any of them: what indexes the slices, what does one slice weigh, and how far does that slice go.
Every family below is those three answers filled in differently.

Every value in every table was computed twice - once from a closed form, once from a formula-blind midpoint sum that knows only the slice picture.

### Family 0 - one end raised, with $H \le L$ (this question)

**Trigger:** "raise one end to a height of $h$", and $h$ is no bigger than the object's length.
**Tool:** $W = \tfrac{1}{2}\lambda g h^2$.
**Why:** the part still on the ground contributes nothing, and $L$ never enters.

| $L$ | $M$ | $h$ | $W$ |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $10$ m | $80$ kg | $6$ m | $1411.2$ J |
| $10$ m | $80$ kg | $4$ m | $627.2$ J |
| $12$ m | $60$ kg | $5$ m | $612.5$ J |

**The structural fact:** $W$ is independent of $L$ except through $\lambda$.
Halve the length while keeping the density and the answer does not move.

### Family 1 - one end raised, with $H \ge L$

**Trigger:** the target height is at least the chain's length, so the whole chain leaves the ground.
**Tool:** $W = \lambda g\left(\tfrac{1}{2}L^2 + L(h-L)\right)$.
**Why:** once the chain is clear, every further metre lifts the *entire* weight, so the cost becomes linear.

| $h$ | $W$ | note |
| ---: | ---: | :--- |
| $10$ m | $3920$ J | the two regimes meet here |
| $15$ m | $7840$ J | $3920$ for the lift plus $3920$ for the extra $5$ m |
| $20$ m | $11760$ J | linear from here on |

**The structural fact:** below $L$ the graph of $W$ against $h$ is a parabola; at $h=L$ it becomes a straight line, and the two pieces join smoothly because the slope $\lambda g h$ saturates at $\lambda g L = $ the whole weight.

### Family 2 - a uniform hoist, where every slice moves the same distance

**Trigger:** "lift the whole chain $6$ m", "raise the object to a height of...".
**Tool:** $W = Mgd$, a product with no integral.
**Why:** the rise is constant, so it comes out of the integral and what is left is the total mass.

Lifting all $80$ kg through $6$ m is $4704$ J - which is exactly Q19.4's trivial upper bound, because that is what "every slice travels the maximum distance" means.
**This family is the commonest wrong answer to Family 0**, and telling the two apart is the entire skill.

### Family 3 - a hanging chain hauled to the top

**Trigger:** "a cable hangs from the top of a building", "pull all the rope up".
**Tool:** $W = \tfrac{1}{2}\lambda g L^2$, with the slice at depth $d$ below the top rising $d$.
**Why:** it is Family 0 with $h = L$, drawn upside down.

| $L$ | $M$ | $W$ |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $10$ m | $80$ kg | $3920$ J |
| $30$ m | $45$ kg | $6615$ J |

**The structural fact worth carrying:** hauling up a hanging $10$ m chain and raising a grounded $10$ m chain's end to $10$ m are **the same number** by two completely different pictures.

### Family 4 - weight per unit length given, so no $g$ anywhere

**Trigger:** "weighs $2$ lb/ft", "a $50$ lb cable", any imperial force unit.
**Tool:** $W = \tfrac{1}{2}w h^2$ with $w$ the weight per length.
**Why:** the pound is already a force; $g$ is inside it.

| $w$ | $h$ | $W$ |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $2.5$ lb/ft | $6$ ft | $45$ ft-lb |
| $3$ lb/ft | $8$ ft | $96$ ft-lb |

This is the family that makes the weight-versus-mass distinction of section 2c cost a mark rather than merely being pedantry.

### Family 5 - variable linear density

**Trigger:** "the density at a distance $x$ from one end is ...".
**Tool:** the same integral, with $\lambda$ inside it rather than outside.
**Why:** nothing about the slice argument changes; only one factor stops being constant.

Worked instance: a $6$ m chain of density $(2+x)$ kg/m at distance $x$ from the raised end, that end taken to $6$ m so the whole chain hangs.
The slice at $x$ rises $6-x$:

$$W = \int_0^6 (2+x)g(6-x)\,dx = g\int_0^6 (12 + 4x - x^2)\,dx = 72g = 705.6\text{ J}$$

The chain's total mass is $30$ kg, and a *uniform* $30$ kg chain of the same length gives a different answer - which is the check that the variable density is actually doing work in the integral.

### Family 6 - a rope plus a payload

**Trigger:** "a bucket of mass $m$ is lifted on a rope weighing ...".
**Tool:** $W = mgh + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho g h^2$, one term from Family 2 and one from Family 0.
**Why:** the payload's rise is constant, the rope's is not.

| Piece | Value |
| :--- | ---: |
| $10$ kg bucket raised $12$ m | $1176$ J |
| $0.5$ kg/m rope, same lift | $352.8$ J |
| total | $1528.8$ J |

**The structural fact:** work is additive over the parts of the system, which is what lets you split a hard problem into two easy families.

### Family 7 - a leaky bucket

**Trigger:** "the bucket leaks at ... while it is raised".
**Tool:** $W = \int_0^h F(y)\,dy$ with $F$ the *weight at height $y$*.
**Why:** this is the **variable-force** shape, not the variable-distance one. The whole object travels the whole distance; it is the force that changes.

A bucket whose mass is $(20 - 0.5y)$ kg at height $y$, raised $10$ m, costs $175g = 1715$ J - less than the $1960$ J it would cost if nothing leaked.

**This family is the reason section 2a exists.**
Family 7 and Family 0 produce structurally identical-looking integrals from opposite physical arguments, and writing the right integral for the wrong reason is how a student passes this question and fails the next one.

### Family 8 - pumping liquid out of a tank

**Trigger:** "pump the water over the rim", "empty the tank".
**Tool:** $W = \int \rho g A(y)\,(\text{rim} - y)\,dy$.
**Why:** the slice is a horizontal layer, so its weight involves the cross-sectional **area**, which may itself vary with $y$.

A cylinder of radius $2$ m and depth $5$ m, full of water, pumped over the rim: $W = 490000\pi \approx 1.5394\times 10^6$ J.
A cone of the same height, narrowing downward, costs less - because more of its water starts near the rim.

This is Family 0's argument with one extra factor, and it is the standard next question after this one.

### Family 9 - a spring, which is Q19.5

**Trigger:** Hooke's law, "stretch beyond its natural length".
**Tool:** $F(x) = kx$, $W = \int_a^b kx\,dx$.
**Why:** variable force again, and $x$ measures extension, not position.

Q19.5's own numbers: $20$ ft-lb stretches the spring $1$ ft, so $k = 2(20)/1^2 = 40$ lb/ft, and stretching it $2$ ft costs $\int_0^2 40x\,dx = 80$ ft-lb.
Note that **no $g$ appears anywhere**, because the pound is a force - the mirror image of Q19.4.

### Family 10 - a general variable force

**Trigger:** "a force of $F(x)$ acts along ...".
**Tool:** $W = \int_a^b F(x)\,dx$, with no modelling at all.
**Why:** the integrand is handed to you, so this is really a Q17-style definite integral wearing a physics costume.

$F(x) = 3x^2 + 2$ from $x=0$ to $x=4$ gives $72$.

### Family 11 - the question run backwards

**Trigger:** "how high must the end be raised for the work to be ...", "find the density given the work".
**Tool:** solve $\tfrac{1}{2}\lambda g h^2 = W$ for the unknown.
**Why:** the relation is invertible on $[0, L]$ because $W$ is strictly increasing there.

For Q19.4's chain, $1000$ J corresponds to $h = \sqrt{2000/78.4} = 5.0508$ m.
Always check the answer lies in $[0,L]$; a target above $3920$ J has no Family 0 solution at all and needs Family 1.

### Family 12 - a difference of works

**Trigger:** "how much *additional* work", "raise it a further ...".
**Tool:** $W(h_2) - W(h_1)$.
**Why:** work is a difference of a state function, so the intermediate history does not matter.

Going from $6$ m to $8$ m costs $1097.6$ J - which is **more** than the first $2$ m cost ($156.8$ J), because there is more chain hanging by then.
That monotone increase is a good structural check.

---

## 9. The trap list

Ranked by how often each actually costs a mark.

1. **Treating every slice as if it travelled the full $6$ m.**
   This is Family 2's formula on Family 0's question, and it gives $4704$ J.
   It is the single commonest wrong answer in this topic, and it is precisely the trivial upper bound - so it is the one error the bracket check cannot mistake for a right answer.
2. **Applying the centre-of-mass shortcut to the whole $80$ kg.**
   $80 \times 9.8 \times 3 = 2352$ J.
   The average rise of $3$ m is correct; the mass it is applied to is not, because $32$ kg never left the ground.
   This is the seductive one, because every individual step in it is true of *something*.
3. **Omitting $g$.**
   $144$ J, exactly the answer over $9.8$.
   Invisible to any check that does not look at units.
4. **Inserting $g$ where the stem already gave a weight.**
   The same mistake in reverse, and the one waiting on Q19.5.
5. **Integrating to $L$ instead of $H$.**
   $3920$ J, which is the answer to a different and perfectly sensible question (Family 1 at $h=L$).
   Nothing about the number looks wrong.
6. **Dropping the $\tfrac{1}{2}$ from $\int y\,dy$.**
   $2822.4$ J, exactly double.
7. **Using $M$ where $\lambda$ belongs**, or dividing by $H$ instead of $L$.
   $14112$ J and $2352$ J respectively.
8. **Measuring the rise as $6-y$ instead of $y$.**
   This one **hides**; see below.

### The census, and which errors hide

Seventeen candidate wrong answers were enumerated, each derived from a named mistake rather than typed, with no point excluded as degenerate.

| Mistake | Value |
| :--- | ---: |
| every slice travels the full $6$ m (whole chain) | $4704$ |
| lifted mass times full length | $4704$ |
| $g$ inserted twice | $13829.76$ |
| mass used as the linear density | $14112$ |
| integrate to $L$ instead of $H$ | $3920$ |
| whole chain's centre of mass rises $L/2$ | $3920$ |
| every slice of the lifted part travels $6$ m | $2822.4$ |
| the $\tfrac{1}{2}$ dropped from $\int y\,dy$ | $2822.4$ |
| answer doubled | $2822.4$ |
| average distance applied to the whole weight | $2352$ |
| density taken as $M/H$ | $2352$ |
| $g = 9.81$ instead of $9.8$ | $1412.64$ |
| **rise measured downward, $6-y$ instead of $y$** | **$1411.2$** |
| answer halved | $705.6$ |
| the rise $(6-s)$ let run over the whole chain | $784$ |
| $y\,dy$ read as $y$, evaluated at $H$ | $470.4$ |
| $g$ omitted entirely | $144$ |

**Exactly one candidate hides**: measuring each slice's rise downward as $6-y$ rather than $y$ returns $1411.2$ J, the correct answer, from an incorrect picture.
It hides because $\int_0^6 y\,dy = \int_0^6 (6-y)\,dy = 18$ - the rise is symmetric about the midpoint of the interval, so reversing it changes nothing.
That symmetry breaks the moment the interval does not start at zero, which is why Drill D3 and Family 5 are worth doing: they remove the hiding point.

**One more is a near-miss rather than a hider:** using $g = 9.81$ gives $1412.64$, which is $1.44$ J away.
That is not an error of method, and if the paper's own convention is $9.81$ it is the right answer.

**The magnitude pattern.**
Twelve candidates are larger than the truth and four are smaller.
Every single one is **positive**, so the positivity repair that rescues Q19.1 and Q19.3 rejects **zero** of them.
Four values are hit by more than one distinct mistake, and $2822.4$ is hit by **three** - it is exactly twice the answer, so the constant-distance-on-the-lifted-part error, the dropped-$\tfrac12$ error and a bare factor-of-two slip all land on it.
Nine of the seventeen candidates sit on a value that some other mistake also produces, which means "two methods agreed" is weak evidence on this question unless the two methods used different origins.

### Which pattern this is: neither Q19.1's nor Q19.2's

The queue has now measured three behaviours of the same repair:

| Question | The repair | What it does |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Q19.1 | "an area is positive" | rescues all three wrong candidates |
| Q19.2 | "an area is positive" | produces a confident **wrong** answer |
| Q19.3 | "an amount is positive" | rescues the one sign error, harmlessly |
| **Q19.4** | "work is positive" | **inert - it rejects nothing at all** |

So Q19.4 is a fourth case, and it changes what you should reach for.
On an area or net-change question the sign is the cheap discriminator; on a work question there is no sign to check, and **the magnitude bracket is the only cheap check that discriminates**.
That is the single most transferable sentence on this page.

---

## 10. Drill set

Score **magnitude** and **setup** separately.
A magnitude error means arithmetic; a setup error means you answered a different family's question, and the fix is a different section.

1. The same $10$ m, $80$ kg chain: raise one end to $10$ m.
2. The same chain: raise one end to $4$ m.
3. A $12$ m chain of mass $60$ kg: raise one end to $5$ m.
4. A rope weighing $3$ lb/ft: raise one end to $8$ ft.
5. Lift the entire $10$ m, $80$ kg chain to a height of $6$ m.
6. A $10$ m, $80$ kg chain hangs from a roof; haul all of it up.
7. Starting from the $6$ m position of the main question, how much *additional* work raises the end to $8$ m?
8. A $6$ m chain has density $(2+x)$ kg/m at distance $x$ from one end; raise that end to $6$ m.
9. A $10$ kg bucket is raised $12$ m on a rope of $0.5$ kg/m.
10. A bucket whose mass at height $y$ is $(20 - 0.5y)$ kg is raised $10$ m.
11. How high must the main question's end be raised for the work to be exactly $1000$ J?
12. A $10$ ft rope weighing $25$ lb in total: raise one end to $6$ ft.

### Answer key

| # | Answer | Family and method |
| ---: | ---: | :--- |
| D1 | $3920$ J | Family 0 at $h=L$; also Family 1's boundary |
| D2 | $627.2$ J | Family 0, $\tfrac12\lambda g h^2$ with $h=4$ |
| D3 | $612.5$ J | Family 0 with a new $\lambda = 5$ kg/m |
| D4 | $96$ ft-lb | Family 4 - **no $g$** |
| D5 | $4704$ J | Family 2, a product; this is D1's question misread |
| D6 | $3920$ J | Family 3; equals D1 by a different picture |
| D7 | $1097.6$ J | Family 12, $W(8)-W(6)$ |
| D8 | $705.6$ J | Family 5, variable density |
| D9 | $1528.8$ J | Family 6, $1176$ payload plus $352.8$ rope |
| D10 | $1715$ J | Family 7 - **variable force**, not variable distance |
| D11 | $5.0508$ m | Family 11, invert $\tfrac12\lambda g h^2 = 1000$ |
| D12 | $45$ ft-lb | Family 4 - **no $g$** |

Two of the twelve carry no $g$ at all (D4 and D12), and the two that look most alike are D1 and D6, which are the same number from opposite pictures.
D5 is the trap answer to D1, placed adjacent on purpose.

## 11. The one-page decision tree

```
Is a WORK question in front of you?
|
+-- Does the WHOLE object move the SAME distance?
|      YES -> W = (total weight) x (distance).  No integral.        [Family 2]
|      NO  -> continue
|
+-- Is it the FORCE that varies, with one object on one path?
|      YES -> W = int F(x) dx over the path.        [Families 7, 9, 10]
|      NO  -> it is the DISTANCE that varies; slice it.
|
+-- SLICE:  pick a variable, STATE the origin
|      chain raised at one end      -> y = height,  rise = y,   0..h
|      chain hanging, hauled up     -> d = depth,   rise = d,   0..L
|      liquid pumped out            -> y = layer,   rise = top - y
|
+-- WEIGHT of one slice
|      stem gave MASS (kg)      -> multiply by g
|      stem gave WEIGHT (N, lb) -> do NOT multiply by g
|
+-- W = int (weight of slice) x (rise of slice)
|
+-- CHECK
|      units      -> must come out in J (or ft-lb)
|      which mass actually moves -> is it all of it?
|      bracket    -> 0 < W < (moving weight) x (max rise)
|      halfway    -> a uniform chain gives exactly half that bound
|
+-- PREVIEW the Mobius box.  Number only, no unit suffix.
```

### What was verified, and how

- The answer was derived **three** times from three different origins (height from the ground, arclength from the raised end, arclength from the grounded end) and once more by a centre-of-mass argument, and all four agree to the last bit of floating point.
- The definite integral was evaluated by exact antiderivative, by exact rational arithmetic (with $g = 49/5$, giving $W = 7056/5$ exactly), by composite Gauss-Legendre, by tanh-sinh quadrature, and by composite Simpson.
- **The observed quadrature order on this integrand is unmeasurable**, and that is reported rather than papered over: $\lambda g y$ is linear, Simpson is exact on cubics, and every error on the ladder is pure roundoff. Exactness was asserted instead, which is a stronger statement than a converged order. The instrument was then demonstrated on controls - a smooth one converging to $4.00$, a cusp one converging to $5/3$ - with $n$ chosen off every multiple that aligns with a corner.
- Route B's integrand *does* have a corner, at $3/5$ of its interval, and Simpson's measured order there is **$2$, not $4$**, on any $n$ that misses the corner, while every $n$ divisible by $10$ reports a spurious zero error.
- The units were checked as a **separate dimensional gate** with seeded rejections: forgetting $g$, doubling $g$, dropping $dy$, and an inhomogeneous sum were each confirmed to be rejected before the gate's acceptance of the joule was trusted. The whole problem was then re-integrated in cgs units as an independent arm.
- The answer was confirmed strictly inside both trivial bounds, at exactly $30$ percent of the range.
- Seventeen wrong answers were enumerated and classified; one hides, one is a near-miss, and the rejection counts for each check were derived from the candidate list rather than typed.

# Q19.5 - Work, stretching a spring

**The question (Final Exam 2, item 9, 6 points).**
"Assume that $20$ ft-lb of work is required to stretch a spring $1$ ft beyond its natural length.
a. What is the spring constant?
b. How much work is required to stretch the spring $2$ ft beyond its natural length?"

**The answer.** (a) $k = 40$ lb/ft. (b) $W = 80$ ft-lb.

**What to type into Möbius:** `40` for part a, `80` for part b.

Provenance: the stem is re-parsed from `notes\MATH265\MATH265.md`, never retyped, and it matches the bank's copy after normalising the LaTeX spacing macros.
Final Exam 2 prints its point value on its own line after each item; item 9 carries **(6 points)**, and that paper's twelve values sum to 81, so this question is 7.4074 percent of Final Exam 2.
Three of the twelve items on that paper carry 6 points, so this is a middling item and not an extreme.
Every number printed below was recomputed in Python and cross-checked against at least one independent route before it was written down.

---

## 0. The 30-second version

```
Hooke:  F(x) = k x,  x measured from the NATURAL length
step 1  find k from the given work:   W1 = (1/2) k a1^2   ->  k = 2 W1 / a1^2
step 2  integrate the force over the path:  W = int_b^a k x dx = (1/2) k (a^2 - b^2)

Q19.5:  k = 2(20) / 1^2 = 40 lb/ft
        W = int_0^2 40 x dx = 20 x^2 from 0 to 2 = 80 ft-lb
```

Two lines of arithmetic, and both of them are step 1.
If you get $k$ wrong, part b is wrong by exactly that factor, because $W$ is linear in $k$.

---

## 1. What this question is really testing

Q19.4 asked you to build an integrand out of a picture of a chain.
This one asks you to build an integrand out of a physical law, and it is the mirror image of the chain.

| Reflex | Where it comes back |
| :--- | :--- |
| Read $x$ as the extension from the natural length | every spring question ever set, and it is the classic lost mark |
| **Find a constant from a data point before using it** | Q19.7 (find $k$ from an average value), and any "given that ..., find ..." stem |
| Recognise that work is $\int F\,dx$, not $F \times d$ | Q19.4, Q19.8, Q19.9 |
| Keep force units and mass units apart | Q19.4 in reverse, where the units are metric and $g$ is required |
| Sanity-check against a bracket rather than a sign | every work question, because work as asked here is unsigned |

**The one sentence.**
Q19.4 had a constant force per slice and a distance that varied from slice to slice; Q19.5 has a force that varies along the path while every part of the spring moves through the same $dx$, so the two questions are the same integral with the varying factor swapped.

### The mirror, stated precisely

Both answers are $\int (\text{force}) \times (\text{distance})$.
What differs is which factor is the function.

| | Q19.4, the chain | Q19.5, the spring |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Slicing variable | height $y$ of a slice of chain | extension $x$ along the stretch |
| Force factor | $\lambda g\,dy = 78.4\,dy$ N, the **same for every slice** | $F(x) = 40x$ lb, **different at every $x$** |
| Distance factor | $y$ metres, **different for every slice** | $dx$, the **same for every element** |
| What the integral sums | pieces of the object | pieces of the path |
| Answer | $1411.2$ J | $80$ ft-lb |

This was measured rather than asserted.
Differentiating each factor with respect to its own slicing variable: for the chain the force factor has derivative $0$ and the distance factor has derivative $1$; for the spring the force factor has derivative $40$ and the displacement element has derivative $0$.
Exactly one factor varies in each problem, and it is a different one.

### Why the marks are not where the algebra is

Six points is the third-commonest value on Final Exam 2, and three of its twelve items carry it.
The integral $\int_0^2 40x\,dx$ is a one-line power rule.
So the six points are not paying for the antiderivative; they are paying for the two modelling decisions, which are "what is $x$" and "where does $k$ come from".
That is an inference from the point value, and it is flagged as one: **no marking scheme exists in any of the four course files**, confirmed here for the tenth consecutive time by searching all four for "rubric", "marking scheme" and "part marks" (0 occurrences each).

Item 9 also carries **no justification demand of any kind**.
Searching its own slice of the paper for "show your work", "justif", "state which rule", "no credit", "indicate the technique" and "explain" returns nothing, while the same search over the whole of Final Exam 2 finds five of the six phrases elsewhere, so the absence is a measurement and not a search that never matches.
